Industry, I, Ashok Mitra, in my capacity as Chairman of the Committee, Present its 
Seventeenth Report. 
2. The Committee has, during its tenure, striven to keep itself abreast with the emerging/ 
trends in the industrial sector and the specific problems afflicting national industrial growth. 
The issue of overall growth apart, the unevenness of industrial expansion, the Committee is 
aware, has acute political and social implications. In the current financial year, the 
Committee chose to undertake a number of field visits in different parts of the country in 
order that members could closely acquaint themselves in on the state of the major industries, 
particularly heavy and capital goods industries, and the factors instrumental for the 
persistence of industrial backwardness in several regions. 
3. For the purpose 'Of the field visits, the Committee divided itself into six Sub-, 
Committees; five of the Sub-Committees concentrated on the problems of 'individual regions, 
while the Sixth Sub-Committee was assigned the task of studying in depth the difficulties 
faced by women industrial workers as well as women entrepreneur~. . ·

10. Ambivalence in public policy in such matters is best avoidable. A number of contrary

In the metropolitan and near-metropolitan pockets, the phenomenon observed is of

n. Two dimensions of the problem of inter-re.l!,~llal economic. imbalances, in the

23. None of these ideas is new. What is however called for is sustained application of 
energy to translate them into reality. No illusion should be entertained about the magnitude of 
the task, involved. The application of energy has to be of a sustained nature, not merely because 
of recommendations made in this or that official report. It will be the product of pressure 
generated from below. This is in a sense the single most important instrumentality for propelling 
industrial growth which the Committee cannot but take cognizance of. There is a stirring of

. of independence. That has not prevented the awakenings of a degr~e of relevant consciousness : 
millions amongst these sections are fully aware of the nature and extent of social and economic

24. Economic retardation, it can be argued, is itself an exclusive function of illiteracy and 
ck of social consciousness. Viewed in that light, perhaps the very first obligation of a 
programme which pledges to cut through industrial backwardness in the dispersed parts of the 
country would be to launch a massive literacy programme in the areas of retared growth. 
25. This, then, is the crux of the issue. The extent of economic progress achievable in a 
particular region is as much a function of the resources that are applied as of the general milieu 
in which activities take shape. It is equally dependent upon the quality of awareness of the 
populace. The development process, to really get going, awaits an impetus to be articulated in 
the hinterland. "The demand for industrialisation and for larger opportunities for work and 
employment has to originate from below. This demand still does not develop in its on, but is a 
function of environmental conditions. The importance of the social factors which give shape to 
enviroment must not be under-rated. Nor can we ignore the reality that the spread of literacy 
plays a major part in the unfolding process. Literacy assists in the absorption of newer 
technology and in the acquisition of new skills even as it makes hitherto deprived and backward 
communities better aware of their rights as free and equal members of this nation. Not that 
social and political awamesss can blossom without an adequate base of literacy. When their time 
comes, historical forces will assert themselves, however, adverse the circumstances. Literacy, 
however, imparts a greater coherence to the impulses which at such states strive to express 
themselves.

26. It is, in this connection, most important to urge for the full-scale association of 
women in the on-going process of industrial aud economic development in backward regions. 
The feudal stigma perSists, women continue to be socially oppressed in several balatant ways 
in almost all parts of the country. Certain current realities are self-evident. Given the limited 
resources a poor country can garner for growth and the built-in inequalities in the system, 
the vast majority of households are in any case at the receiving end of gross social injustice 
and rough, unfair treatment. Women in these households are generally far more subjected to 
social exploitation than the other numbers. This is on account of the traditional roles 
assigned to men and women from which easy exits are not possible in an ambience marked 
by horrendous feudal legacies. On the other hand, as developments particularly in Kerala 
illustrate, once literacy and nutritional standards improve for women, social mobilisation 
gains in strength, and stirrings from below for better economic advancement assume an 
immensely superior thrust. 
27. The plight of millions and millions of women engaged in industries such as coir and 
bidi manufacture or in other small-scale activities often beggars description. Irrespective of 
the provisions of our Constitution and those of the United Nations Charter of Human 
Rights, women workers are discriminated against in industry after industry in more ways 
than one : they suffer from low wages that are paid at irregular intervals and are very often 
victims of social indignities of assorted kinds at the workplace. The ultimate remedy of 
cour-ce lies in the better mobilisation of women under the umbrella of organised trade union 
' movements. The spread of mass literacy is likely to help the process of such mobilisation, 
but this is one area where it would not be prudent to leave things to autonomous market 
forces. The administration both at the Central and State levels have to step in and eDsure that 
\ 
statutory minimum wages for women in the specified industries are not only announced 
~ regularly but are duly implemenied. The hoUsing and security arrangements for migrant 
" ( women workers should be carefully monitored and superintended. Hours of work for women 
workers also need to be strictly regulated. Not only should the law be laid down in these 
areas; where necessary, special regulatory .bodies must be set up to ensure that the statutory 
injunctions are strictly followed. 
28. While our attention cannot veer away from the problem of poor, helpless 
unorganised women engaged in cottage crafts and similar other activities, and sometimes in 
large-scale industrial undertakings as well, it would not be irrelevant to take cognizance of· 
the problems faced by women who have entered the arena of industrial entrepreneurship or

encouraged to set up cooperative institutions and are helped to obtain both rmancial 
accommodation and entrepreneurial advice from rmancial agencies including the NABARD 
and the IDBI. One interesting suggestion put forward in this connection is the earmarking of 
a quota for purchases at both State and the Central levels from establishments presided over 
by women entrepreneurs. 
l9. It is far from the Committee's intention to under-emphasise the role of good roads 
or rail and communication links to propel. development, nor would it ignore such a 
worthwhile suggestion that, apart from a solid primary education base, all backward areas 
should be blanketed by technical training institutions and polytechnics so that the supply of 
skilled labour does not lag when the development process really catches on.

ments must be made to associate technical advice of the appropriate kind with this cell.

at the national level for infrastructural growth, the priorities hitherto followed need to be 
reversed, and project which would help enlarge the growth potential in hitherto retarded and 
deprived areas should be lifted to the top of the ageuda. That is to say, where the choice is 
between allocating funds at the margin on a project either in a backward region or in an 
area already r~~atively economically advanced, the decision should, as far as possible, be in 
favour of the hitherto retarded area. This is in fact the outstanding challenge the nation will 
have to face at the level of national decision-making in the coming years. In case, because of 
resource constraint, a temporary halt is ordered in capacity expansion of telecommunications 
or rail or road links in a metropolitan or semi-metropolitan region, it may have 
repercussions on the pace of growth in. the region for some while. On the other hand, such 
an embargo on the expansion of basic infrastructures might conceivably also lead to a more 
rational use and elimination of waste from out of existing capacity. True, such slackening of 
the pace of expansion of infrastructural facilities could inconvenience some interest groups 
and activate lobbies in their support. The authorities would do well not to yield to such 
developing pressures. That apart, the system of fiscal and monetary incentives should be so 
worked out that private entities, whether foreign or domestic, receive the appropriate signals 
at each point of time. Whatever the other compulsions, the persistence of economic 
backwardness over large stretches of the country has ominous social and political 
implications. Priorities at the national level must change in response to this challenge; the 
nature of this change must be det~rmined by impulses triggered from below. 
33. That a poor country is always hamstrung by lack of resources is a cliche. But 
because it is a cliche, its relevance is not reduced. What is essential is that Central and State 
Governments, as well as the dccentralised agencies further down the hierarchial line, must 
not -work at cross purposes and thereby fritter away resources. Political and ideological 
· positions of decision-makers at different levels will often tend to be at variance with one 
another in such a huge, big country such as ours. It would still be extraordinary if a large 
measure of agreement is not reached on the priority tasks in particularly retarded area. 
34. One point deserves separate mention. It would be neither desirable nor feasible to 
take away the executive and monitoring functions of the panchayat institutions in 
programmes aimed at eradicating industrial backwardness. No outside agency can fit into the 
format of decentralised development assigned to representative institutions the office-bearers 
of which have been elected on the basis of a democratic mandate. The panchayat bodies will 
continue to be the pivotal element for prepaiing the blueprint of growth at the local level 
and its subsequent implementation. It is for consideration whether during the on-going 
process, the panchayat agency concerned should not invite representatives of the State 
Government, the Union Government, banks and principal financial institutions to participate 

9 
in an advisory capacity. Reconciling the points of view of the different entities is not as 
difficult a task as it might seem initially, Once, through close interaction with one another, 
the realisation dawns that. their mutual roles are neither adversary nor competitive, the 
impulse to cooperate would being to gain instrength among the participating agencies, 
thereby facilitating the realisation of objectives the panchayat institution had set for itself. 
35. Some infrastructures, such as opening up rail and telecommunications links, belong 
to the exclusive domain of the Union Government. The creation of new rail connections has 
currently been reduced to a political football; priorities are more often than not determined 
on the basis of the clout of individual interest groups or individual Members of Parliament 
or particular State Governments. The time, has certainly come, the Committee feels, when 
this pattern is substituted by a more rational system of priority fixation. As argued earlier in 
this Report, the demand for industrialisation emanating from hitherto neglected regions will 
call for a shift in the agenda. In the view of the Committee, the Ministry of Industry and the 
Ministry of Railways may consider constituting a joint decision-making body in association 
with the Planning Commission to decide the aggregate sum to be set aside for railway 
development in the country's backward regions over a five-year period, indicate its region­
wise breakdown and settle the sequence according to with the projects are to be executed. 
State Governments will have the right to approach these inter-ministerial Committees with 
their suggestions and recommendations. Similarly, within each State, while deciding the 
priorities and Scheduling of infrastructure development, the State Government may consider 
taking into account representations from below and have them processed for onward 
despatch to the Centre. 
36. The Committee envisages no difficulty. in case a similar pattern were to emerge with 
respect :to the planning and implementation of other infrastructural activities, such as road 
building and creation of new telecommunications facilities. The State Government will 
express its views on the determination of priorities, but it will exercise no veto, just as no 
Central agency will have a veto either. The endeavour will be to reach a consensus on the 
basis of continuous efforts at accommodating pne another's point of view. This, after all, . 
constitutes the core of a genuinely federal arrangement. 
37. The Union Government, particularly in the Ministries of Industry and Finance, 
should, in the view of the Committee, exercise appropriate moral suasion so that State 
Governments desist from competitive soliciting of private investment in their respective 
States by, for example, lowering local taxes such as sales taxes. Such a practice reduces 
realisable revenue for all the States and thus reduces their overall capability to finance 
industrial development on their. own. It would at the same time be desirable that the Union 
Government takes a sympathetic view of representations about the desirability .of granting 
certain prerogatives to State Governments in terms of Articles 268 and 269 of the 
Constitution, a gesture which· is unlikely to alfed the revenue growth potential for the Centre. 
The nation can develop only on the basis ol endeavours shared by the Union and State 
Governments; a dog-in-the-manger policy can scarcely help the cause of balanced national 
economic growth. 
38. The Committee would like to append a further observation. The package of policies 
for promoting industrial growth in backward areas had tended to be applied in the past in 
piecemeal fashion, often sequentially, without taking into account the total picture of 
possibilities; For instance, there have been announcements from time to time of 'holidays'. 
from income and corporate taxes on behalf of the Centre and sales tax on behalf of the 
States, or of transport subsidies, of supply of inputs at subsidised rates, and so on. What bas, 
however, been missing is an intearated approach which bas also the imprimatur of approval of 

10 
banks and financial institutions. The Committee would like-to see this disarray substituted 
by a blueprint of recommendations vetted jointly by all agencies concerned for, say, a five­
year period, which will then be rolled over from year to year. Such blueprints should be 
made. prepared for all levels of administration. The blueprint at the national level should 
be dovetailed into the State and panchayat level blueprints. Requests for alterations and 
adjustments on a year-to-year basis could emanate either at the national level or the State 
level or from the panchayat bodies themselves. 
39. A measure of confusion may be inevitable in the beginning in such exercises. That 
is. only to be expected. Once the agencies and institutions operating at different levels are 
forced to interact with one another, the sheer weight of circumstances would perhaps 
persuade them to agree on a common set of goals and a common set of instrumentalities 
to attain these goaly / 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
.. 1. The Ministry of Industry should assume the main responsibility to implement 
Pfogramme of industrial growth in hitherto backward areas. It should draw up detailed 
btbeprints of projects in collaboration with the Planning Commission and the State 
Governments. Detailed prescriptions of task for each area should embrace, apart from 
infrastructural planning such measures as the opening of a single window arrangement to 
cater to the requirements of potential entrepreneurs. 
2. The Planning Commission should, in collaboration of the State Governments and the 
Union Ministry, set up a cell to monitor the availability of basic infrastructural facilities 
such as railway net-work, power, roads and water. 
3. There is need to formulate clear-cut policies with regard to the -role the Union 
Government intends to play in respect of its public sector undertakings, particularly with 
reference to disinvestment of its share holding. 
4. The Government also n~eds to r.e-derme its policy concerning the public undertakings 
which are under reference to the Bureau for Industrial and Financial . Reconstruction 
(BIFR). In this connection, possibilities may be explored for cqmmon production planning 
by a group of sick public sector units located in reasonable proximity to one another and 
specialising in a similar range of products. 
5. The banks have not been till now very enthusiastic about projects under the Prime 
Minister's Rozgar Yojana. It is necessary to ensure that time-bound measures are taken for 
examination, allocations and release of funds for such of these projects as are considered 
viable. It is desirable that the Ministry of Finance evolves special stipulations and norms for 
facilitating speedy implementation of projects with high employment generating and output· 
boosting po~ential, in particular in the designated backward are~s. 
6. In order to provide an integrated approach for the industrial development, blueprints 
of recommendations should be vetted jointly by all agencies concerned for, say, for a five 
year period. Such blueprints should be worked out at all levels of administration. The 
blueprints at the national level shoul~ be dovetailed into those for the States and panchayats. 
7. The North-Eastern States have had been long neglected. It isnecessary that a time­
bound programme is drawn up for economic development of this region, with emphasis on 
the development of basic infrastructures such as rail links, roads, air services, power and 
water. 
8. Transport and tax subsidies to backward areas and the North-Eastern regions should 

11 
continue; care should also be taken that transport subsidies are also paid in time and adjusted 
upwards when considered appropriate. 
9. The Ministry. of Industry should take special time-bound measures for development 
and promotion of smali scale units in the island territories of the country, namely, Andaman 
and Nicobar Islands; the transport subsidy prevalent here should continue without restric­
tions; the port facilities in the islands must also be improved. 
10. The Union Government should sympathetically consider representations about the 
desirability of granting certain prerogatives to the State Governments in terms of Articles 268 
and 269 of the Constitution so larger funds become available for industrial growth on the 
initiative of State Government~ 
11. Requests from State Governments for declaration their States as industrially 
backward should be considered sympathetically, and the criteria for declaring a State 
industrially backward should be reviewed from time to time so as to take into account shifting 
realities. 
12. All backward areas should be blanketed by technical and vocational training 
institutions and polytechnics so as to ensure supply of skilled labour when the development 
process catches on. 
13. District panchayats should play much greater role than at present for planning 
industrial growth. Special cells should be set up in the district panchayats and arrangements 
made to provide technical advice of the appropriate kind with such cells. 
14. The Union and State Governments should earmark funds to ensure that projects 
formulated at the local level on the basis of local resources are not allowed to die out. 
15. Panchayat institutions should be vested with executive and monitoring IJ9Wers for 
implementing programmes aimed at eradicating industrial backwardness. The responsibility 
for preparing blueprints of growth at the local level and its subsequent implementation should 
rest with the panchayats. 
16. The Ministries of Industry and Railways should constitute a joint decision-making 
body alongwith the Planning Commission to decide on the aggregate sum to be set aside for 
railway development in the country's backward regions over a five year period, indicate its 
region-wise break-down and settle the sequence according to which the projects are to be 
executed. 
17. In order to cut through industrial backwardness, massive literacy programme should 
be launched in the areas of retarded growth. · 
1 18. Women should be associated in the on-going process of industrial and economic 
development in the backward regions. The administration both at the Union and State levels 
must-ensure that statutory minimum wages for women in the specified industries are not only 
announced but also duly implemented. 
19. The housing and security arrangements for migrant women WQrkers need to be 
carefully monitored and superintended and working hours for women should be strictly 
regulated and adhered to. 
20. Women entrepreneurs, especially in the relatively backward regions, should be 
encouraged to set up cooperative institutions and help may be provided to them to obtain both 
financial accommodation and ~ntrepreneurial advice from rmancial agencies including the

industries in Rajasthan. Despite having great potential for automobiles, electronics and 
· petroleum based industries in Rajasthan no significant development of such industries had 
taken place in the State. He attributed inadequate road, rail and airlinks as the main reasons 
.for slow industrial developll}ent of Rajasthan. Accor,ding to him ceramics, wool based 
industries, leather industrie~. ·electronics, agro processing and mineral processing industries

development. Number ·of'' effective steps had been taken such ~S- development of industrial 
areas, entrepreneurial development programme, and ade,'luate arrangement for finance.

The Management of HhJdustan Copper Limited 
The Sub-Committee had been given to understand by th~ management that copper 
mining industry in India had some inherent constraints due to low grade of Indian ore and 
poor geometry of the Indian ore body. As agatnst 3-4% copper content in ore in most of the 
o~er copper producing countries in the world, the average copper content of Indian ore was 
just around 1%. Though mining cost in terms of per tonne ore in India was more or less 
comparable with international standard but in terms of metal it was 2.5-3 times higher than 
the international cost because of poor grade of ore. 
In the initial years, the company incurred losses because of teething troubles, 
unremunerative administered prices not related to the cost of production from very low 
grade of copper ore available in India and lack of investments ·in mines. However, the 
company continued its efforts for increasing production and productivity through various in-

Metal Scrap Trade Corporation (MSTC) 
The management informed the Sub-Committee that MSTC was primarily engaged in 
two activities viz., (i) Foreign Trade, and (ii) Domestic Trade. 
In Foreign Trade, MSTC was the sole Canalising Agency for import of scrap till 
February, 1992. Import during the last two years of canalisation were 15,44,000 tonnes and 
2,80,000 tonnes. Imports.during 1992-93 went upto 6,82,000 tonries. However, in subsequent 
years, only 307,000 & 278,000 tonnes were imported. Total imports of scrap by the country 
have also come down during these years resulting in market share of MSTC being around 
30% . MSTC had, therefore, embarked upon a Corporate Planning exercise to identify areas 
with potential for diversifying so as to remove dependence on one item, namely, scrap. It 
has also simultaneously been trying to expand the basket of imports by including other items 
such as Pig Iron, "Billets, Coke, HR Coils, etc. 
The management suggested that MSTC should diversify into imports of other items, 
develop export business as well as set up joint ventures for manufacturing steel relate<I 
items. 
In case of Domestic Trade, MSTC is handling disposal of scrap worth about Rs. 300 
crores for over 100 Public Sector Undertakings Government Departments. Hewever, this 
number and volume can be substantiall~ increased if Railways and Defence also entrust the 
disposal of their scrap to MSTC. The management suggested that it is imperative that the 
Government renders support to MSTC both in Foreign Trade and Domestic Trade since 
there are definite disadvantages to the country in decanalisation of imports of important raw 
materials like scrap. 
Similarly in case of Domestic Trade, organisations like Defence, Railways and some 
other Public Sector Undertakings are utilising the services of private auctioneers who are 
offering such low rate of servi~. charges that it does not even justify the bare minimum cost 
of the operation. This ·means that there are c;>ther incentives available to the privat~­
auctioneers which is at the cost of the Public Sector Underta~ings depriving them of the 
necessary revenues. 

44 
The management was of the view that the proposed diversification project of MSTC 
should be given top priority for clearances by the Ministry, Planning Co11;1mission, CCEA 
etc. so as to enable MSTC to create its own productivity and give sufficient business volume 
to its existing infrastructure. 
On enquiring as to what has been the impact of liberalisation on the Company, the 
management clarified that liberalisation has l)rimarily involved decanalisation of import of 
scrap, -reduction of import duties and simplification of systems and procedures in this sphere. 
A-s a result of these measures, following developments have taken place:-
( a) A .number of private units including large organisations such as Reliance, TISCO, lTC, 
etc. and international traders as well as individual furnace upits have come into the field 
of import of scrap. This has resulted in foreian suppliers taking advantage of a number 
of players in the field and dilution of strict quality criteria follo~ed by MSTC during the 
canalisation period. MSTC has also had as a result to follow suit, since the prices offered 
to MSTC otherwise were necessarily higher and as such uncompetitive. 
The mushrooming has led to simultaneous import by a number of parties and avoidable 
infructuous cost by way of bunching of vessels at ports, demurrage, necessity to keep 
material in stock for extended periods due to inability to sell in advance, introduction of 
extra commercial practice. 
(b) Impact of Reduction of Duties 
Import Duty on melting scrap has been reduced to 5%. Simultaneously, duty on finished 
products has also been reduced. For example, duty on billets stands at 20%. As a result, 
billets are being imported in preference to scrap import since billets produced out of 
imported scrap after melting in furnaces is .costlier than the landed cost of imported 
billets. As a result of this as well as th~ hike in international price of scrap, a large 
number of furnaces have closed down, resulting in gross under-utilisation of investment 
and capacity built up. 
(c) Impact of Removal of Definition qf Heavy Melting Scrap Rerollable Scrap 
HEAVY MELTING SCRAP (HMS) was defined in the import policy in 1985-88. 
However, in the last few years, this definition has been withdrawn and as a result large 
scale imports of HMS are being undertaken now. Material actually coming under this 
category however is in higher sizes which can only be categorised as rerollable scrap. 
Duty on rerollable scrap ranges upto 40%, whereas duty on HMS is just 5%. This leads 
to large scale evasion of duty. 
MSTC cannot obviously be party to such practices and is not in position to import HMS,_ 
being otherwise unviable. In the present decanalisation regime, HMS is being imported 
from sources which include zones of conflict. As a result there have been a number of 
cases of presence of explosives in these consignments which have led to loss of life. This 
is primarily due to non-eQforcement of quality control, due to inability of private 
importers to enforce such a discipline on the sellers . • 
The management has highlighted the following facts regarding import of scrap after 
decanalisation:-
1. There have been several instances where scrap imported by private importers have 
been accompanied by explosives and· on a few occasions there have been serious 
casualities. 
/ 

45 
2. There has been every possibility of radio-active contamination being present in such 
material imported. 
3. Due to substantial differential in customs duty between HMS and rerollable scrap, 
there is every possibility/tendency on the part of private importers to import 
rerollable -scrap in the guise of HMS which naturally results in revenue loss to the 
country. 
4. Price manipulation through under-invoicing/over-invoicing depending .upon the 
circumstances cannot be ruled out which evidently is at the cost of revenue and loss 
of foreign exchange to the country. 
0~ th~ basis of evidence of the m$magement and the papers/documents submitted before 
it the Sub-Committee feels that though it would be difficult to extend full monopoly to the 
Com.pany in the field of importing Scrap but Govem~ent may still help out MSTC by

expedite clearance of the diversification proposal, of the company. Ministry of Railways and

_ Study note on the visit of the Sub-Committee-Ill of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Indu,St(y to Bihar from 4th to lOth November, 1995 
The Sub-Committee-III of the D.R.P.S.C. Committee on Industry was constituted to 
study the problems of Industrialisation in backward areas and Capital Goods Industry. The 
Sub-Committee consisted of seven members, namely:-
1. Shri Naval Kishore Rai 
2. Shri Raj Nath Singh 
3. Shri V. Rajeshwar Rao 
4. Shri Manjay Lal 

93 
5. Shri Rajendra Agnihotri 
6. Shri Rama Krishna Konathala 
7. Shri Puma Chandra Malik 
Shri Naval Kishore Rai was the Convenor of the Sub-Committe~. 
2. The Sub-Committee visited Bihar from 4th to 11th November, 1995 for the purpose 
and held disc;:ussions with the representatives of Chambers of Commerce and Industries, 
Officers of the State Industry and other Departments, District authorities of Patna, Ranchi, 
Bokaro, Mu:zaffarpur and Sitamarhi and other workers organisations. The salient features of 
the outcome of the study are as under:-
Brleling wltb the omcJaJs of the State GovernmeDt 
On 4th November, 1995 the Sub-Committee held its first meeitng with the Officials of 
the State Government where it apprised them about the purpose and objectives of the visit. 
The Sub-Committee also directed that representatives of various concerned department may 
be present in the concluding meeting of the Sub-Committee with the State Government on 
lOth November, 1995 so that matter concerning their department can be clarified then and 
there. The Sub-Committee directed that meeting with the representatives of the concerned 
Industrial Area Development Authorities where the Sub-Committee is visiting may be 
arranged at the respective places of visit of the Sub-Committee and the representatives of 
remaining Industrial Area Development Authority of places where the Sub-Committee is not 
visiting may appear at the meeting at Patna on lOth November, 1995. · 
On learning that matter regarding approval of the Growth Centre for Bihar is pending 
with IFCI the Sub-Commi~tee directed that representatives of IFCI may also be called from 
New Delhi to appear before the Sub-Committee at its meeting with State Government 
officials on lOth November, 1995 so that matter can be sorted out in the presence of State 
Government officials. 
Meeting with Worhers Unions HEC, Ranclli 
On 5th November, 1995 the Sub-Committee reached Ranchi, where it met with the 
worker's unions of HEC. The Sub-Committee cam~ to understand that once a prestigious 
profit making organisation and pride to nation, HEC is now on the verge of death. 
As a natural corollary to the company's sad state, the Sub-Committee came to 
understand that diverse labour problems have cropped up. The employees of HEC are 
facing a very tough time as all the facilities extended to them have been curtailed/suspended 
due t.o shortage of funds. · 
The workers apprised that their wage revision is pending for last four years and they are 
not getting L.T.A., leave encashment and due D.A. point anymore. For the last two years 
even salaries to workers have not been paid in time and the casual workers have not been 
regularised. The managem~nt was not able to deposit CPF and even the transport subsidy 
has been withdrawn. The Sub-Committee was told that due to a fear psyschosis in workers 
that HEC will not run, the work force is fast depleting and many experienced workers have 
opted for VRS resulting in qualitative degradation of work. Even some foreign trained 
technicians have been given .administrative jobs rather than technical work showing lack of 
professionalism in regard to utilisation of work force. 
The Sub-Committee was also apprised that unorganised labourers engaged in the plant 
are given minimum wages fixed for the construction work rather than that of engineering 
industry which is higher. 
The Sub-Committee also came to understand that due to deteriorated state of HEC the 

94 
basic civic amenities to workers are also affected. In plant hospital at Ranchi where the 
facilities used to be very good, qualified doctors have left under V.R.S. and doctors present 
are also indulging in private practice resulting, only those patients -who attend their private 
clinics get good medicines (though free of cost) from the hospital. Majority of medicines are 
not available at the plant hospital and though HEC reimburses for the local purchase, the 
procedure is time consuming and causes a lot of inconvenience to workers. There are also 
apprehensions that the hospital may be given to some private organisation. At the township, 
the petty maintenance works are not being attended to. 
The representatives of Trade Unions told that no land has been· allotted for their office 
and there are cases of disciplinary action on workers on anonymous complaints. 
The workers, naturally apprehensive about their fate, pleaded that­
( a) sufficient work order may be provided to HEC, 
(b) financial aid may be given to the compauy immediately, 
(c) HEC may be taken out from B.I.F.R. 
Meeting with Trade and Industry Representatives, Ranchi 
The second meeting of Sub-Committee at Ranchi was with the Trade and Industry 
Representatives where it came to understand that the industrialists are facing diverse 
problem, in setting up/runmng successfully their industrial units. Firstly, there is a prevalent 
insecurity among the entrepreneurs, due to law and order problem in the region which is not 
conducive to industrialist for installing industrial units. Secondly there's lack of adequate 
basic infrastructure in the State. The poor condition of roads results in high costs of 
transportation of raw materials and finished products. The supply of power to industriaL 
units is very erratic and is moving from bad to worse and above all there are draconian rules 
of minimum guarantee, and minimum electricity charges which again contribute to higher 
cost of production and poor productivity. Telecom services are also not upto the mark in the 
region. The industrial areas are not well connected by local and STDIISD lines and there is 
frequent breakdown of the system. 
The entrepreneurs also told the Sub-Committee about rampant corruption in the local 
bureaucracy, including RIADA. There the attitude of officials is not to guide but to grab the 
entrepreneurs the moment they commit a mistake and rules are interpreted in such a way so 
as to corner the entrepreneurs. 
Contrary to assertions made by the State Government there is still widespread 
prevalence of Inspector Raj, and the entrepreneurs are invariably harassed and threatened 
by the inspecting officials from various department such as Labour, Sales Tax and Central 
Exdse, Pollution Control, Transport and there are many administrative procedural wrangles 
which are not existing in other States. Thus in place of producing anything worthwhile, the 
entrepreneurs are mentally engaged in these activities only. The attitude of Bihar State 
Financial Corporation, too, is more of a Money-lender than that of an agency for industrial 
development. Its rehabilitation programmes are neither timely nor constructive. The 
industrialists feel that they should be given representation in its Board of Directors. 
The entrepreneurs did not approve the recent policy of deducting P.F. of worker who 
has worked in an establishment a single day and stated that this scheme is not favourite even 
among the workers. 
Another big problem faced by the industrialists is the shortage of coal, though the area 
is situated on the pit-head of coal reserves. This problem is actue during rainy season and 
whatever the entrepreneurs manage to get is at high rates. 

95 
The present state of HEC is also affecting the industries in and around Ranchi, since 
most of them are its ancilliaries or are indirectly dependant on HEC. 
Apart from this the entrepreneurs stated that there are no compelling reasons for 
entrepreneurs to start industry in the region and in order to allure the entrepreneurs the 
Government should give certain incentives such as-
(i) tax holiday for Jharkhand area and more powers to Jharkhand Autonomous Council; 
(ii) uniform tax system throughout the country; 
(iii) modernisation of Ranchi airport for night landing; 
(iv) maintenance of National highway by Central Government; 
(v) offices of all major Central Government in Ranchi; 
(vi) settlement of E.S.I. cases in Ranchi not in Patna; 
(vii) increase in railways facilities and availability of wagons; 
(viii) simplified administrative procedure and restriction on the visit of Government 
Officials in the industries. 
On the basis of the evidence tendered, the Sub-Committee observed that one of the 
main reasons for the sickness in industrial units in and around Ranchi is the sickness in 
HEC. Therefore revival of HEC is must for the health of units in and around Ranchi. 
Besides this, the sub-Committee observed that erratic power supply is contributing to further 
sickness in the industrial units and therefore needs to be improved. The entrepreneurs are 
also suffering due to different tax structure in different States. Accordingly the Sub­
Committee recommends that there should be a uniform tax structure throughout the 
country. The Sub-Committee further recommends that development of infrastructure such as 
good road conditions, modernisation of airport, availability of wagons and increase in 
Railway facilities are the need of the hour for creating industrial atmosphere. 
On the functioning of RIADA the Sub-Committee observed that it should hetp the 
entrepreneurs instead of engaging them in procedure wrangles. For this the Sub-Committee 
recommends that administrative procedure may be simplified and the visit of Government 
Officials may be reduced to once in a year. 
The Sub-Committee also observed that functioning of SISI is not satisfactory and 
therefore recommends that it must aggravate its activities to help out the entrepreneurs. 
IHeeting with District Collector and Representatives of State Industry Department, Ranchi 
The Sub-Committee held its next meeting with District Collector and representatives of 
states industry department where it was informed that in Ranchi there are mainly 
engineering and mineral industries with other units which have also started in the area. The 
performance of Ranchi in achievement of PMRY is good and last year, (1994-95) out of the 
target of 900 loan 427 proposals were actually disbursed. The Sub-Committee observed that

The recoveries of B.S.F.C. are not good and out of the 414 units financed by it, 217 are

On the working of RIADA the Sub-Committee was informed that all the land under it 

96 
has not been allotted and there is no sickness in the industrial area under it. The Sub­
Committee examined the issue of sickness and found that it is contradictory to the statement 
given by B.S.F.C. which has also financed certain units presently sick under RIADA. The

The Sub-Committee also came to know that among other things unpleasant state of

About the local industries and handicraft the Sub-Committee came to know that

(i) bad recoveries

The administration was of the opinion that in PMRY it has moved proposal· to forward

Meeting with Management ol HEC, Ranchi 
On 6th November, 1995, the Sub-Committee met with the Management of HEC, 
Ranchi where it came to understand the HEC needs financial help from Central 
Government, for its revival. The Management stated that it was also trying to improve its 
internal financial condition with active cooperation of its workers. The Sub-Committee was 
told that the Corporation was engaged in the manufacture and supply of capital equipments, 
machine tools and spares needed for the core sector industries, namely, Steel, Coal, 
Cement, Power, Defence, Aluminium, Ship buildina, Railway, etc. The Corporation has 
been a major contributor in the indigenisation and expansion of steel plants and has also t. 
played a significant role in the modernisation ·Of the coal sector in the Country. It has so far, 
the Sub-Committee was told, supplied over one lakh ton of Mining Equipments to coal 
mining industries the Corporation is among the few exclusive companies in the world to 
manufacture draglines. It has a turnkey project division which has succesfully completed 
projects in different core sectors of the economy, viz, Steel, Coal, Power, Cement besides 
carrying out modernisation of a cement plant in Bangladesh. Currently it is engaged in the 
execution of Raw Material Handling Plant at Rourkela Steel Plant. 
The Management also gave the details of the equipment supplied by it to Railways, 
Aluminium Industry, Ship Building, Sugar Industry, Cement and Defence Industries. 
The Management then represented to the Sub-Committee about the problems being 
faced by it and the assistance it needed from Government. Firstly, it pleaded that to revive 
operations of HEC, Group of Ministries had taken a decision to given certain financial 
assistance to company according to whicb for 1995-96 interest free loan to compensate cash 
losses of Rs. 80.61 crores were sanctioned. 
This decision of Group of Ministries was communicated to BIFR to which the company 
has been referred. The Sub-Committee· was further informed that du.ring the current year 
only 18 crores has been released by the Government. The management further submitted 
that despite the Government's intentions, efforts made by the company, and suggestion from 

97 
BIFR, the attitude of the S.B.I., sole bankers to HEC, poses a series concern in the revival 
of the company. To bring their point home, the management informed that S.B.I. has 
adjusted Rs.2.7 crores as 15% deduction (adjustment against the frozen account) and 
Rs. 8.84 crores against interest leviable as on September, 1995, thus taking away Rs. 11.6 
crores out of the funds of Rs. 18 crores provided by the Government for Salary/Wages. 
Despite the assurance that the company's performance is improving and therefore the 15% 
of collection would adequately service the interest burden is not accepted by the Bank. 
To compound the problems, bank is now planning to further restrict HEC's ability to 
utilise fund fully. This gives a feeling as if bank is behaving in a manner to negate the 
purpose of the Government's financial assistance to the company and therefore its revival. 
The management pleaded that instead of restricting HEC's ability to utilise its funds 
properly the S.B.I. should help the company within the guarantees provided by Government 
and RBI guidelines. Secondly, the company pleaded that Coal India Ltd., which was 
extensively using equipments supplied by HEC, is now turning towards foreign countries. 
The Government should direct CIL, to continue buying its equipments from HEC which are 
no less efficient than any other product. Thirdly, the company informed that it was running 
into problems with B.S.E.B. to which the Chairman, B.S.E.B. has agreed to consider 
sympathetically .. Fourthly, the management pleaded that the revised performance targets for

Meeting with the Officials of Government of Biha1· 
The final meeting of the Sub-Committee was held on the lOth November,. 1995 with 
the State Government officials, where it was apprised that the Chief Minister has recently 
taken a lot of initiatives for the creation of industrial environment and promotion of 
industrial development in Bihar. Thus new Industrial Policy was announced by the State 
Government which came into force on September 1, 1995, with the aim and objectives of 
creating on environment for optimal utilisation of State's agro climatic, mineral and 
human resources; reviving potentially viable and closed industries; boosting exports; 
providing quality infrastructure and simplifying procedure to expedite and impart 
transparency in decision making. 
The Sub-Committee came to understand that Bihar is currently facing vast magnitude 
of problems. For the improvement of infrastructure, Government is taking steps for 
improving telecom, power, transport, roads, etc. Role of private sector has been utilised 
in the concept of Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) for development of infrastructure in the

Committee was informed that Government is actively going to seek help from private 
sector for power generation and distribution. Further the Government would encourage 
setting up of captive power plant to meet the existing as well as future demand for 
power of industrial unit and would review the tariff rate besides granting certain 
exemption/incentives to new units. 
The Sub-Committee was. told that under the new policy for attracting investment for 
sustaining industrial development, the State Government is going to allow sales tax 
incentive to new units. The earlier ceiling of Rs. 15 crores on industries for aid has also 
been removed and new units get sales tax deferment benefit on purchase of raw materials 
and finished goods for 8-10 years, irrespective of their investment. This is a big 
advantage and in many industries like telecommunication, computer software/hardware 
and electronics, its limit is 300% of the fixed investment. The freight equalis,ltion policy, 

109 
due to which Bihar's industries were not gaining from proximity to raw material like coal, 
iron ore,. etc., has been abolished. Policies regarding coal have also been modified. 
The Sub-Committee was told that the Chief Minister had a campaign during which

Directorate of Industries to work out a revival package for the SSI units which are outside

On the basis 9f the evidence tendered, the Sub-Committee observed that the condition 
of industrial units in Bihar is in bad shape due to scores of reasons, main being the shortage 
of funds and erratic power supply position in the State. 
The Sub-Committee observed that the other reason for backwardness in the region is 
the deteriorated conditions of big industries on which many small and medium industries 
were dependant. Accordingly, the Sub-Committee recommends that banks must increase

Industry Department of the Central Government and the State Government on the

Bihar. The Sub-Committee was informed that out of the six Growth Centres allotted for 
Bihar, two Growth Centres viz., Begusarai and Hazaribagh have been sanctioned and the 
Central Government has released a sum of Rupees 50 Lakhs to each of these centres. It was 
further informed that appraisal reports in respect of Growth Centres at Bhagalpur, Chhapra 
and Muzaffarpur have been received from IFCI and the Ministry of Industry has sought 
clarification on certain points from the State Government. On being asked to specify the 
points on which the Ministry of Industry have sought clarifications, the State Government 
officials informed that IFCI wants an agreement from State Government on the availability of 
requisite electricity. The lFCI further seeks State Government comments as to why 
agricultural land is being acquired for these Centres and lastly the IFCI also wants to be 
convinced about presence of perennial water resource for the Centres. 
The Sub-Committee impressed upon the State Government officials to expedite their 
replies to objections raised by IFCI. The Sub-Committee strongly recommends that much 
awaited appraisal report from IFCI, regarding Growth Centre at Darbhanga may be expedited 
on urgent basis. 

115 
The next item in the agenda was Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme. The 
Sub-Committee has been given to understand that the Scheme was initiated in June, 1992 
for promoting and strengthening small, tiny and village Industries in ruraVbackward areas 
with active participation of State Government/financial institutions. Under the Scheme 50 
Centres are proposed to be set up at the cost of Rupees 5 crores which will be paid by the 
Government of India and SIDBI in ratio of 2:3. The State Officials infonned that the State 
Government has selected Fatuha (Patna), Belchampa (Garhwa), Alamnagar (Madhepura) 
and Gopalganj for Integrated Infrastructure Dcvel"pment Scheme. BITCo had been 
authorised to prepare project report for the LI.D. Scheme in June, 1994. IADA Patna, 
Ranchi, Darbhanga and Muzaffarpur was selected nodal agency for implementation of the 
Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme. BITCo has prepared the project report of 
Integrated infrastructure Development Scheme at Fatuha (Patna) and Belchampa 
(Garhwa). 
The Sub-Committee noted that Government of India has been communicating with State 
Government on the issue of setting up liD centres but no response coming forth. The Sub· 
Committee further noted that the State Government has not even sent its report on the liD 
centre for Sitamarhi to Government of India. The Sub-Committee urges upon State 
Government to explore the possibilities of setting up of more liD Centres in the State in the 
interest of overall industrial development of the State. 
Bharat Coldng Coal Limited (BCCL) 
\ 
The Sub-Committee met the workers .and management of BCCL at Dhanbad with 
regard to the status of the company in overall industrial scenario of the State. 
The Sub-Committee gathered that the coal region of the company is spread from 
Bardhman to Ranchi in an area of 300 kms. The production is 30 mt. per annum. Around 
4.5 mt. of coal is sent to steel plants through washeries. At present 6 to 7 mt. coking coal 
is imported as the internal availability of the same is very less. The company is incurring 
loss to the tune of Rs. 350 crores per year .and presently referred to BIFR. There is 30% 
coking coal and rest non-coking coal. About 40 mt. good quality coal is under fire. The 
management informed that world bank has extended aid for controlling the fire. The 
project report is being prepared. According to the management, if the population of Jharia 
is evacuated, the mines could live for 50 lllOre years. 
Highlighting the reasons for losses, the management pointed out that SAIL is not 
extending the required cooperation. SAIL is paying Rs. 3300/t on coal imported from 
Australia while it pays only Rs. 1500/t to BCCL. According to the management if SAIL 
agrees to pay Rs. 2000/t BCCL could not go to BIFR. Thus SAIL is earning profits at 
BCCL's losses. 
Other problems include a number of coal theft cases. Though the company is bearing 
Rs. 2 crores per month wages bill of CISF still the small theft cases here and there have 
been very difficult to be controlled. The management further mentioned about the 
depleted condition of 92 washeries. These washeries have lost efficiency and atleast 55 
crores are required for their modernisation·. The management also informed that the work 
culture and the discipline in the company is very bad. 
While interacting with the workers union the Sub-Committee gathered that company's 
production can be increased by inviting workers participation in management. On the 
question of mechanisation and planning the workers wanted both mechanised and semi 
mechanised patterns on the lines of China. The workers further wanted that open cast 
mining be suspended and better working condition for workers be created. As regards· 

116 
work culture the unions felt that the same can be improved by workers participation 111 
management. 
The Sub-Committee feels that it is still time to improve the work culture. For this the 
management and the workers should sit together and set up a joint committee to monitor 
the same~ 
Meeting with District Collector, Dhanbad on Industrial backwardness 
At Dhanbad, the Sub-Committee first met the District authorities about the overall 
industrial status of the district. The District Collector informed that in Dhanbad there are 6 
large scale, 26 medium scale industries and about 4076 (435 SSI units and 3641 Tring units) 
registered units out of 435, 106 SSI units are sick. No foreign investment has so far come in 
the district. However NRis have been suggested to set up Food Processing Industry. 
Under Prime Minister Rozgar Yojana last year out of a target of 1250 cases only in 302 
cases loan could be disbursed. This year the target is 1719 out of which disbursment has 
been done in only 147 cases. That means only 11.6% achievement. The District Collector 
informed that the reasons for poor performance is that bank's efficiency is calculated with 
.deposits it has and not by disbursments. The district authorities have brought to the notice 
of different agencies the poor performance of banks. 
When asked whether any utilisation survey has been undertaken in respect of the 
disbursed cases, the District Collector replied that all units are working. The District 
Collector however made it clear that the banks are notaccountable to State Government 
and if district authorities are to be asked about Stattbovernment's performance on PMR Y 
some con.trol on banks could be desirable at district level. 
The Sub-Committee feels that the District Collector may be empowered to analyse the 
performance of banks under the scheme. The Sub-Committee equally feels it important that 
bank authorities should also realise the seriousness of the scheme and cooperate with district 
authorities to the maximum possible in making the scheme a success. 
The Sub-Committee was very disappointed togather that the CD ratio in the district is 
18%. It wonders as to how the area can industrially grow with such a low CD ratio. The 
Sub-Committee suggested to the bank representative that a meeting of district bankers be 
held on urgent bases and a note on reasons and suggestions for improving CD ratio be 
prepared and sent for consideration of State Government, Central Government and the Sub­
Committee. 
In a communication subsequently sent to the Sub-Committee the Bank of India, 
Dhanbad indicated following suggestions for improvement in CD ratio:-, 
1. Identification of potential units in the District; 
2. Injection of working capital and term loan as per requirement; 
3. Financing in aggressive manner to Self-Help Group for prospective projects; 
4. Removal of Bank notion for non-recovery of debts; 
5. Adequate powers to be vested with the individual banks 111 line with the Non­
Banking Financial Companies; 
6. Setting up proper industrial climate in the District; 
7. Government sympathy for adequate power supply. This is one of the major 
impediments for industrial growth and improvement in Credit Deposit Ratio; 
8. Adequate linkage of coal and timely delivery should be ensured by CIUBCCL; 

117 
9. Infra-structural development is to be strengthened; 
10. Setting up commercial trade complexes at strategic places like, Jharia, Chirkunda, 
Katrasgharh, Kirkend and Bank More; and 
11. Composite plan for industrial growth, service oriented industries along side G.T. Road. 
-Viz : transport repair shops/ garage motel facilities, breakdown van etc. 
The Sub-Committee hopes that the Central as well as the State Government would take 
note of the aforesaid suggestions and devise some concrete method in consultation with the 
Bank Authorities to improve the CD ratio. 
Hindustan Steel Wol'lfS Construction Limited (HSCL) 
The · management informed the Sub-Committee that Hindustan Steel Works 
Construction Limited ~as incorporated in the year 1964 with the primary objective of 
creation of public sector organisation capable of undertaking complete construction of 
modern integrated steel plants from the stage of site investigation to the stage of 
commissioning of the plant. Pooling up the available expertise and know-how in the 
company today has within its ambit of activities a wide range of specialised work in steel 
sector, power plants, dam construction, bridge, coal handling plants, underground 
communication and transport system, industrial and township e,omplexes etc. involving high 
degree of planning, coordination and sophisticated construction techniques. 
Elaborating the highlights of the company the management informed that the company 
earned profit till 1977-78. However slowing down of construction tempo in steel plants 
coupled with unplanned requirement of workforce resulted in accumulated losses. Turn 
around started from 1994-95 under a no profit no loss situation. The turnover of the 
company has risen from Rs. 239 crores in 1990-91 to Rs. 390 crores in 1994-95 with a 
projection of Rs. 411 crores in 1995-96. Even under the existing financial strain, HSCL 
generated Rs. 380 crores which takes care of 97% of direct annual expenditure. 
The management informed that last year Bokaro Steel Plant gave an order of Rs. 117 
crores which is not sufficient enough. Highlighting the turnover position of the company the 
management indicated that the company has taken up I completed certain important 
assignments such as Reheating Furnace No.4, Modernisation Package of Continous Casting 
Plant and Rebuilding of Coke Over Battery No. 4. The management pleaded before the 
Committee that a little work support from SAIL awarding even 25% of its annual outlay of 
additional, modification and repair works I operational jobs approximately valued at Rs. 200 
crores only will enable the company to gainfully engage its workforce. On the front of Non­
Steel Sector, HSCL has completed prestigious work of International Stadium at Cochin. 
The Sub-Committee has been given to understand that HSCL directly employs over 
14000 employees and indirectly supports half a lakh contract workforce besides other 
ancillary support services. Out of this technical strength of the company is 2100. There has 
been no recruitment in the company during last five years. Infact there is an excess man­
power of six thousand. 
On the basis of the evidence of the Management and the papers I document submitted 
before it, the Sub-Committee has come to the conclusion that the company is faced with the 
problems such as (i) Lack of adequate orders, (ii) Lack of strong technology base, (iii) Low 
Equity base and huge burden of Government loan & interest and (iv) Virtual withdrawal of 
purchase & price preference. The Sub-Committee hopes that Government of India would 
sympathetically look into these problems and come to the help of the company as. far as 
possible keeping in view the contribution of the company in the steel sector of the country. 

118 
The Committee also urge upon Government to ensure orders for the company so. that it may 
be able to strengthen its technological base. It should also be well within the consideration of 
Government of India to restore the purchase and price preference of the company. SAIL may 
perhaps be in a better position to work out some solution for revival of the company. 
Bharat Refractories Limited 
The Management informed the Sub-Committee that the Bharat Refractories Limited 
was incorporated on 22nd July, 1974 and at present it has three Units viz (i) Bhandaridah 
Refractories Plant at Bhandaridah, (ii) Ranchi Road Refra~tories Plant at Ramgarth and (iii) 
Bhilai Refractories Plant at Bhilai. The Company is incurring losses and referred to BIFR 
since 1992. BIFR had appointed IDBI as the operating agency for working out the revival 
plan. The recommendation of the BIFR on the revival plan submitted by IDBI is awaited. 
Highlighting the problems faced by the Company the Management informed that the 
Company is not getting the orders. The following major constraints were indicated:-
!. Increase in the cost of inputs such as raw materials, fuel, power, salary and wages, 
etc. Although -some of the finished products fetches higher price, the price rise is not 
in proportion to the price rise of cost of inputs, 
2. Frequent power failures particularly units situated in Bihar, 
3. Shortage of Raw Materials, 
4. Lack of Working ~apital, 
5. Accumulation of Inventory leading to liquidity problems, 
6. Lack of adequate orders, particularly for premium products such as Mag-Carbon 
Bricks, Refractories for Sliding Gate Systems, Blast Furnace Bricks and Masses etc. 
When asked, the Management indicated that help from Government I SAIL I Financial 
Institution of the following sectors would be very useful in revival of the Company:-
1. Financial: 
(A) Approval of Revival Package consisting, inter-alia:-
(a) Waiver of interest on loans to Government amounting to Rs. 60.36 crores, 
(b) Conversion of 50% of Plan Loan amounting to Rs. 39.76 crores into equity, 
(c) Conversion of Non-Plan loans amounting to Rs. 12.05 crores to '0' rate interest 
of Debentures. 
(B) Sanction of Additional working capital facilities. 
2. New Projects: 
Government to fund Refractories for Continuous Casting Project costing Rs. 2v.00 crores 
approx. This would help the Company to meet growing demand for hi-tech refractories. 
3. Marketing: 
(a) To secure more orders for Mag-Carbon Bricks, Blast Furnace Bricks and Masses. 
(b) SAIL to help in lifting the inventory of finished goods against orders. 
The Sub-Committee takes· note of immense contribution of the Company in growth of 
Steel Sector over the years. It is somewhat unusual that inordinate delay in proceedings of 
BIFR in respect of Companies like BRL leads to demotivation amongst the workers. The Sub­
Committee would urge upon Government of India to expedite the revival of the Company on 
the basis of suggestions put forth by the IDBI. 

119 
Meeting with Bokaro Steel Plant 
The Sub-Committee before visiting Bokaro Steel Plant had received answers from the 
management on a questionnaire prepared by it on the basis of a discusson earlier held with 
the management in November, 1995. Apart from that the management informed the Sub­
Committee about certain problems the plant is facing. It was given to understand that BCCL 
would not be able to supply the required quality of coal for the Coke Oven and Blast 
Furnace. Further elaborating the position of coal, the management informed that the Blast 
Furnace requires more quantity of coal. Similarly lack of coal is also adversely effecting the 
growth in hot metal sector. When enquired as to why the plant is preferring import of coal 
at a much higher price to that coal available from BCCL, the management informed that 
they will import coal only to the extent of its requirement not met by CIL. It was further 
clarified by the management that the heat value of coal is determined by the ash, fixed 
carbon, Volatile Matters and Inherent Moisture. Sulphur has no affect on heat value. 
Though Indian Coal has low sulphur, but due to presence of high ash, the heat value is low 
compared to low ash imported coking coal. 
When the Sub-Committee enquired about the constraints in extending civil works to 
HSCL, the Bokaro Steel Plant Management informed that of late HSCL has been 
transferring the work to some other agencies on contract basis which could be stopped. On 
the question of support to Hindustan Engineering Corporation the management informed 
that Bokaro Steel Plant has extended full support to HEC whenever required by giving 
Advance payment against purchase orders. Sometimes raw materials as well as bought out 
items have been provided for completion of urgent jobs although it is not stipulated in the 
scope of BSL. Apart from this regular orders are being placed by Projects Division, Project 
Modernisation as well as Contract Cell for IPU schemes. Delivery extension has been 
accorded without any financial recovery. 
On the question of future requirement of steel in the country the management informed 
that the perception of BSP about future requirement of steel in the flat product category is 
to be around 16 MT for the domestic market alone out of which HR products will comprise 
a market demand of 8.5 MT and CR products near about 7.5 MT. Considering the futuristic 
d'emand, BSP is considering to expand its capacity to the level of 5.25 MT of liquid steel 
corresponding to saleable steel production of 4.74 MT. 
The Sub-Committee thereafter enquired about the reasons of not reporting 45 theft 
cases of scrap/finished product in the plant since 1987. The management clarified that in 
most of these cases recovery of scrap has been made from outside the perimeter wall of the 
plant. In every such case an enquiry is initially made to find out and fix responsibility. But in 
these cases most of the property is found in an abandoned condition or it is being collected 
by miscreants outside the plant for petty gain. CSF regularly checks the area and wherever 
such collection is found it is brought inside the plant. 
The Sub-Committee thereafter deliberated qn the purchase policy .of the plan~ 
particularly purchase of clothes. The Sub-Committee desired that the management may 
approach National Textiles Corporation for such purchases. The management informed that 
NTC cannot meet the requirement but assured that possibilities would be explored this time. 
On the issue of deputing employees abroad for training, some discriminatory attitude of the 
management was pointed out by the Committee. The management assured that any case if 
brought to its notice would:/ be examined.

under forest cover. The State is served by a large number of streams and rivers which are 
not suitable for inland water transport. It has abundant reserves of sub-soil water and the

border of Tripura is international. About 50,000 tribal refugees from Bangladesh are 
sheltered in South Tripura district. The State has three Industrial Training Institutes.

cropping intensity of the major crops of rice, wheat, maize, oilseeds, pulses etc. Fruits like 
jackfruit, coconut, lichi, pineapple, mango etc. grow in the State. ·~ 
The Committee was also informed that the State was industrially backward mainly 
because of geographical isolation, lack of infrastructure, non-availability of raw material and 
associated problems. The State as a whole had been declared 'No Industry District' under 
Category 'A'. The State had been assigned special status for the purpose of rapid 
industrialisation. The industrial units set up in the State were in small scale and rural

costs.
