Kashmir.
                   (iii)18 to 45 years for Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, Ex-serviceman, Physically Disabled and Women.
            2.Educational Qualification : VIIIth passed. Preference will be given to those who have been trained for any
trade in Government recognised/approved institutions for duration of at least six months.
            3.Family Income : Neither the income of the beneficiary along with the spouse nor the income of parents of the
beneficiaries shall exceed Rs.40,000/-per annum.
            4.Residence : Permanent resident of the area for at least 3 years. (Relaxed for married
men in Meghalaya and for married women in rest of the country. For married men in
Meghalaya and for married women in the rest of the country, the residency criteria applies
to the spouse or in-laws).
            5.Defaulter : Should not be a defaulter to any nationalised bank/financial institution/cooperative bank. Further, a
person already assisted under other subsidy linked Government schemes would not be eligible under this
scheme.
            6.Activities Covered : All economically viable activities including agriculture and allied activities but excluding
direct agricultural operations like raising of Crops, purchase of manure etc.
            7.Project Cost : Rs. 1.00 lakh for business sector. Rs 2.00 lakhs for other activities, loan to be of composite
nature. If two or more eligible persons join together in a partnership, project up to Rs. 10.00 lakhs are
covered. Assistance shall be limited to individual admissibility.
9.2   Keeping in view the inflation and general increase in the income level and also the fact that some States like West
Bengal, Gujarat, Pondicherry etc. are running their own self employment schemes with better subsidy provision as
compared to PMRY, the Committee recommends the following modification in the existing criteria of PMRY scheme:
           (i)Enhancement of the eligibility criteria of family income from Rs. 40,000/- per annum to Rs. 1,50,000/- per
annum.
           (ii)Enhancement in project cost ceiling under the scheme may be enhanced from 
Rs. 1,00,000/- to Rs. 2,00,000/- for business sector and from Rs. 2,00,000/- to 
Rs. 5,00,000/- for service and industry sector.
           (iii)Enhancement in subsidy from Rs. 7,500/- per beneficiary (except for NER, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and
Uttaranchal) to Rs. 20,000/- per beneficiary other than NE States, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal.
In case of NE States including Sikkim, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal, the subsidy ceiling may be
enhanced i.e. Rs. 25,000/- per beneficiary.

12.0  STATUS OF RECOVERY OF LOANS UNDER PMRY
12.1  As per the reports received from RBI, the overall status of recovery under PMRY is around 35 
per cent i.e. 34.9 per cent, 35.2 per cent and 34.96 per cent for the half year ending March, 2002, 2003 and 2004.
12.2  The RBI and Govt. of India have initiated the following steps for improving the recovery of loan overdues under
the Scheme:
           (i)Emphasis has been laid on improving the success rate under the Scheme by ensuring backward and forward
linkages for the units set up under the Scheme. Higher success rate of the units under the Scheme is
necessary to ensure regular repayment of loan overdues under the Scheme.
           (ii) Revised Training curriculum for training of PMRY beneficiaries has been prepared by the Ministry of ARI
through Rural Development and Self Employment Training Institute (RUDSETI), Karnataka.
           (iii)Banks have been advised to conduct joint recovery drives with concerned Government Departments viz.
District Industries Centres (DICs).
           (iv)Government of India has advised all State Government to notify PMRY loan overdues as revenues dues under
their respective Revenue Recovery Acts.
           (v)The State/UTs are requested to improve recovery of loan overdues while communicating annual targets to
them.
           (vi)   All implementing banks have been advised to file criminal complaints against the borrowers who misutilise
loans sanctioned under the Scheme.
           (vii)  A meeting of RBI, implementing banks and State Directorate of Industries was held on 10.2.2004 in which
the States having low recovery of loan under the Scheme were urged upon to adopt the pattern followed in

13.0         CHANGING THE MINDSET OF BANKERS
13.1  The Committee was informed that the RBI has initiated following steps for changing the mindset of bankers to
remove their reluctance to sanction/disburse loans under the Scheme.
           (i)Banks have been instructed that they should impart necessary training programmes for the branch level
officials to sensitize them and bring about an attitudinal change towards the needs of this sector.
           (ii)Banks have been instructed by the RBI to dispose off applications involving loan amount of Rs. 25,000/-
within 2 weeks and those of higher amount within 4 weeks, provided the loan applications are completed in
all respect.
           (iii)Cut off date for lapsing of sanctions and completion of disbursements have also been prescribed to ensure
timely sanctions and disbursement of loan under the Scheme.
           (iv)Banks have been advised to adhere to the quarterly schedule of sanctions and disbursement of loan under the
PMRY.
13.2The Committee desires that public sector banks must yield to the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India in
regard to disbursement of loans on the PMRY. The managers at the top level should also direct the branch managers to
adopt client-friendly approach and create such atmosphere that the general opinion about the mindset of the bankers
should itself change. It is possible through making PMRY more popular among the unemployed youth. The Committee
comment the role of RBI for suitable intervention from time to time whereby the RBI issued guidelines for
consumer/client-friendly working of banks. As the banking sector is being empowered with functional autonomy, the
onus/lies on the public sector banks and its administrative Ministry to implement the guidelines of RBI in the best
interest of the industries its an objective to serve the nation and not use this functional discretion for denying the
prospective entrepreneurs in harnessing the opportunity for contributing to economic growth and industrial
development.
13.3 The Committee further desires that the financial institutions, respective State Governments and the Ministry of ARI
should coordinate and monitor the working of PMRY in such a way as to enable the process of sponsoring, sanctioning
and disbursement of applications by the States and banks by avoiding the stoppage/delay of disbursement in PMRY on
flimsy grounds and for quick disposal of application on the part of DICs and forwarding the same to the banks.
Adequate mechanism may be adopted for timely communication of targets to the banks for necessary action on their
part; coverage of SCs\STs/OBCs under the scheme as per the norms stipulated by the Government of India; effective
orientation programmes conducted by DIC for the target groups at block/taluka level to enlighten/popularisation of
PMRY and giving accordance to the provision of PMRY for advancing loans in the ratio of 50 per cent; 30 per cent and
20 per cent in respect of industry, service and business sector.
14.0         (STRENGTHS, WEAKNESSES, OPPORTUNITIES AND THREATS) SWOT ANALYSIS OF PMRY
         Strengths:
           (i)   PMRY has emerged as a major Central Sector Scheme creating employment opportunities for about 31.6
lakh persons since inception of the Scheme in the year 1993. The employment under the PMRY will further
increase over the years as the PMRY is ongoing Central Sector Scheme.
           (ii)The coverage of the Scheme is spread over both for Rural as well as Urban areas. As per findings of 2 nd
round of evaluation on PMRY, conducted by the Institution of Applied Manpower and Research (IAMR),
disbursement of PMRY beneficiaries in Rural and Urban areas is 49.9 per cent and 50.1 per cent
respectively.
           (iii)The evaluation study has also revealed that assets have been created in 89.7 per cent of cases disbursed loans
under the PMRY.
           Weaknesses:
           (i)The recovery of loan over dues under the PMRY Scheme has not been satisfactory. The recovery of loan over
dues was 34.9 per cent for the half year ended March, 2002 which stands at 34.96 per cent for the half year
March, 2004.
           (ii)Banks are under financing the projects. The amount of loan disbursed under PMRY is stagnating around Rs.
60,000/- per beneficiary.
           (iii)There is gap between the cases sanctioned and disbursement made under PMRY by banks. A total of 21.1

           (iv)Export potential.
           Threat :
           (i) Competition from handlooms, powerloom and other synthetic products,
           (ii) Increasing inventory with NGO.
16.1  The Committee expects that the Ministry of ARI would take stock of SWOT analysis of Khadi industries and
make all out efforts for combating weaknesses and threats to Khadi industries and capitalize on its strength and
opportunities for fast track promotion and proliferation of Khadi industries in India in general and in the States like
Bihar, Maharashtra and Jharkhand where the Khadi industries has to make its way.
17.0         PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY KHADI INDUSTRIES
            (i)Quality:- In the market economy, is an important aspect. As such, to make khadi products competitive in the
market it is necessary to enhance the quality of the products as such to enhance the budget support for such
schemes.
            (ii)Sales outlets:- Shabby & dilapidated conditions of khadi institutions is a weak area which require
improvement for attracting the customers. A scheme has been launched for this purpose by formulating a
plan for modernization and renovation of sales outlets. KVIC has already renovated and modernized one of
the prestigious DSOs located at Connaught Place, New Delhi and another private sales outlet at Khan
Market, New Delhi. Further under UNDP-KVIC project, computerization of inventory management and
financial accounting is one of the important element and in this regard, 10 major sales outlets were
identified and upgraded. The proposal for renovation of other DSOs and Institutional Sales Outlets need
adequate budgetary support. Similarly, the efforts initiated by KVIC by launching the PRODIP for
improving the Product Design and Packaging also taken up for vigorous follow up with adequate financial
support.
            (iii)    Working capital:- Shortage of working capital is another major problem blocking the progress of khadi
programme. Earlier, the institutions were enjoying working capital assistance from KVIC’s budgetary
support at zero rate of interest. Subsequently, in view of budgetary crunch, the khadi institutions have been
directed to avail of funds from banking sector, against which KVIC issues interest subsidy eligibility
certificate. However, the financial institutions are not honouring the ISEC issued by KVIC to its full extent
as such there is shortage of working capital in the Khadi Sector. Further, large amount of pending rebate
with various State Governments adds to the burden.
            (iv)Consortium Bank Credit (CBC):- As on 31 st January, 2005, Rs. 238.02 crore was lying as outstanding
balance with Khadi Implementing Agencies under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) for which they have to
pay interest @ 4.5 per cent in addition to refunding the same in instalments whereas under the working
fund system adopted for khadi programme the institutions are permitted to keep the working capital in the
form of working fund as long as they maintain certain level of production. The Government has now
approved the conversion of outstanding balance under CBC scheme into working capital and for this
purpose KVIC has executed necessary documents and forwarded to the lead bank - State Bank of India.
            (v)Outdated and obsolete charkhas and looms:- Another area which required immediate assistance to khadi
institutions is tools and implements. The fact remains that the charkhas and looms available with them are
mostly outdated, which require replacement or renovation.
17.1  The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should take up the issue of requirement of working capital and
budgetory support with the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission for modernisation and renovation of sales
outlets, alongwith the strategy and time frame to execute the same. Adequate steps must also be taken for modernisation
of Charkhas and looms, for which a separate fund and scheme i.e. modernisation of traditional industries has been made.
17.2  The Committee feels that conversion of outstanding balance i.e. to the tune of Rs.238.02 crore which was lying as
outstanding balance with Khadi implementing Agencies under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) into working capital
would solve the problem of requirement of working capital to a certain extent.

19.0  SWOT ANALYSIS
           Strength :
               (i)Low per capita investment and highly employment oriented,
               (ii) Involvement of low technology which can be adopted without much specialized knowledge,
               (iii)Easily accessible-even in remote villages.
           Weaknesses :
               (i)Largely decentralised nature of operation,
               (ii)Inadequate Research & Development,
               (iii)Lack of quality control and standardization facilities.
           Opportunities :
               (i) Capacity to generate both Self-employment as well as wage employment,
               (ii) Substitute to rural farm sector employment without replacing the workforce in rural areas,
               (iii)Increasing employment among rural youths.
           Threats :
               (i)    Migration of artisans/entrepreneurs from villages to other areas,
               (ii) Competition from organized sector.
19.1  The Committee is of the view that the Government must give the utmost attention to the Village Industries by
undertaking serious study of SWOT analysis and outlining the "Key Areas for Massive Action" as India being a country
of villages and undergoing industrial development must tap the opportunities and bank upon its strength and remove the
weaknesses and threats for rapid and ensured rural industrialization and development. Special/specific strategic
programme should be sketched out for developing and consolidating village industries in Bihar, Jharkhand and West
Bengal, basing the strategy on the availability of local raw material and providing adequate working capital and
budgetary support.

21.0         MARKETING STRATEGY FOR KVI
21.1  The marketing strategy of KVIC is to focus on its eco friendly and natural product range. Khadi and Village
Industries sector produces goods and services both. In village industries service based units basically cover local area
needs. With regard to non-consumer goods normally units established have good market as most of such products are
intermediary products used by other industries. Main difficulty is in consumer goods and khadi. For both these products
areas of intervention involves a detailed marketing strategy for publicity, branding and brand promotion, design input,
better packaging etc. Accessing private marketing channel, modernization of existing channels, organizing large scale
exhibitions are important aspects. Design/packaging development scheme and renovation of marketing outlets scheme
has been launched.
21.2  For the consumer goods, KVIC has developed “Sarvodaya Brand” consisting of FMCG products like Toilet Soap,
Pickles, Honey, etc., “Khadi” for exclusive up-market and export products like Essential Oils, Herbal Products,
Designer Garments etc. and “Desi Aahaar” for Organic foods like Cereals, Spices Powder, Pulses, etc. and the same
have been launched at Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata etc. in select Outlets. Based on the experience it is felt that a
professional Marketing Agency / Federation is required, so that KVIC does not get involved in Departmental Trading
Activities, since institutions and marketing professionals can play a better and effective role in marketing these
products. Accordingly a Marketing Confederation has been constituted out of existing Khadi & VI Federations and has
also been accorded provisional recognition by KVIC. The Confederation is expected to take up aggressive marketing for
KVI products with active support of KVIC.
22.0         MARKETING OF PRODUCTS UNDER KVIC
22.1  There are 7050 Sales Outlets under KVI Sector and in addition, KVIC has launched a scheme of Franchise Outlets
as well as marketing into private channel of distribution. A scheme for opening Sales Outlets under REGP Scheme has
also been introduced. There is a need for supporting inputs like CFCs in a big way for providing infrastructural support
to marketing like raw-material godown, processing facilities, quality control laboratories, packaging, etc.
22.2  In addition, exhibitions are conducted every year for sale as well as promotion of KVI goods. The institutions
working under KVI sector also conduct Mobile Sales as well as door-to-door sales for sale of their goods. Most of the
goods produced in VI as well as REGP units go through the marketing through private trade channel. There is an
eminent need to strengthen the distribution channel of VI goods by setting up Gramodyog agar on the lines of Khadi
Vastragar.
22.3         Government Supply also forms a major part in marketing the KVI products. Under DGS&D, Rate Contract,
KVIC used to supply Khadi as well as other village industries product to different organizations, prominent among them
being the Indian Railway, Defence, Paramilitary Forces and other Government Departments.

25.0         ORGANIZATIONAL-FUNCTIONAL RESTRUCTURING OF KVI
25.1  Arthur Anderson’s report suggested to change the present structure of Commission. It has also suggested that
besides khadi and V.I. expert members, representatives from Social Marketing/Rural Marketing, Research Institute,
Development Institute are should also be included in the Commission. Regarding Organisational Structure it was
desired that the Organisational structure of Khadi and Village Industries and other Directorates should be changed so
that they should be end to end structure. Other key recommendations included Commission’s Central office needs to
play role as a policy making body and delegate implementation to the field officers; KVIC needs to be a promotional
and developing agency
rather than financial agency: KVIC needs to concentrate on creating Marketing Demands and focused on marketing :
Focus on product, process, research, technical support, marketing under Khadi: Focus on establishment of rural
industries clusters for providing common facilities and Capacity building of Khadi Institutions: KVIC to function brand
promotion, advertising and other market promotion activities: KVIC to develop capacity of institutions including
Management system and technology transfer to institutions: To develop proper human resource information system,
performance management system, strengthening of audit and financial control process and strengthening of IT.
25.2  As per the National Common Minimum Programme, the Government has declared to revamp the KVIC. Towards
this objective, the Government has dissolved the KVIC with effect from 14 October, 2004 and also set up a ten-Member
Expert Committee to Examine the Structure, Functioning and Performance of KVIC and Recommend Measures to

26.0         PROFESSIONALISATION OF KVIC
26.1  KVIC has recently constituted a Confederation for Promotion of Khadi & Village Industries (CPKVI) in order to

26.2  The Committee expects that the Ministry of ARI would examine the recommendations of the Expert Committee
within a specific time-frame and suitable recommendation which are accepted by the Ministry would be implemented in
a time-bound manner. The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI would furnish the Committee the report of the
Expert Committee along with comments of the Ministry on the recommendation contained therein and the possible
impact on the structural and functional pattern of KVIC. It is now the time for KVIC to deliver as it is being hoped that
the revamped KVIC with new structural and functional pattern would be in a better position to serve the KVI sector in a
more professional and effective manner.

35.0  STATUS OF COIR INDUSTRIES IN ORISSA AND WEST BENGAL
35.1  In the State of Orissa, the Board has opened a Regional office at Bhubaneswar for implementing various schemes
and programmes for the development of coir industry in the State. A coir testing laboratory has been established at the
office to facilitate the testing of coir products and coir pith samples.
35.2  In the State, women are imparted training in spinning under Manila Coir Yojana of the Board. They are provided
Motorised Ratt at 75 per cent subsidized cost on completion of the Training. Field training units are imparting training
in spinning to rural artisans in association with local NGOs and Co-operative Societies. During 2004-05, about 160
candidates were trained and 300 candidates are undergoing training in 10 centres. It is expected that during the year, 920
artisans including women would be provided training in spinning coir yarn and production of value added items. Coir
Board supplied 30 motorised traditional ratts for training and two exposures tours for coir artisans/entrepreneurs were
arranged to Kerala and other coir producing States. Entrepreneurship Development Programmes and Quality
Improvements Programmes were also organized through the Regional Office of Coir Board in Bhubaneswar.
35.3  Under the Co-operativisation Scheme of the Board, an amount of Rs.83.40 lakh has been released to the State for
modernization of a rubberized coir manufacturing unit of the Orissa State Coir Corporation Ltd. In the State of West
Bengal, the Board is imparting training to rural artisans through Non Governmental Organisations. The trainees are paid
a stipend of Rs.500 per month and Rs.3000 to the trainer towards honorarium. During the year, the Board has approved
for payment of a sum of Rs.2.00 lakh to the Government of West Bengal for organizing a Seminar on Coir Industry.
Under the scheme of Development of Production Infrastructure, assistance to the tune of 50 per cent (Limited to Rs.1.50
lakh) of the cost of building and machinery is provided to set up/renovate coir units. The entrepreneurs are also paid 50
per cent of II Class Train Fare/Bus fare for conducting exposure tour to coir producing centers in other States. In
addition, the Board organizes Entrepreneurship Development Programmes in the State for attracting new entrepreneurs
to the sector. The Board also approved a proposal for purchase of coir manufacturing machineries worth Rs.6 lakh by
the State Government.
35.4  The Committee desires that the Coir Board should implement its action plan in West Bengal in letter and spirit and
promote the coir industries in Orissa and Jharkhand through various schemes and programmes including Co-
operativisation Scheme and the Mahila Coir Yojana so that the prospects of coir industries must be vitalised in the non-
traditional zones

opportunities at low cost to local artisans by utilising the local raw materials. To support such traditional industries,
Government has been giving loans for Khadi and Village Industries to be set up in rural areas through the KVIC. The
KVIC in turn lent this money to Khadi and VI institutions for meeting their working capital fund requirements. With the
expansion of KVI programme the budgetary support being provided by the Government of India has become
insufficient to meet the funds requirement of this sector. To overcome this difficulty, the ISEC scheme was introduced
in May, 1977 which provides Interest Subsidy to the extent of the difference between the actual interest charged by the
banks and 4 per cent born by the institutions. In view of the recommendations made by the High Power Committee
(HPC) in 1994, the ISEC scheme is now extended only to Khadi and Ployvastra Programme with effect from 1995-96.
However, under Village Industries activities fund already committed earlier ISEC are also provided, which constituted
only in a small quantum. As the Khadi institutions were to pay zero per cent interest on this loan till 2003 and 4 per cent
thereafter, KVIC have hardly been able to pay any interest or return the loan advanced by Government to KVIC. The
amount of interest accrued to KVIC on loan has been subsidized by the Government through payment of subsidy in lieu
of interest over the years.
36.2  The Committee was informed by the Ministry of ARI that the subsidy in lieu of interest is not actually released to
the KVIC but is provided for in the budgetary provision both Plan and Non-plan for book adjustments, against the
interest payable by KVIC to Government. The Committee endorses the provision made for the purpose. The budgetary
provision for interest subsidy as a book adjustment is arising on account of the fact that the sanction of Khadi and VI
loan at different points of time over the years has borne varying rates of interest, (varying between 11.8 per cent to 14
per cent) whereas KVIC being a developmental agency for promoting rural employment through Khadi and VI activities
has in turn lent to its beneficiaries at zero per cent interest till 16 March, 2000 and at 4 per cent afterwards (Khadi Loan)
and VI loan at the rate of 4 per cent per annum. The subsidy is therefore towards this difference in the rate at which
KVIC borrows from the Government and the rate at which it lends to beneficiaries. The Committee finds it reasonable
that since the amount of interest subsidy has been accumulating every year, the budgetary provision for interest subsidy
has been kept at the level of Rs. 39.10 crore to meet the requirements of annual book adjustment.
37.0         INSTITUTIONAL CREDIT TO KVI SECTOR
37.1  The institutional credit flow to KVI Sector is just 50 per cent to 60 per cent of the expectation. The RBI has issued
separate guidelines after Kalia Committee report in July, 1994. Wherein clear-cut guidelines have been issued for
calculation of the credit requirement of the khadi institution, to remove the gap in Interest Subsidy value vis-a-vis fund
provided by bank. All the banks has to follow the guidelines given by RBI in July, 1994 based on following points:
            (i)KVIC will furnish the worksheet for assessment of Working Capital.
            (ii)KVIC assessment may be accepted if it does not exceed the assessment made by the banks by more than 10
per cent.
            (iii)    In case KVIC assessment of W.C. exceed the bank assessment more than 10 per cent. The W.C. may be
arrived at by mutual dialogue between KVIC/institution and financing branch.
37.2  In case of sharp difference between the peak level and lean season credit requirements additional credit limits may
be sanctioned by the banks, KVIC will indicate such peak level credit requirements also in the interest subsidy
certificate.

38.1  The plan expenditure has been earmarked to the tune of Rs. 4.50 crore and non-plan expenditure to the tune of
Rs.5.36 crore during 2004-05 over other village industries (than Khadi Industries). Since the expenditure indicated
above is only book adjustment, there is no achievement or target against this fund. As far as Interest Subsidy is
concerned, both Plan and Non Plan are by way of book adjustment without any cash flow.
38.2  The Village Industries being supported by KVIC have been categorized into seven broad groups viz. agro and food
processing industry, forest based industry, handmade paper and fibre industry, mineral based industry, polymer and
chemical based industry, rural engineering and bio-technology industry and service industry. The major problem for
setting up of such village industries have been the availability of credit at nominal interest rates, marketing of products
and technology upgradation.
38.3  The KVIC has been making available finance to VI institutions at the nominal rate of 4 per cent. Subsequently,
they have introduced the REGP scheme, which provides a capital subsidy but no interest subsidy. Further, the KVIC has
built up a large network of rural Cottage Industrial Units producing wide range of goods and articles catering the rural
and partly urban markets. Some of them have achieved high standards for export as well but a vast majority lack support
in maintaining standard quality and for want of technical Back-up to upgrade the technology of their products. Keeping
this in view, the KVIC had set up Technical Back Up Units who will provide S&T inputs to the entrepreneurs engaged
in KVI activities.
38.4  The main implementing agencies of village industries are individual entrepreneurs, however, the subsidy in lieu of
interest was meant only for VI institutions and entrepreneurs were not covered. By launching Margin Money scheme
(REGP), this lacuna has been removed and Margin Money is provided to both individuals as well as institutions. After
the introduction of Margin Money, a considerable number of individual entrepreneurs have been covered under the
purview of KVIC and proved it as a successful instrument to set up village industries projects in rural areas by
channelising the institutional credit with corresponding of Margin Money from KVIC. Initially the Margin Money
component is kept with the Banks for a period of 2 years under fixed deposit in the name of the entrepreneurs. If the
project fails, this margin money will not be released to the entrepreneurs. Further as the banks are providing loans to the
entrepreneurs under REGP they may initiate recovery measures as per terms and conditions stipulated in their loan
sanction.
38.5  The experience gained so far is quite encouraging and there is much demand for REGP in the field. The
Government of India has already decided to continue REGP till the end of Xth Five Year Plan. Seeing the encouraging
result of this scheme, with all probability the scheme may continue beyond X the plan provided no other better
substitute is formulated.
38.6  The Committee acknowledges the improvement in the scheme of Margin Money over subsidy in lieu of interest as
the Margin Money is provided to both individuals as well as institutions while the subsidy in lieu of interest was meant
only for VI institutions and entrepreneurs were not covered. Since the experience gained so far is quite encouraging and
there is much demand for REGP in the field, the scheme should continue beyond Tenth Plan provided no other better
substitute is formulated. The Committee further recommends that KVIC should undertake following actions for
promoting Village Industries:-
            (i)     to trigger and strengthen rural industrialization through timely, continuous and appropriate S&T inputs,
R&D support, innovative ideas and technologies for value addition as well as for strengthening academic-
industrial linkages.
            (ii)proactive steps to give a fillip to the marketing of VI products through brand promotion, exhibitions,
marketing tie up with the Departmental Bhawans and sales outlets, etc.

Industrialisation to set up 100 rural industrial clusters in the country every year so that it can boost up the rural economy
by creating more employment avenues for the rural youth in the non-farm sector, and slow down the migration of the

programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments are having their own programmes in this area which
could be coordinated and their synergies exploited for greater impact.

Implementation Committee (SLIC) and District Level Implementation Committee (DLIC) for implementation of the
programme at State and District Level. The programme is being implemented by KVIC, NABARD, SIDDBI and the
States.

42.4  The performance under the NPRI Scheme has not been satisfactory at all. Some of the reasons to this could be the
meager financial assistance of Rs 5.0 lakh per cluster for cluster-wide interventions, fill-in-gaps arrangements, non-
availability of credit-linked subsidy component, inadequate synergy with the Ministries/departments with their own
schemes in this area etc. Therefore, the Ministry proposes to subsume the NPRI Scheme into the new proposed Scheme
namely, Scheme of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI). The liability of the NPRI may be met
out of the subsequent provisions of budget under NPRI/ other schemes of the Ministry.
42.5  The revised scheme, titled the Scheme of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) has been
drafted. This scheme is based on cluster development approach and also addresses the concerns raised by the Ministry
of Finance (MoF). The EFC note along with the revised draft scheme has been circulated to the Ministries/Departments
concerned for their comments on 15 February, 2005.
42.6  The Committee takes stock of the fact that NPRI which was announced in the budget 
1999-2000 with the objective of setting up of hundred rural industrial clusters in the country every year for boosting
rural economy by creating more employment avenues and to arrest the migration of the rural artisans or town/cities. The
irony of the programme was that no separate fund was made available to implement the programme and it was
conceived that since the various Ministries/Departments are having their own programme in this “coveted areas and
their co-ordination and synergistic harnessing would be significant/harness the objectives of the programmes. The result
that comes out is that the expectation regarding the success of the programme felled apart, and that was bound to happen
with the programme without financial support.
42.7  The Committee observes that the co-ordination and synergetic approach so conceived among various Government
Ministries/Departments to make NPRI a success could not succeed the test of the time and the administrative (Ministry
of ARI) which was supposed to implement the NPRI spent no time in screwing the bureaucratic skill for advocating the
countless reasons for “unsatisfactory performance of NPRI i.e. meagre financial assistance of Rs. 5.00 lakh for lakh per
cluster for wide intervention, fill in gap arrangements, non-availability of credit linked subsidy component and also the
inadequate synergy with the Ministries / Departments with their own scheme in this area. When this Committtee
recommended for comprehensive over hauling and synchronization of all schemes and programmes for employment
generation and poverty alleviation, it the Ministry of ARI who beautifully referred the allocation of transaction of
business among various Government’s Ministries/Departments with a stress that sufficient co-ordination and syenergy
exists among various Government’s Ministries/Departments. The Committee wonders as how the same Ministry of ARI
is now wanting out the lack of co-ordination and synergy as the reason for unsatisfactory performance of NPRI. This
Committee is of the view that logic and argument of the Ministry of ARI is of selective nature.
42.8  Regarding NPRI, the Committee in its Report on Demands for Grants (2004-05) that NPRI has the potential for
actual rural industrialization and consolidation of rural economy and had recommended that the Government should
undertake concrete measures to combat the problems in achieving the objectives, targets credit-flow, implementation
and monitoring mechanism and “Key Concern Areas” of NPRI. But of no avail. Sensing the slow but sure death knell of
the NPRI, the Ministry of ARI has now decided to abandon the so acclaimed programme (NPRI) and the Ministry
comes out with re-christened programme, coincidently, the name of the programme is SFURTI, Scheme of Funds for
Re-genration of Traditional Industries. NPRI had made a slow start, therefore, it seems that the name of the new
programme is carefully drafted as SFURTI, obviously to instill the hope among those who is using their heart in the
efficient working of the Government machinery.
42.9  The Committee is awefully shocked to observe the pathetic working of the programmes/ schemes and the
monitoring mechanism as maintained within the Governmental structure which is being imparted to make the
programme a success. The Committee is of the considered view that re-christening of schemes is not the guarantee to
make the new scheme a success unless and until the scheme is back by adequate financial fund and willing
administrative backup to deliver in the system.The Committee has no objection with launching of new programme like
SFURTI or with whatever names it comes in future but the Committee strongly feels that NPRI has cherished national
goal and appropriate objectives and had no inherent weaknesses/problems as such except the lack of allocation for a
separate fund, the Committee therefore, reiterates that NPRI must continue in order to achieve those goals/objectives
and a separate fund must be allocated to NPRI.

of priority sector and they should be provided various facilities accordingly.
44.2  For regeneration of traditional industries like coir, handloom, handicrafts, sericulture, leather, pottery and other
cottage industries, the Finance Minister in his Budget Speech of July, 2004 announced the decision to set up a Fund
with an initial allocation of Rs. 100 crore. In view of the comments of the Ministry of Finance (MoF) on initial draft
scheme drawn up by this Ministry, a revised scheme, titled the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional
Industries (SFURTI) has been drafted. This Scheme is based on cluster development approach and also addresses the
concerns raised by the MoF. The EFC note along with the revised draft scheme has been circulated to the
Ministries/Departments concerned for their comments on 15 February, 2005. As such no fund has been released under
this scheme so far. The allocation of Rs. 100 crore in BE 2004-05 under Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries
where the budget allocation was reduced to Rs. 1 crore in RE 2004-05 as a token amount, as the scheme could not be
finalised in view of comments of Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission on the initial draft scheme circulated.
44.3  The allocation of Rs. 30 crore (including Rs. 3 crore for NE Region) keeping in view the fact that the scheme is
expected to start in 2005-06, after necessary approval of the EFC/Cabinet and keeping in view the financial outlay in the
draft scheme in the first year.
44.4  The Committee extends its best wishes for the success of the scheme for re­generation of Traditional Industries
based on cluster development approach and hopes that the programme would make a head start without further delay as
SFURTI has lost one financial year at the drafting/approval stage. The Committee therefore, recommends that the
Ministry of ARI should expedite the process to get the approval of EFC/cabinet with adequate and required financial
support. The scheme may prove effective in re­generation of traditional industries like coir, handloom, handicrafts,
sericulture, leather, pottery and other cottage industries.
44.5  The committee reiterates that since the artisans are facing various problems including non-availability of timely
credit and raw material, lack of market opportunities, it can be hoped that that the budgetary provision made to the tune
of Rs 27.00 crore in the year 2005-06 would be able to solve the problems faced by the artisans. Moreover, since the
Traditional Industries are functioning in the remote rural areas in a most decentralized manner, efforts should be made
for organizing them under appropriate organizational structure.

49.0         STRATEGY TO PROMOTE INTER-SECTORAL CO-OPERATION AND ASSISTANCE
49.1  Regarding the suggestions for inter-sectoral cooperation and assistance among various sectors of economy to
promote Agro and Rural Industries. The Ministry of ARI stated that the Ministry of ARI, Rural Development and Food
Processing are quite different and do not overlap except in a few areas. The work of M/o Food Processing relates to the
promotion of industries like processing and refrigeration, technical assistance planning, development and control
of/assistance to the industries in the food sector viz. bread, oilseeds, beer, alcoholic drinks from molasses base, aerated
water etc. whereas, the work of M/o Rural Development relates to public cooperation including the matters relating to
Panchayati Raj/Panchayati Raj institutions rural development etc., rural employment, integrated rural development,
matters relating to rural connectivity including Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, rural housing etc. The work of the
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries is to coordinate the development work of village andcottage industries and tiny
and micro enterprises in both urban and rural areas and the matter relating to all rural industries.
49.2  It was further stated that though the role of M/o Rural Development is poverty alleviation and that of M/o ARI is
employment generation, in case of Ministry of Rural Development, the projects taken up are meant for the people below
poverty line and per unit investment is around Rs. 50,000/-, whereas in Ministry ofARI, the emphasis is on employment
generation through individual entrepreneurs and the project cost can go upto Rs. 25 lakhs. Thus in case of M/o ARI, the
individual enterprises are encouraged for setting up projects for generating  employment opportunities. In case of
Ministry of Food Processing Industries, the focus is on the specialized area of food processing and covers all types of
projects including large scale projects.
49.3  The Ministry of ARI advocated that the holistic planning for overall development of rural economy is already
being done at the level of Planning Commission. The Planning Commission has broken down the national targets with
the targets at the Ministry level in consultation with the concerned Ministries/State Governments for the Tenth Plan
period. These targets are reviewed regularly. Further, the Planning Commission also sets up Inter-Ministerial Task
Force (1MTF) whenever it is felt necessary to integrate the efforts of more than one Ministry. During 2004-05, the
Ministry of ARI was in several such IMTFs viz. Household and Artisanal Manufacturing, Agriculture and allied
activities, etc.
49.4  The Committee understands that each Ministry has been interested with specific mandate and each of them
functions on the areas as per the mandate. The Committee also understands that Planning Commission coordinates the
programmes on various issues. However, governance can not be water compartmentalised all together in the cases were
the areas/issues/concerned are of similar nature or overlap each other as is the case with the ARI sector which has to
promote industries in the rural areas and thus generate avenues of employment generation with the ultimate objectives
of poverty alleviation and thus contributing the national economy. Therefore, the Committee is of view that strategy to
promote inter-sectoral co-operation and assistance among Rural Development, poverty alleviation programmes, Food
Processing sector and other such programmes/schemes with the Agro & Rural Sector in order to give greater thrust and
coordinated efforts and synergistic approach towards implementation of rural infrastructural development projects,
employment Generation and Rural industrialization & Development and poverty-alleviation. The Government should
adopt the Unified and Integrated and holistic approach to strike out the very roots of poverty and undertake the
implementation of well knitted policies/programmes to develop the rural economy with co-ordinated and concerted
efforts, then and only then benefits of the programmes would percolate down to the targets contributing to “Bharat
Nirman”.

            (v)    to reach electricity to the remaining 1,25,000 villages and offer electricity connection to 2.3 crore

50.2  The Committee welcomes the announcement of the Finance Minister on Bharat Nirman and is of the opinion that
the implementation of programmes under Bharat Nirman will go a long way forward in developing rural connectivity
and infrastructure, thus providing better access to the rural areas. It will give a boost to marketing goods produced by
rural industries. In fact such initiatives are as much requires as subsidy for setting up rural industries. The Committee
hopes that the programmes on Bharat Nirman would incorporate also the components of Agro and Rural Industries.

51.0         IMPACT OF GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALIZATION
51.1  The impact of liberalization has enhanced the competitive nature of the whole industrial set up as such. Open
market mechanisms have come in place of regulated and protected nature of pre-liberalized economy. The challenge
posed by globalized economy has enhanced and enabled nurturing of the inherent competitive and resilient nature of the
Agro and Rural Industries sector as such.
51.2  The sector mainly consists of Khadi, Village Industries, cottage industries (handicrafts), Coir, Tiny and Micro
enterprises. The products of this sector by their very nature are traditional, location specific and exclusively indigenous.
This adds to the specialized and exclusive nature of the sector as such and gives it a dynamic and resilient character. For
example, herbal products, organic manure, organic food, honey production, traditional crafts items, etc are so exclusive
by nature that it offers immense export potential which is almost non-competitive in the world economy. This defines
the future outlook of the sector. The emphasis would be to highlight the exclusivity of ARI products and its suitability to
specific local area both for production as well as marketing as it addresses the felt local needs and to develop quality
diversification and aggressively enter the world market.
51.3The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI should make strategy to protect the Agro Rural Industries

52.0  LEGAL FRAMEWORK SUPPORTING OF THE AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES
52.1  The existing legal framework pertains to specific Acts framed for the implementing agencies like the KVIC Act
and the legislations relating to Coir sector. Within the broad legislative frameworks of these Acts, the Khadi and Village
Industries Commission as well as the Coir Board frame their rules of business and conduct their activities. Some
modifications, as required, in the basic legal framework have also been made.
52.2  Further, in the National Common Minimum Programme, the Government has declared to revamp the KVIC.
Towards this objective, the Government has dissolved the KVIC with effect from 14 October, 2004 and also set up a
ten-Member Expert Committee to Examine the Structure, Functioning and Performance of KVIC and recommend
Measures to revamp the KVIC and launch new programmes, with the following terms of reference:
            (i)     to review the existing structure, functioning and performance of the KVIC since its inception;
            (ii)     to review the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956 (No. 61 of 1956), KVIC Rules 1957,
and the Regulations made thereunder and to recommend restructuring, along with modifications, if any, in
these statutes, to achieve the objectives of (a) development of Khadi and Village Industries (KVI) and (b)
making KVIC a more professional and effective body for implementation of the existing KVI
programmes/schemes and/or launching new programmes/schemes with a view to enhancing employment
and income generation in the rural areas and expending the markets for (including export of) Khadi and
Village Industry products; and
            (iii)    to recommend any other measure(s) considered necessary by the Committee to revamp the KVIC and to
launch new, appropriate programmes/schemes.
52.3  The Expert Committee is expected to give its recommendation shortly. The Government will take necessary action
on the recommendations of the Expert Committee including changes in the legal framework as required to make KVIC
more effective in generation of employment opportunities in the rural areas and small towns.
52.4  The Committee hopes that the recommendations of the expert Committee on revamping KVIC would go a long
way in reorienting the organisational and functional pattern of KVIC for the promotion and proliferation of Khadi and
Village Industries.
53.0         NATIONAL POLICY FOR AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES
53.1  Reacting to the suggestion of the need for formulation of the national policy of Agro and Rural Industries, the
Ministry of ARI the viewed that the present policy relating to Agro and Rural Industries adequately addresses the issues
and potentials of the sector. Khadi and Village Industries sector through its Khadi package tackles the issue of
liberalization and its after effects effectively. The policy framework at present is adequately ensures optimal support and
promotion to the units functioning in this sector. Policy initiatives in response to the changed economic scenario and its
challenges are being consistently addressed by the Ministry through a dynamic process of policy amendments and
positioning.
53.2  The Committee feels that the Ministry of ARI should give serious thought for formulation of National Policy for
Agro & Rural Industries for the growth of rural industries, instead of rejecting the suggestion on the first instance. Had
the every thing been right with the existing policy measures, India’s Agro Rural Industries would have been in a better
position contributing the national economy and particularly consolidating the rural economy. The Committee
understands that the Ministry through a dynamic process of policy amendments and positioning is consistently
addressing policy initiatives in response to the changed economic scenario and its challenges, however, the colossal
problem of India is also persisting and that too consistently. Therefore, it is desirable that the Ministry of ARI should act
and not react on the recommendation of the Committee without giving a proper thought to the ideas behind the
recommendations.
54.0         PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES
54.1  The Major problems faced by the Agro and Rural Industries, are primarily relating to lack of Infrastructural
facilities, marketing linkages and updated technology. The same is being addressed by way of providing emphasis on
development of market linkages, modernization of outlets, diversification of products, exposure to foreign markets and
infrastructural back up through cluster development. The impact of liberalization and WTO regime on the market
scenario are being responded by the Sector through policy initiatives which enhances the resilient nature of the sector as
a whole.
54.2  The Committee is of the view that Ministry of ARI should interact with the concerned sector/department
for facilitating infrastructural facilities, marketing linkages and updated technology to the Agro and Rural
Industries.

55.0  CREDIT FLOW TO AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES
55.1  Major credit flow to the Agro and Rural Industries is through banks. Credit flow to units in this sector is supported
by way of Margin Money/subsidy/loan/working capital. The loan part is accessed through the financial institutions and
the subsidy and margin money part of the project is borne form the budgetary allocations to the concerned implementing
agency. Problems by way of unviable projects, cutting down financial size of the projects, lengthy procedural
formalitiesare faced in general by the beneficiaries or entrepreneurs in accessing credit for their units. This may be, to a
certain extent linked to unsatisfactory recovery of finances advanced. Hence the attempt is to constantly, vigorously
pursue recovery dues and at the same time ensure easy accessibility to new entrepreneurs.
55.2  The Committee feels that the fiscal measures/issues may be undertaken by the Ministry of ARI with the Ministry
of Finance to boost investment in Agro and Rural Industries through credit enabled private investment and enhanced
public investment effective measures for Agro & Rural Industries for striking an equilibrium for balanced regional
growth and overall national economic growth and development.
55.3  The rural industries provide the critical forum needed for a balanced regional growth due to its unique resilient and
vibrant qualities as a sector which spans the Nation as a whole. With the sector being a combination of traditional skills
coupled with modern technology provides a very strong and potential weapon to combat the negative effects of
liberalization. It is an accepted fact that in our country, with regional imbalances as they exist, liberalization without the
presence of this sector would have made the existing imbalances extreme and a potent threat to the objectives of rural
industrialization and poverty alleviation. It is in this scenario that this independent Ministry, focusing totally on this
sector, formulating policies to withstand the effects of liberalization, assumes its critical role in shaping the national
economic scenario. The measures taken so far by the Ministry should effectively enable the achievement of balanced
regional growth.
55.4  The Committee acknowledges the contribution of ARI sector and awareness of the  responsibilities of Ministry of
ARI for a balanced regional growth, however, the Committee expects that the Ministry of ARI would undertake
effective measures for Agro and Rural Industries for striking an equilibrium for balanced regional growth and overall
national economic growth and development.
56.0         EMPLOYMENT GENERATION IN AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
56.1  Under the Khadi and Village industries sector so far approximately 74.01 lakh persons have been provided
employment. Similarly under PMRY employment up to January, 2005 has been generated to the tune of 31.6 lakh
persons. In the Coir sector about 5.8 lakh coir workers are being gainfully employed. The disguised employment in this
sector is primarily of the Khadi artisans whereas in other avenues it is not so pronounced. However, the Government has
not undertaken any survey so far in this regard.
56.2  The Committee is of the considered view that there is the tremendous potential for employment generation in the
Agro and Rural Industries, need is to frame the policy measures and chalking out suitable strategy to harness the
inherent potential of employment generation in the ARI sector. In this regard, the Committee desires the Government
would come out with integrated and holistic programme for employment generation and poverty alleviation. Investment
- employment generation - enhancement in purchasing power - improvement in standard of living and the consequent
poverty alleviation route would root out the inherent problems India’s economy. The Committee hopes that the Ministry
of ARI would understand its responsibility towards changing the status of the country from the developing to a
developed one and act upon with all efforts.
57.0  CO-ORDINATED AND CONCERTED EFFORTS TO TACKLE THE PROBLEM OF
UNEMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION
57.1  In regard to the Committee’s query as to the suggestion of the merger of all Government scheme for employment
generation into one programme in order to undertake co-ordinated efforts to root out the problem of unemployment and
poverty alleviation, the Ministry of ARI explained that the major schemes of employment generation are being
implemented through its agencies by the Ministry of ARI. Poverty alleviation is not the main objective of the schemes
implemented by the Ministry. It certainly is a ‘consequent’ to the programmes of the Ministry. Hence, schemes which
basically aims at poverty alleviation or other related facets but which may result in employment generation are
substantially different from the schemes implemented by the Ministry of ARI and it is submitted that there is
coordination at the Government of India level as well as at the level of implementation with regard to all these schemes
as they are all focused on mutually inclusive geographical area.
57.2  The Committee refers to the concern expressed by the Finance Minister in the General Budget (2005-06) and the
need to tackle the twin problem of unemployment and poverty with focused and co-ordinated approach. The Committee
appreciates the approach of the Finance Minister as stated in the General Budget 2005-06 which is in consonance with
the recommendation of the Committee given in its Report on Demands for Grants (2004-05). The Committee’s

170th Report of Committee On Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/170thReport.htm[04-07-2016 12:54:33]
observation in that report reads as under:-
           “The  Committee is pleased to note that the Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector
and especially the Agro and Rural Industries. The Committee, however, desires that the Government should
come out with pragmatic planning for Agro and Rural Industries keeping in view the twin objectives of
employment generation and poverty alleviation. The Committee wishes to highlight that the Agro and Rural
Industries has the potential of employment generation and since large chunk of Indian population dwells in rural
areas under the abject poverty therefore, holistic and comprehensive planning for rural sector and its effective
implementation is the need of the hour.”           (Para 31.4 of Report No. 152nd)
57.3  The Committee in its 124th Report on Demands for Grants 2003-04 had recommended as under:-
       “The Committee is of the opinion that Government should fix the target under PMRY keeping in mind the
stark reality of population growth rate, quantum of poverty and absolute number of unemployment (disguised
unemployment as well as seasonal employment). Need of the hour is formulation of Integrated and Total
Planning after having objective assessment of empirical fact and figures. The rate of employment generations
must be twice/thrice than the population growth rate so that the problem of unemployment gets out rooted in a
time bound manner. The Committee would be pleased to observe that the planning is done for exploring
employment generation at the geo­metrical rate and population growth be limited at the arithmetical rate.
Though at the first instance the suggestion may seem illusive but to change the fate of India it has to be done and
Government must strive in this direction. This is possible only through co-ordinated and total Planning and when
the problems of Population, Poverty and unemployment are studied and visualized in a holistic manner and
policy-maker has to go beyond the cocoon of department/ministries of the Government.”       (Para 7.6.3 of 124th
Report)
57.4 What the Finance Minister is pronouncing in the General Budget (2005-06), the Committee has been observing and
making recommendations since its report on Demands for Grants 
(2003-04). The Committee therefore, expects that the two wings of the Government should not act in water tight
compartmentalization manner. The problem of unemployment and poverty are intrinsically related to each other
therefore, focused and co-ordinated approach is required, then and only then India’s Developing Economy can be
converted into a developed one at a rapid track and within stipulated time-frame.
58.0         INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
58.1  At the level of Centre-State as well as the Districts there is both structural as well as informal coordination and
exchange of ideas and information. The District level implementing agency for most of the programmes and schemes
devolve at the level of the District Collectors and his offices. Hence, at the District level there is one agency, which
ensures coordination both effectively and efficiently. State-level, again, agencies for coordination are also specified and
interaction relating to policy as well as implementation is ensured. At the apex level also there is frequent and both
formal and informal interaction with the related Ministries to achieve better coordination and collaboration amongst
agencies involved in similar activities. The Ministry of ARI, along with management of its activities, functions on the
basis of its avowed objective/mission, which is to promote and strengthen the Agro and Rural Industries sector.
58.2  The Committee is of the considered opinion the Ministry of ARI must undertake measures for better co-ordination
and collaboration among various agencies/ operating at centre, state and district level so that agro and rural industries
may be given a look of organized sector where all activities can be carried out/managed by stated objectives and
cherished Mission. In this regard, the Ministry of ARI should be guided by Management by Objectives (MBO )and not
merely management by activities.
59.0  “NEW DEAL” FOR RURAL INDIA
59.1  The Prime Minister in his address to the Nation has laid stress on overall growth of the national economy.
Employment generation has been identified as a tool to banish poverty, hunger and homelessness and improve the
standard of living of the mass of our people. The employment should be generated through environmentally sustainable
rural industries. The Prime Minister has also focused on expanding opportunities for gainful employment in agriculture
and in non-farm rural activities.
59.2  Since the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries is functioning in the rural sector, the interaction between farmner
and agro industries has greatly picked up. To improve interaction between farmers and agro industries, KVIC has taken
several measures to strengthen activities in the rural areas like bee-keeping, food processing industries, handmade paper
industries etc. These programmes along with other activities of the Ministry in the agro and rural sector will continue to
receive focus in the Ministry in line with the message enshrined in PMs speech with a view to empower disadvantaged
sections of the society.

59.3  The Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries through its various employment generation programme is focusing on
setting up of industries in the rural areas in the non-farm sector. The Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP)
being implemented by the Ministry of ARI through KVIC since 1995 has successfully generated employment
opportunities to 25.55 lakh persons up to January, 2005. Similarly, under Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY)
since 1993, 31.6 lakh educated persons have been provided employment up to January, 2005.
59.4  The Committee understands that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries is functioning in the rural sector and
thus ARI sector can be a party to the “New Deal” for rural India in respect to rural development and welfare and for
achieving sustained overall annual growth of generating employment. The “New Deal” for rural India would benefit to
the agro rural industries lead to empowerment of disadvantaged sections of the society. The Committee is of the opinion
that suitable steps should be taken to boost the growth of agro based industries and diversification and development of
agro processed products for enhancing it contribution in Bharat Nirman.
60.0  RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FUND (RIDF)
60.1  The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) being operated by NABARD under Ministry of Rural
Development is for the purpose of financing projects like irrigation, flood protection, watershed management,
construction of rural roads and bridges etc. in the rural areas, whereas the Ministry of ARI is concerned with providing
employment in the non-farm sector through setting up of agro and rural industries. As such, the RIDF is not directly
concerned with this Ministry. However, because of better connectivity to be created in the rural areas by way of roads
and bridges under RIDF, the setting up agro and rural industries would definitely be helped in so far as quicker
availability of raw materials and marketing of the products are concerned. This will have spiraling effect on further
growth of agro and rural industries.
60.2  The Committee understands that the announcement of re-launching Rural Infrastructure Development Fund
(RIDF) with a corpus of Rs. 8000.00 crore would go a long way in the proliferation and setting up of new units of agro
and rural industries in the country. Even if the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) is operated by NABARD
under Ministry of Rural Development, the basic infrastructure and better connectivity is to be created in the rural areas
by way of roads and bridges under RIDF, which would lead to promotion and proliferation of ARI in the country. The
Ministry of ARI may co-ordinate with the Ministry of Rural Development for apportioning the fund also in the better
interest of ARI.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
STRENGTHENING AND FUNCTIONING OF THE ARI SECTOR
         The Committee understands that the creation of an independent Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has
reinforced and strengthened the functioning of the ARI sector as a whole, by highlighting its present status and ensuring
timely policy interventions needed. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI should further streamline and
strengthen the ARI sector by ensuring timely and, adequate delivery of credit, technology upgradation, marketing
support in the form of financial support as the mandate of the Ministry of ARI.(Para 1.4)
TARGETS FOR EMPLOYMENT GENERATION
         The Committee is of the view that all efforts should be taken to achieve the targets set for employment generation
under REGP, KVIC and PMRY. Efforts should also be taken that targets under these schemes are evenly distributed
throughout the year.(Para 4.3)
MONITORING MECHANISM
         The Committee is of the view that ARI sector can contribute to the national economy in terms of production and
employment generation through setting up of village industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. The efficacy and
effectiveness of the schemes-largely depends upon intensive review of implementation of the schemes of KVIC, Coir
Board and the PMRY.    (Para 5.8)
INADEQUATE BUDGETARY SUPPORT TO MINISTRY OF ARI
         The Committee expresses its concern over the provision of inadequate budgetary support to Ministry of ARI as the
projected demand was to the tune of Rs. 1150.10 crore against which Rs. 859.00 crore has been provide which may
affect the progress of the programmes undertaken by the Ministry. The Committee is of the considered view that since
ARI has potential for generating more employment opportunities in the rural areas and small towns, the Ministry of ARI
must vigorously and effectively take up the issue with the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance urging for
additional allocation as per requirement at RE Stage.         (Para 5.13)
MODIFICATION IN THE EXISTING CRITERIA OF PMRY SCHEME
         Keeping in view the inflation and general increase in the income level and also the fact that some States like West
Bengal, Gujarat, Pondicherry etc. are running their own self employment schemes with better subsidy provision as
compared to PMRY, the Committee recommends the following modification in the existing criteria of PMRY scheme:
            (i) Enhancement of the eligibility criteria of family income from Rs. 40,000/- per annum to Rs. 1,50,000/- per
annum.
            (ii) Enhancement in project cost ceiling under the scheme may be enhanced from 
Rs. 1,00,000/- to Rs. 2,00,000/- for business sector and from Rs. 2,00,000/- to 
Rs. 5,00,000/- for service and Industry sector.
            (iii) Enhancement in subsidy from Rs. 7,500/- per beneficiary (except for NER, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and
Uttranchal) to Rs. 20,000/- per beneficiary other than NE States, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal.
In case of NE States including Sikkim, J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal, the subsidy ceiling may
be enhanced i.e. Rs. 25,000/- per beneficiary.  (Para 9.2)
UTILIZATION OF FUNDS UNDER THE PMRY SCHEME
         The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI and Ministry of Finance should ensure the optimum
utilization of funds under the PMRY Scheme by basing the release/utilization of funds under the Scheme on
performance/achievement of target by the State/UTs. The funds released to State/UTs should be expensed during the
same year.(Para 10.2)
STATUS OF RECOVERY OF LOANS UNDER PMRY
         The Committee observes that the measures taken by the RBI and Government have not yielded the desired results
as the rate recovery is not satisfactory at all and needs to be imposed. The Ministry mechanism of the banks in the post
sanctioned share has to be strengthened is enhance in recovery.         
                (Para 12.3)
CHANGING THE MINDSET OF BANKERS
         The Committee desires that public sector banks must yield to the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India in
regard to disbursement of loans on the PMRY. The managers at the top level should also direct the branch managers to
adopt client-friendly approach and create such atmosphere that the general opinion about the mindset of the bankers
should itself change. It is possible through making PMRY more popular among the unemployed youth. The Committee
comment the role of RBI for suitable intervention from time to time whereby the RBI issued guidelines for
consumer/client-friendly working of banks. As the banking sector is being empowered with functional autonomy, the

interest of the industries its an objective to serve the nation and not use this functional discretion for denying the
prospective entrepreneurs in harnessing the opportunity for contributing to economic growth and industrial
development.         (Para 13.2)
COORDINATING AND MONITORING THE WORKING OF PMRY
         The Committee further desires that the financial institutions, respective State Governments and the Ministry of
ARI should coordinate and monitor the working of PMRY in such a way as to enable the process of sponsoring,
sanctioning and disbursement of applications by the States and banks by avoiding the stoppage/delay of disbursement in
PMRY on flimsy grounds and for quick disposal of application on the part of DICs and forwarding the same to the
banks. Adequate mechanism may be adopted for timely communication of targets to the banks for necessary action on
their part; coverage of SCs/STs/OBCs under the scheme as per the norms stipulated by the Government of India;
effective orientation programmes conducted by DIC for the target groups at block/taluka level to enlighten/
popularisation of PMRY and giving accordance to the provision of PMRY for advancing loans in the ratio of 50%; 30%
and 20% in respect of industry, service and business sector.         (Para 13.3)
SUBSIDY AND CEILING LEVELS FOR LOANS
         The Committee takes note of the fact that the recommendation of Parliamentary Standing Committee in its report
on Demand for Grants for 2004-05 regarding increase in the subsidy and ceiling levels for loans under business and
industry category are under active consideration of the Government, however, the Committee desires that Government
should expedite the process of its active consideration on the issue.         (Para 14.2)
ASSESSMENT OF SWOT ANALYSIS
         The Committee hopes that the Ministry of ARI and the financial institutions would undertake intensive assessment
of SWOT analysis on working of PMRY and make out strategy for making the scheme successful.         (Para 14.3)
ALLOCATION MORE FUND FOR R&D IN THE KHADI FIELD
         The Committee understands that Khadi has been the mode of national identity since the days of India’s struggle
for Independence, therefore, all programmes for the furtherance of Khadi would amount to enhancing the national
culture, traditions and identity. On this ground, the two major components of Khadi programmes i.e. the rebate and
interest subsidy is desirable (Rs.73.10 crores in 2004-05 and Rs.75.00 crores in 2005-06 as rebate on retail sales of
Khadi and Rs.24.04 crores in 2004-05 and Rs.25.00 crores for the financial year 2005-06 as interest subsidy on bank
finance for Khadi working fund). However, the Committee would like to stress that Government should allocate more
fund for R&D in the Khadi field as the actual expenditure remained confined to the tune of Rs.0.22 crore during the year
2004-05 as the more and more R&D activities would lead to reduction in the cost of production; product
development/modification and diversification enabling the Khadi product to compete with others in the market.         
(Para 15.6)
REBATE AND INTEREST SUBSIDY
         The Committee would also like to give a word of caution to the managers of Khadi industries that since we are
living in the WTO regime, therefore, Khadi Industries should now starts to think to stand on its own without depending
upon rebate and subsidy. Per se the Committee is not against the rebate and interest subsidy but such a caution is based
on the ground realities indicating the need for preparing the Khadi Industries self-sufficient and competitive.         (Para
15.7)
SWOT ANALYSIS OF KHADI INDUSTRIES
         The Committee expects that the Ministry of ARI would take stock of SWOT analysis of Khadi industries and
make all out efforts for combating weaknesses and threats to Khadi industries and capitalize on its strength and
opportunities for fast track promotion and proliferation of Khadi industries in India in general and in the states like
Bihar, Maharashtra and Jharkhand where the Khadi industries has to make its way.         (Para 16.1)
PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY KHADI INDUSTRIES
         The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should take up the issue of requirement of working capital and
budgetary support with the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission for modernisation and renovation of sales
outlets, alongwith the strategy and time-frame to execute the same. Adequate steps must also be taken for modernisation
of Charkhas and looms, for which a separate fund and scheme i.e. modernisation of traditional industries has been
made.         (Para 17.1)
         The Committee feels that conversion of outstanding balance i.e. to the tune of Rs.238.02 crore which was lying as
outstanding balance with Khadi implementing Agencies under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) into working capital
would solve the problem of requirement of working capital to a certain extent.      (Para 17.2)
OTHER VILLAGE INDUSTRIES SWOT ANALYSIS

national economy. The Committee desires the problem of national economy should be tackled through comprehensive
and integrated planning and having coordination and collaboration among Government Departments/Ministries for
effective outcome/result within a stipulated time-frame. Of course, the role of private enterprising units would also be
significant in achieving such national goal, therefore, their participation should also be encouraged.         (Para 20.9)
