INTEREST SUBSIDY FOR KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES COMMISSION (KHADI COMMISSION)
         The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that the institutional credit to KVI sector is just 50 per cent
to 60 per cent of its requirement. It is all the more disturbing due to the fact that despite the RBI’s clear cut and repeated
guidelines on the issue the credit flow to KVI sector. Credit flow has remained far short of actual requirement.
Therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI and KVIC should take up the issue with the financial
institution as the priority basis and ensure that the KVI sector get the credit as per requirement. For calculation of the
credit requirement of khadi institution it must be ensured that there should not be any gap interest subsidy value vis-a­-
vis credit provided by the bank. The Committee recommends that the banks should follow the guidelines of RBI in letter
and spirit for the calculation of the credit requirement of the khadi institution.(Para 37.5)
MARGIN MONEY OVER SUBSIDY UNDER OTHER VILLAGE INDUSTRIES
         The Committee acknowledges the improvement in the scheme of Margin Money over subsidy in lieu of interest as
the Margin Money is provided to both individuals as well as institutions while the subsidy in lieu of interest was meant
only for VI institutions and entrepreneurs were not covered. Since the experience gained so far is quite encouraging and
there is much demand for REGF in the field, the scheme should continue beyond Tenth plan provided no other better
substitute is formulated. The Committee further recommends that KVIC should undertake following actions for
promoting Village Industries :-
            (i)To trigger and strengthen rural industrialization through timely, continuous and appropriate S&T inputs, R&D
support, innovative ideas and technologies for value addition as well as for strengthening academic -
industrial linkages.
            (ii)Proactive steps to give a fillip to the marketing of VI products through brand promotion, exhibitions,
marketing tie up with the Departmental Bhawans and sales outlets, etc.
(Para 38.6)
RURAL EMPLOYMENT GENERATION PROGRAMME (REGP)
         The Committee observes that Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) is reaching to its stabilization
phase and is almost capable of overcoming its teething problems marked at the initial stage of starting of the
programme. The programme is becoming popular with the Bankers as more and more number of beneficiaries are
interested to avail finance under the scheme for establishment of their projects. The Committee desires that the efforts
should be made to make REGP a success to generate additional employment in the Rural Industry Sector, by facilitating
margin money to first generation entrepreneurs financed and under the scheme help should be extended through
Backward & Forward Linkages under the umbrella of KVIC. The Backward & Forward Linkages must include EDP
training, Marketing support through outlets and District/State/Zonal Level exhibitions for display and marketing their
products, Quality Control Assistance, etc. The Committee further recommends for modification in the eligibility criteria
for REGP:-
            (i)At present the lock in period of margin money is two years. It is proposed to extend it to 3 years so that the
sustainability and continuity of project as well as employment can be ensured.
            (ii)Fiscal  concessions in Terms of Tax exemption relating to establishment and running of the units, Octroi
exemption, Transport and Power subsidy may be provided atleast for 3 years.
            (iii)    In each backward block of the District, a Rural Industrial Estate may be established with all infrastructure
support, so that REGP Units can grow without any hurdles.
(Para 40.3)
NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION
         The Committee takes stock of the fact that NPRI which was announced in the budget 
1999-2000 with the objective of setting up of hundred rural industrial clusters in the country every year for boosting
rural economy by creating more employment avenues and to arrest the migration of the rural artisans or town/cities. The
irony of the programme was that no separate fund was made available to implement the programme and it was
conceived that since the various Ministries/Departments are having their own programme in this coveted areas and their
co-ordination and synergistic harnessing would be significant/harness the objectives of the programmes. The result that
comes out is that the expectation regarding the success of the programme felled apart, and that was bound to happen
with the programme without financial support.   (Para 42.6)
         The Committee observes that the co-ordination and synergetic approach so conceived among various Government
Ministries/Departments to make NPRI a success could not succeed the test of the time and the administrative (Ministry
of ARI) which was supposed to implement the NPRI spent no time in screwing the bureaucratic skill for advocating the
countless reasons for unsatisfactory performance of NPRI i.e. meagre financial assistance of Rs. 5.00 lakh for lakh per
cluster for wide intervention, fill in gap arrangements, non-availability of credit linked subsidy component and also the

170th Report of Committee On Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/170thReport.htm[04-07-2016 12:54:33]
inadequate synergy with the Ministries/Departments with their own scheme in this area. When this Committtee
recommended for comprehensive over hauling and synchronization of all schemes and programmes for employment
generation and poverty alleviation, if the Ministry of ARI who beautifully referred the allocation of transaction of
business among various Government’s Ministries/Departments with a stress that sufficient co-ordination and syenergy
exists among various Government’s Ministries / Departments. The Committee wonders as how the same Ministry of
ARI is now wanting out the lakh of co­ordination and synergy as the reason for unsatisfactory performance of NPRI.
This Committee is of the view that logic and argument of the Ministry of ARI is of selective nature.     (Para 42.7)
         Regarding NPRI, the Committee in its Report on Demands for Grants (2004-05) that NPRI has the potential for
actual rural industrialization and consolidation of rural economy and had recommended that the Government should
undertake concrete measures to combat the problems in achieving the objectives, targets credit-flow, implementation
and monitoring mechanism and “Key Concern Areas” of NPRI. But of no avail. Sensing the slow but sure death knell of
the NPRI, the Ministry of ARI has now decided to abandon the so acclaimed programme (NPRI) and the Ministry
comes out with re-christened programme, coincidently, the name of the programme is SFURTI, Scheme of Funds for
Re-generation of Traditional Industries. NPRI had made a slow start, therefore, it seems that the name of the new
programme is carefully drafted as SFURTI, obviously to instill the hope among those who are having their heart in the
efficient working of the Government machinery.       
                (Para 42.8)
         The Committee is awefully shocked to observe the pathetic working of the programmes/ schemes and the
monitoring mechanism as maintained within the Governmental structure which is being imparted to make the
programme a success. The Committee is of the considered view that re-christening of schemes is not the guarantee to
make the new scheme a success unless and until the scheme is backed by adequate financial fund and willing
administrative backup to deliver in the system. The Committee has no objection with launching of new programme like
SFURTI or with whatever names it comes in future but the Committee strongly feels that NPRI has cherished national
goal and appropriate objectives and had no inherent weaknesses/problems as such except the lack of allocation for a
separate fund, the Committee therefore, reiterates that NPRI must continue in order to achieve those goals/objectives
and a separate fund must be allocated to NPRI.      (Para 42.9)
SWOT ANALYSIS OF THE TRADITIONAL INDUSTRIES
         The Committee extends its best wishes for the success of the scheme for re­generation of Traditional Industries
based on cluster development approach and hopes that the programme would make a head start without further delay as
SFURTI has lost one financial year at the drafting/approval stage. The Committee therefore, recommends that the
Ministry of ARI should expedite the process to get the approval of EFC/ cabinet with adequate and required financial
support. The scheme may prove effective in re­generation of traditional industries like coir, handloom, handicrafts,
sericulture, leather, pottery and other cottage industries.(Para 44.4)
         The Committee reiterates that since the artisans are facing various problems including non-availability of timely
credit and raw material, lack of market opportunities, it can be hoped that that the budgetary provision made to the tune
of Rs 27.00 crore in the year 2005-06 would be able to solve the problems faced by the artisans. Moreover, since the
Traditional Industries are functioning in the remote rural areas in a most decentralized manner, efforts should be made
for organizing them under appropriate organizational structure.  (Para 44.5)
LUMPSUM PROVISION FOR PROJECTS SCHEMES FOR THE BENEFIT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION
AND SIKKIM
         The Committee acknowledges that the development of the NER region requires the special attention of the
Government because the region has immense potential but due to lack of communication facilities, poor infrastructure,
difficult terrain etc. have atributed to the region’s economic backwardness. Since the region has lagged behind in
progress as compared to other regions of the country, special attention is required to strengthen and reinforce focused
implementation of various schemes under the ARI sector. Targets under REGP, PMRY coir industries should be
accordingly set for the region.         (Para 47.5)
         The Committee is in agreement with the relaxation in parameters of eligibility which have been made specifically
for this region to ensure effective implementation of schemes specially under PMRY. Performance under various
schemes in the regions must be monitored by the implementing agencies at various level both at the Centre and State in
order to have effective result.         (Para 47.6)
KVIC’S REVAMPING ACTIVITIES IN THE NORTH EASTERN REGION
         The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI and revamped KVIC should not delay much (as two years has
already been elapsed in making the feasibility study ) in undertaking revamping activities in the North Eastern Region
and the scheme on utilization of potential for silk khadi particularly the variety of Endi and Muga Silk must be done in a

170th Report of Committee On Industry

time bound manner.    (Para 48.2)
STRATEGY TO PROMOTE INTER-SECTORAL CO-OPERATION AND ASSISTANCE
         The Committee understands that each Ministry has been interested with specific mandate and each of them
functions on the areas as per the mandate. The Committee also understands that Planning Commission coordinates the
programmes on various issues. However, governance can not be water compartmentalised all together in the cases
where the areas/issues/concerned are of similar nature or overlap each other as is the case with the ARI sector which has
to promote industries in the rural areas and thus generate avenues of employment generation with the ultimate objectives
of poverty alleviation and thus contributing the national economy. Therefore, the Committee is of view that strategy to
promote inter-sectoral co-operation and assistance among Rural Development, poverty alleviation programmes, Food
Processing sector and other such programmes/schemes with the Agro and Rural Sector in order to give greater thrust
and coordinated efforts and synergistic approach towards implementation of rural infrastructural development projects,
employment Generation and Rural Industrialization & Development and poverty-alleviation. The Government should
adopt the Unified and Integrated and holistic approach to strike out the very roots of poverty and undertake the
implementation of well knitted policies/programmes to develop the rural economy with co-ordinated and concerted
efforts, then and only then benefits of the programmes would percolate down to the targets contributing to “Bharat
Nirman”.  (Para 49.4)
“BHARAT NIRMAN”
         The Committee welcomes the announcement of the Finance Minister on Bharat Nirman and is of the opinion that
the implementation of programmes under Bharat Nirman will go a long way forward in developing rural connectivity
and infrastructure, thus providing better access to the rural areas. It will give a boost to marketing goods produced by
rural industries. In fact such initiatives are as much requires as subsidy for setting up rural industries. The Committee
hopes that the programmes on Bharat Nirman would incorporate also the components of Agro and Rural Industries.
(Para 50.2)
SWOT (STRENGTH, WEAKNESS, OPPORTUNITIES AND THREATS) ANALYSIS OF AGRO AND RURAL
INDUSTRIES
         The Committee is of considered opinion that the role of Agro and Rural Industries may be crystallized so as to
inject competitive edge in the system and process of Agro and Rural Industries so that it could play pro-active role in
national economy and in changing the status of Indian economy from developing to a developed one. The Committee
desires that the Ministry of ARI would chalk out Key areas for massive action basing its understanding on the SWOT
analysis of Agro and Rural Industries and should always be guided by Management by Objectives (MBO) and not
merely by Management by Activities (MBA).   (Para 50.4)
IMPACT OF GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALIZATION
         The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI should make strategy to protect the Agro and Rural
Industries from the adverse impact of globalisation and Liberlisation and promote the ARI products in the domestic and
the global market by injecting the required competitive resilience under the WTO regime.     (Para 51.3)
LEGAL FRAMEWORK SUPPORTING OF THE AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
         The Committee hopes that the recommendations of the expert Committee on revamping KVIC would go a long
way in reorienting the organisational and functional pattern of KVIC for the promotion and proliferation of Khadi and
Village Industries.(Para 52.4)
NATIONAL POLICY FOR AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
         The Committee feels that the Ministry of ARI should give serious thought for formulation of National Policy for
Agro and Rural Industries for the growth of rural industries, instead of rejecting the suggestion on the first instance. Had
the every thing been right with the existing policy measures, India’s Agro and Rural Industries would have been in a
better position contributing the national economy and particularly consolidating the rural economy. The Committee
understands that the Ministry through a dynamic process of policy amendments and positioning is consistently
addressing policy initiatives in response tothe changed economic scenario and its challenges, however, the colossal
problem of India is also persisting and that too consistently. Therefore, it is desirable that the Ministry of ARI should act
and not react on the recommendation of the Committee without giving a proper thought to the ideas behind the
recommendations.    (Para 53.2)
INFRASTRUCTURAL FACILITIES
         The Committee is of the view that Ministry of ARI should interact with the concerned sector/department for
facilitating infrastructural facilities, marketing linkages and updated technology to the Agro and Rural Industries.(Para
54.2)
CREDIT FLOW TO AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES

         The Committee feels that the fiscal measures/issues may be undertaken by the Ministry of ARI with the Ministry
of Finance to boost investment in Agro and Rural Industries through credit enabled private investment and enhanced
public investment effective measures for Agro & Rural Industries for striking an equilibrium for balanced regional
growth and overall national economic growth and development.         (Para 55.2)
CONTRIBUTION OF ARI SECTOR
         The Committee acknowledges the contribution of ARI sector and awareness of the responsibilities of Ministry of
ARI for a balanced regional growth, however, the Committee expects that the Ministry of ARI would undertake
effective measures for Agro and Rural Industries for striking an equilibrium for balanced regional growth and overall
national economic growth and development.         (Para 55.4)
EMPLOYMENT GENERATION IN AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
         The Committee is of the considered view that there is the tremendous potential for employment generation in the
Agro and Rural Industries, need is to frame the policy measures and chalking out suitable strategy to harness the
inherent potential of employment generation in the ARI sector. In this regard, the Committee desires the Government
would come out with integrated and holistic programme for employment generation and poverty alleviation. Investment
- employment generation - enhancement in purchasing power - improvement in standard of living and the consequent
poverty alleviation route would root out the inherent problems India’s economy. The Committee hopes that the Ministry
of ARI would understand it responsibility towards changing the status of the country from the developing to a
developed one and act upon with all efforts.     (Para 56.2)
CO-ORDINATED AND CONCERTED EFFORTS TO TACKLE THE PROBLEM OF UNEMPLOYMENT
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION
         The Committee refers to the concern expressed by the Finance Minister in the General Budget 2005-06 and the
need to tackle the twin problem of unemployment and poverty with focused and co-ordinated approach. The Committee
appreciates the approach of the Finance Minister as stated in the General Budget 2005-06 which is in consonance with
the recommendation of the Committee given in its Report on Demands for Grants (2004-05). The Committee’s
observation in that report reads as under:-
“The Committee is pleased to note that the Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector and
especially the Agro and Rural Industries. The Committee, however, desires that the Government should come
out with pragmatic planning for Agro and Rural Industries keeping in view the twin objectives of employment
generation and poverty alleviation. The Committee wishes to highlight that the Agro and Rural Industries has
the potential of employment generation and since large chunk of Indian population dwells in rural areas under
the abject poverty therefore, holistic and comprehensive planning for rural sector and its effective
implementation is the need of the hour.”
(Para 31.4 of Report No. 152nd)
         The Committee in its 124th Report on Demands for Grants 2003-04 had recommended as under:-
“The Committee is of the opinion that Government should fix the target under PMRY keeping in mind the stark
reality of population growth rate, quantum of poverty and absolute number of unemployment (disguised
unemployment as well as seasonal employment). Need of the hour is formulation of Integrated and Total
Planning after having objective assessment of empirical fact and figures. The rate of employment generations
must be twice/thrice than the population growth rate so that the problem of unemployment gets out rooted in a
time bound manner. The Committee would be pleased to observe that the planning is done for exploring
employment generation at the geo­metrical rate and population growth be limited at the arithmetical rate.
Though at the first instance the suggestion may seem illusive but to change the fate of India it has to be done
and Government must strive in this direction. This is possible only through co-ordinated and total Planning and
when the problems of Population, Poverty and unemployment are studied and visualized in a holistic manner
and policy-maker has to go beyond the cocoon of department/ministries of the Government.”
(Para 7.6.3 of 124th Report)
         What the Finance Minister is pronouncing in the General Budget (2005-06), the Committee has been observing
and making recommendations since its report on Demands for Grants 
(2003-04). The Committee therefore, expects that the two wings of the Government should not act in water tight
compartmentalization manner. The problem of unemployment and poverty are intrinsically related to each other
therefore, focused and co-ordinated approach is required, then and only then India’s Developing Economy can be
converted into a developed one at a rapid track and within stipulated time-frame.     (Paras 57.2, 57.3 and 57.4)
INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES

         The Committee is of the considered opinion the Ministry of ARI must undertake measures for better co-ordination
and collaboration among various agencies/operating at center, state and district level so that agro and rural industries
may be given a look of organized sector where all activities can be carried out/managed by stated objectives and
cherished Mission. In this regard, the Ministry of ARI should be guided by Management by Objectives (MBO) and not
merely management by activities.         
                (Para 58.1)
“NEW DEAL” FOR RURAL INDIA
         The Committee understands that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries is functioning in the rural sector and
thus ARI sector can be a party to the “New Deal” for rural India in respect to rural development and welfare and for
achieving sustained overall annual growth of generating employment. The “New Deal” for rural India would benefit to
the agro and rural industries lead to empowerment of disadvantaged sections of the society. The Committee is of the
opinion that suitable steps should be taken to boost the growth of agro based industries and diversification and
development of agro processed products for enhancing it contribution in Bharat Nirman.         (Para 59.4)
RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FUND (RIDF)
         The Committee understands that the announcement of re-launching Rural Infrastructure Development Fund
(RIDF) with a corpus of Rs. 8000.00 crore would go a long way in the proliferation and setting up of new units of agro
rural industries in the country. Even if the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) is operated by NABARD
under Ministry of Rural Development, the basic infrastructure and better connectivity is to be created in the rural areas
by way of roads and bridges under RIDF, which would lead to promotion and proliferation of ARI in the country. The
Ministry of ARI may co-ordinate with the Ministry of Rural Development for apportioning the fund also in the better
interest of ARI.         (Para 60.2)

INTRODUCTION
           I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised by the
Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Seventy first Report on Demands for Grants (2005-06) pertaining to the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries.
2.      The Committee in its meeting held on 30 th March, 2005 heard the Secretary, Ministry of SSI and the representative of the attached
organisations/offices of the Ministry on the issue of Demands for Grants 
(2005-06). A detailed questionnaire was forwarded to the Ministry of SSI which were accordingly replied. The report has been prepared
on the basis of the replies received from the Ministry and the oral evidence of the Ministry of SSI on the various aspect  of the budgetary

REPORT
1.1    The Small Enterprises sector is a vibrant segment of the Indian economy which contributed over 39 per cent of the industrial sector
output and 34 per cent of the nation’s exports, and provided employment to over 270 lakh persons through 114 lakh units (2003-04)
spread both in rural and urban areas of the country. The major contribution of the small enterprises sector lies in creation of employment
opportunities at lower per capita capital cost. Alongwith agriculture, the small enterprises sector including both SSI and services provides
the largest employment generation potential in the country. During 2003-04, the small enterprises sector registered a growth rate of 8.6
per cent as against a growth rate of 7.0 per cent for the overall industrial sector.
1.2    To enhance their competitiveness both in domestic and global markets by facilitating technological upgradation and adoption of
international quality standards, the investment ceiling in some high-tech and export oriented SSI units has been raised from Rs. 1 crore to
Rs.5 crore in respect of stationery, drugs and Pharmaceuticals, hand tools & knitwear. Various sub-sectors of the SSI are Ancillary
Industrial Undertakings, High-Tech And Export Oriented Units, Tiny Enterprises, Small Scale Service and Business (Industry Related)
Enterprises, etc.
1.3    In the context of globalisation and for facilitating growth with wider employment generation, there is a growing realization that
India should also adopt the SME concept. On 9 th January 2004, the then Finance Minister announced the establishment of a fund of Rs.
10,000 crore for the SME sector. While presenting the budget for 2004-05, the Finance Minister observed that there was need to provide
some space for small-scale industries (SSIs) to grow into medium enterprises.
1.4    The Committee understands that the Small Scale Industries is today on the move world wide, therefore, Small Scale
Industries in India should be given top priority by the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance in plan-allocation so
that small scale units may get adequate space for maturing into medium enterprises to catch the global trend. The Ministry of
SSI should provide the logistic support to the SSI sector. The Ministry of Small Scale Industries must strengthen the SSI sector to
enable it to remain competitive in market-led economy and generate additional employment opportunities. The Ministry should
assist the SSI sector in accessing (or provide) proper and timely inputs like adequate credit from financial institutions banks;
funds for technology up-gradation and modernization; adequate infrastructural facilities; modern testing facilities and quality
certification laboratories; modern management practices and skill up-gradation through suitable training facilities; marketing
assistance; and level playing field at par with the large industries sector.
2.0    ORGANISATIONAL SET-UP AND RETRAINING OF STAFF
2.1    The Ministry of SSI designs policies, programmes, projects and schemes in consultation with its organizations and various
stakeholders and monitors their implementation with a view to assisting the promotion and growth of small scale industries. The Ministry
also performs the function of policy advocacy on behalf of the SSI sector with other Ministries/Departments of the Central Government
and the States and Union Territories.
2.2    The Ministry of Small Scale Industries designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for the promotion and
growth of small scale industries. The implementation of policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructural and
support services to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached offices, namely Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO), its field offices, and National Small Industries Corporation Limited (NSIC), a public sector undertaking under the Ministry of
SSI.
2.3    The Committee feels that the organizational set-up of the Ministry must be made effective through reorientation of form
and retraining of staff to enable them to make full use of the opportunities and challenges fast emerging liberalization and
globalization process under post-WTO-regime by undertaking following steps:—

            (ii)    ascertaining best practices within the Central Government and also abroad for promotion and development of SME
sector and their adoption/adaptation in the Indian SME context;
            (iii)   closer and more structural interaction with the stakeholders;
            (iv)   improving synergies among the constituent organization of the Ministry and the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries;                                                                                                                
            (v)    promoting constructive competitiveness among field-level organizations based on well defined objectives and action

to the promotion and consolidation of Small Scale Industries. The reduced allocation may already affect the implementation of
these schemes.
3.4    The Committee however understands the financial crunch with the Government and the consequent problems being faced
by the Planning Commission in judicious and equitably allocation among various Departments/Ministries as per their
requirement.
3.5    The Committee is of the opinion that even the Planning Commission would appreciate the potential of Small Scale Industry
in the employment generation and its contribution to the poverty alleviation. It is not a secret that SSI sector is the fate-fixture of
common man as the SSI units require low investment but effects the lives of millions. Therefore, the question of resurrection of
the SSI sector would mean the improvement in the standard of living of millions. Moreover, the global trend of promoting the
SSI sector is an observable fact. The Finance Minister of India is even tired of stressing the need for providing SSI sector the
adequate space to grow and thrive as medium enterprises therefore, the Committee feels that the Ministry of SSI should get the
sufficient line allocation to implement its schemes/programmes.
3.6    The Committee is also of the opinion that there is a need for better coordination between the Ministry of SSI, the Ministry
of Finance, Planning Commission so that the financial requirement of SSI sector is well communicated to the Planning
Commission as per the actual requirement of SSI sector. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry of SSI should
take up the matter with the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance at the RE Stage for plan allocation as per the basic
needs of SSI sector.

4.3    The Committee is in agreement with the revision in the Tenth Five Year Plan target of annual growth rate of Twelve per
cent and additional employment of 44 lakh for the SSI Sector. The Committee is however constrained to note that the revised
growth is yet to be achieved. The Committee therefore desires that resilient monitory mechanism must be set up for timely and
effective implementation of schemes/programmes/Action Plan on whose assumption the revised target has been set up. Since SSI
Sector is emerging as one of the largest employment provider after agriculture, therefore, all Governmental impetus must be
given on the promotion of SSI sector, recognizing and treating SSI as a “real Engine of national growth and development”.
4.4    There is no major policy shift for the year 2004-05 as compared to 2003-04. The endeavor of the Ministry is to strengthen and
facilitate the SSI sector to enable it to remain competitive in the global economy and generate additional employment. The national
economic policy, as enunciated in the National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP) and in the Budget Speeches of the Finance
Minister is, in the context of the SSI sector, focused on employment generation, technology Upgradation and marketing and credit
support to the sector. The budget allocation, accordingly, has been raised to Rs. 408.91 (exclusive of Rs. 3.35 crore for Works Outlay
provided in the Demands of Ministry of Urban Development) crore in 2005-06 compared to Rs. 362.25 crore (exclusive of Rs. 3.75 crore
for Works Outlay provided in the Demands of Ministry of Urban Development) in 2004-05. Efforts are being made to achieve the goals
of NCMP to facilitate the growth of the sector, which in turn will generate employment.
4.5    To address the issues flowing from the process of liberalization and gloablisation for the SSI sector and to assist the sector to
function in a competitive environment, emphasis has been given on technology upgradation of the SSI units. An enhanced budget
provision of Rs.l 8 crore has been provided during 2005-06 under the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS). A budget
provision of Rs.22.61 crore has also been provided in 2005-06 under the ISO 9000/14000 Reimbursement Scheme. Under the Scheme, a
maximum grant of Rs.75,000 is provided to the SSI units for adopting ISO-9000/14000 quality and environment standards to help them
become globally competitive.
4.6    To help the SSI sector face the challenges posed by liberalisation and globalisation, the Government has been taking several policy
initiatives. These include dereservation of items reserved exclusively for manufacture in the SSI sector in a phased manner, enhancing the
investment limit in plant and machinery from Rs.l crore to Rs.5 crore in 71 select hi-tech and export oriented sectors, etc. The
Government is also in the process of finalizing a Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005 to facilitate the promotion and
development of these enterprises and enhance their competitiveness.
4.7    In the Budget 2005-06, the allocations for ‘Promotion of SSI Schemes’ has been enhanced to Rs.l73 crore from Rs.135 crore
provided in 2004-05. Further, SIDBI has established a SME Growth Fund to provide equity support to the small and medium units in the
knowledge- based industries such as pharma, biotech, IT, etc. The above measures would help in promotion and development of small
and medium units and also setting up of new units in the emerging areas of pharma, biotech, IT, etc, leading to generation of more
employment opportunities. In addition a Budget provision of Rs.200 crore (including NE Region) has been made for Credit Guarantee
Fund Trust Scheme, which covers collateral free credit facility (term loan/working capital) extended by eligible lending institutions to
new and existing SSI units. This would help in removing the problem of collaterals  faced by the first generation entrepreneurs,
particularly in the tiny sectors as well as in enhancing the credit flow to the SSI sector.
4.8    The Committee understands that the SSI has to grow and thrive in the global competitive environment unleashed by the
globalization and liberalization process, therefore, concerted efforts should be made for holistic and integrated course of action
for consolidation and promotion of SSI sector by focusing on searching avenues for employment generation on the one hand and

11.1  The inclusion of services and the enlargement of the scope of the Ministry to medium establishment are important in the context of
the emergence of sunrise knowledge-based industries as the harbinger of a new industrial revolution. New knowledge based industries
like Pharmaceuticals and biotechnology industries to be internationally competitive and will require encouragement and support in the
initial period of their development. The emergence of IT and of software in a large way in this country also suggests the need for bringing
the service sector prominently into the ambit of encouragement and support given to small and medium establishments.
11.2  The Committee is of the view that the Government should re-christen the name of Ministry of SSI into the Ministry of Small
and Medium Enterprises (SME) in order to implement the objectives, achievement and targets of Indian SMEs as set by Finance
Minister in General Budget 2005-06. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech 2005-06 also stated that “In recent years, our
approach to small scale industry has evolved, and now we are inclined to treat the sector as the small and medium enterprises
sector”, the Committee is of the view that creation of two separate Departments, e.g., Department of Small Scale Industries and
the Department of Medium Enterprises under the re-christened name of the Ministry of Small and Medium Enterprises and
same could be effectively monitored by the present Ministry directly. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech 2004-05 stated
that “Small scale industry is, and must be regarded as, an engine of growth. At the same time SSI units must also be given the
space to grow into medium enterprises. World over, policies are devised to meet the requirements of small and medium
enterprises (SME)”. The Committee also endorses the view of the Finance Minister and the scope of Ministry of SSI should be
enlarged to cover the service sector in addition to the manufacturing sector to define and include medium establishment.

15.0  ROLE AND RELEVANCE OF THE OFFICE OF DC (SSI)
15.1  The Office of the Development Commissioner (Small Scale Industries) [DC (SSI)] is an attached office of the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries and performs a dual role. On the one hand, it advised the Government on formulation of appropriate policies, schemes,
projects and programmes and, on the other, implements these policies, schemes, etc., for the overall development of the small enterprises.
15.2  The Office of the DC (SSI) currently maintains liaison with the Central Ministries, Planning Commission, State Governments and
financial institutions through the Ministry as well as directly, as per requirement. Secretary (SSI) is a member of the Standing Advisory
Committee of the RBI, which deals with the credit policy for the small scale sector. DC (SSI) is on the Board of Directors of the SIDBI.
Each Director, SISI in the State is a member of the State Level Inter-Institutional Committee, which deals with the revival of sick SSI
units. These arrangements are adequate.
15.3  The Office of DC (SSI) maintain liasion with the Central Ministries, planning Commission, state Governments and
Financial Institution. DC (SSI) is on the Board of Directors of the SIDBI. Each Director, SISI in the State is a member of the
State Level Inter-Institutional Committee, which deals with the revival of sick SSI units. Steps may be undertaken to strengthen
and streamline the liasion mechanism of office of SSI for the furtherance of Small Scale Industries.
15.4  The monitoring mechanism currently in operation includes regular reviews of the performance of individual schemes at various
levels within the Office of the DC(SSI) through periodical meetings, field visits, seminars on selected topics, etc. Periodical interaction
with the State Governments and associations of enterprises also constitutes part of the monitoring mechanism. Finally, periodical reviews
are conducted in the Ministry with DC(SSI) and other officers of the Ministries of SSI and ARI.
15.5  Monitoring mechanism steered by office of DC (SSI) as an apex body for formulating, 
co-ordinating and monitoring policies and programmes for promotion and development of Small Scale Industries in the country.
While the basic structure and process of the monitoring mechanism are adequate, the same may be further strengthened and
streamlined by taking into account the experience of implementation of the proposed legislation, viz, the Small and Medium
Enterprises Development Bill.
16.0  NATIONAL SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES BOARD
16.1  The scope of the policies and programmes for the development of the SSI sector extends over several Departments /Ministries and
Organisations of Central/State Governments. To facilitate co-ordination and inter-institutional linkages, the Small Scale Industries Board
has been constituted. It is an apex advisory body, constituted to render advice to the Government on all issues pertaining to the small
scale sector. The Board meets periodically. The Board has so far met 48 times till January 2004, and has been discharging its functions
satisfactorily.
16.2  The Committee acknowledges the functioning of National Small Scale Industries Board in facilitating co-ordination and
inter-institutional linkages, however, its role may be made more effective and instrumental in organizing the Small Scale Sector.
It would be helpful in enlightening the understanding the small scale industries, if the major decision of the National Small Scale
Industries Board is made known to this Committee.
17.0  STATUS OF POLICY PACKAGE ANNOUNCED BY PRIME MINISTER ON 30
TH AUGUST, 2000
17.1  Out of the 29 action points, which emerged out of the Policy Package announced by the Prime Minister on 30 th August 2000, action
has already been completed on 27 points, which include enhancement of excise exemption from Rs.50 lakh to Rs.100 lakh,
implementation of 12 per cent Capital Subsidy Scheme for technology up-gradation, credit guarantee for loans up to Rs.25 lakh, raising
the composite loan limit to Rs.25 lakh (now it is Rs.100 lakh), raising of project cost limit under National Equity Fund to Rs.50 lakh,
extension of Integrated Infrastructural Development (IID) Scheme, establishment of new testing centres with involvement of Industry
Associations, introduction of Market Development Assistance Scheme for Small Scale Industries. (MDA-SSI), conduct of 3rd Census and
enhancement of investment limit for SSSBEs from Rs.5 lakh to Rs. 10 lakh.
17.2  The Comprehensive Policy Package was announced in order to help the growth of the small enterprises and enable them to face the
challenges of growing national/international competition. Major strength of the policy package 2000 is that it provided much needed
support to the SSI Sector due to which it could sustain the pressure of opening of economy and WTO regime and grew on a faster rate
than the overall industrial sector. The number small units which was more than 97 lakhs during 1999-2000 was more than 113 lakhs
during 2003-04. Similarly the production grew from Rs.2,34,255 crores at current prices to Rs.3,57,733 at current prices, employment
from more than 229 lakh to more than 271 lakh persons during the same period. Exports also grew from Rs. 54,200 crore in 1999-2000 to
Rs.86,013 crore in 2002-03. Opportunities include up coming of sunrise industries like IT and service sector.
17.3  However, there still remain certain weaknesses which need to be addressed. These are non-availability of sufficient and timely

18.0  THIRD CENSUS OF SSIS (2001-02) AND NEED FOR NATIONAL POLICY FOR SMALL INDUSTRIES
18.1  The Third All India Census of Small Scale Industries for the First time made an estimation of the unregistered sector also, based on
a sample survey. It revealed that out of the total 105.21 lakh units, 13.75 lakh were registered units and the remaining 91.46 lakh
unregistered. Out of the 22.62 lakh registered units, 13.75 (61 per cent) were found to be working. 39 per cent were found to be closed
(though the reasons or periods of such closure were not elicited during the census. 99.5 per cent of the total SSI units comprised tiny
units, viz., with investment upto Rs. 25 lakh. The total employment provided by the sector was 249.32 lakh of which 61.63 lakh were in
the registered sector and 187.69 lakh were in the unregistered sector. The total gross output was Rs. 2,82,26,998 lakh with the share of
the registered sector at 72 per cent and the contribution of the unregistered sector at 28 per cent. The share of the service sector
comprising the SSSBEs constituted nearly 58 per cent of the total number of units. The bulk (92 per cent) of the SSSBEs were in the
unregistered sector. Within the registered sector, 56 per cent of the units were in urban areas and 44 per cent in rural areas. Most of the
units were proprietary concerns, both in the registered and unregistered sectors. While about 89 per cent of the registered units were
proprietary concerns, 97 per cent of the unregistered-sector were in this category.
18.2  The results of the Third Census throw light on the structure and characteristics of SSI sector. The unregistered sector, which
constitutes almost 87 per cent of the total units, has remained largely outside the net of official statistics and also not benefited from the
various policy measures formulated for the support and development of SSI. This would be evident from the fact that the number of units
having outstanding loan with institutional credit within the unregistered sector was only 3.09 per cent. Even within the registered sector,
the extent of accessibility to institutional credit is low. Only 14.26 per cent of the registered units were availing of institutional credit.
Using the definition of sick units given by the Kohli Committee appointed by the RBI, i.e., number of units with erosion of net worth by
more than 50 per cent or delay in repayment of institutional loan by more than 12 months, it was found that 17.8 per cent of the units
having outstanding loan with institutional sources were sick.
18.3  Information was collected from the units about the source from which technical know- how was obtained by them. More than 85
per cent of the registered units indicated that they were dependent on traditional technology/skills. The registered sector showed that 36
per cent of the units had their plant and machinery installed during the seventies and eighties. 26 per cent of the registered units were not
using power as against 42 per cent in the unregistered sector. This is a pointer to the gap in technology upgradation which needs to be
remedied.
18.4  About 63.45 per cent of the registered units were in manufacturing/assembling/processing as compared with 36.12 per cent in the
unregistered sector. The registered sector had only a small share (2.10 per cent) in repairs and maintenance as compared with a higher
share (18.50 per cent) in the unregistered sector. Services constituted an important category with the share of the registered and
unregistered sectors at 34.45% and 45.38% respectively. The emergence of a vibrant service sector (SSSBE) merits special attention.  The
findings of the Third Census have shown that the unregistered sector has overtaken the registered sector in terms of the size (number of
units) and employment. However, the registered sector is significant in terms of contribution to output, which is almost 72% of the total
output.
18.5  The Committee is of the view that the national policy and programmes/schemes should be suitable, and effective for
supporting the promotion and development of small scale industries. The main emphasis should be on easy credit availability,
technological Upgradation and modernization, Infrastructural development, marketing support, etc. Moreover, for uniform and
sustainable growth of small scale industries with an objective for greater employment creation and equitable distribution of
wealth all over the country, there is a need for a national policy for small industries. To address the needs in the changed
economic scenario, the Government must come out with a promotional policy package at the earliest. The findings of the Third
Census can be used for policy formulation as follows:-
            (i)     Liberalise credit policy to make institutional credit more accessible to SSI units, including the unregistered units,
            (ii)    Identify industries requiring technological upgradation which can be assisted either under the on-going
programmes/schemes or new appropriate schemes for the same,
            (iii)   Target sub-sectors which have high employment potential, for assistance under different schemes.
            (iv)   Assistance for improving quality and productivity, especially of registered units which account for bulk of the output.

            (vii) Evolve a system for regular collection of data through sample surveys at shorter intervals.

20.0  EFFORTS OF DC (SSI) ON DEVELOPMENT OF ACCREDITED CLUSTERS
20.1  Cluster can be defined as a sectoral and geographical concentration of enterprises, in particular small and medium facing common
opportunities and threats. 1. Cluster Development approach has been recognized as an effective tool for development of small scale
sector in India and abroad also. There are successful precedents of cluster development in Italy , Taiwan and few other countries. Abid
Hussain Committee and Dr. S.P. Gupta Committee Reports as a development tool in Indian industrial scenario have also advocated this
approach.
20.2  As per the 3
rd All India Census of SSI units conducted in 2001-02, there are 1223 clusters in Manufacturing Registered SSI Sector
having 285150 number of units and 819 clusters in unregistered SSI Sector having 12,50207 number of units. As per the estimates of
UNIDO there are about 388 clusters.
20.3  Cluster Development initiatives in India are being undertaken by various agencies like ”Ministry of Small Scale Industries,
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, UNIDO, State Government, financial institutions etc. Under cluster development a
holistic approach is adopted to address identified needs of a particular cluster. To find out needs of the cluster, a diagnostic study is
carried out in the cluster by Cluster Development agent(s). Under this diagnostic study report, the problems of Cluster are identified,
solutions are suggested and action plan is drawn in consultation with various stakeholders including Associations, Representatives of
Industry, financial Institutions etc. Generally the interventions are undertaken in areasTechnology Upgradation, Market
Development,Capacity Building.
20.4  Small Scale Industries contribute significantly in industrial production of the country. They produce a variety of products ranging
from traditional to hi-tech. Although the volume of production from Small Scale Industries is quite large, the quality of the product,
productivity, energy and environmental issues has always been a concern. These concerns have accentuated with the opening of the
economy where productivity and quality play a major role for the survival of the Small Scale Industries. The Office of the Development
Commissioner (Small Scale Industries) has launched a scheme namely the ‘Integrated Technology Upgradation and Management
Programme’ (UPTECH) in 1998, now renamed as ‘Small Industry Cluster Development Program’. The scheme applies to any cluster of
industries where there is a commonality in the method of production, quality control and testing, energy conservation, pollution control
etc. among the units of the cluster. The scheme aims to take care of the modernisation and the technological needs of the cluster. It covers
a comprehensive range of issues related to technology upgradation, improvement of productivity, energy conservation, pollution control,
product diversification and their marketing, training needs etc.
20.5  The Office of DC (SSI) has started a number of Cluster Development initiatives under with holistic approach and active
involvement of beneficiary units through their Associations in their implementation. The activities taken up for development of the
clusters are demand-based. The programmes viz Programme for Development of Rajkot Engineering Cluster; National Programme for
the Development of Indian Machine Tool Industry; National Programme for the Development of Indian Lock Industry; Auto
Components Development Programme, Chennai are being implemented by DC (SSI).

20.6  In regard to the fate of 60 clusters identified by DC (SSI) and submitted to RBI for improving the flow of credit therein, the
Ministry of SSI stated that The RBI had sought the Ministry of SSI’s advice regarding selection of 60 SSI clusters to be identified for
coordinated approach towards meeting their credit requirements. It was also decided that RBI will disseminate the list of such clusters to
all Public Sector Banks for initiating further necessary action and incorporating their credit requirements in State Credit Plans. At the
State Level Bankers Committee (SLBC), a sub group of bankers and the State Government officials will be set up to resolve various
issues arising on financing in the clusters and to report the development to SLBC.
20.7  Accordingly, the Ministry selected 60 clusters from all over the country including the backward areas and the North-Eastern
Region. The list has been forwarded to the RBI for dissemination of public sector banks for incorporating the credit requirements of
clusters in the State Credit Plans. It has also been recommended that one Lead Bank be identified for each cluster for coordinating the
Credit Plan.
20.8  The Ministry has also sensitized the concerned State Secretaries/Directors of Industries by writing to them to draw their attention to
implementing the decision of incorporating the credit requirements of SSI units in the identified clusters in the State Credit Plan. At the
SLBC’s meetings, issues relating to credit to SSI sector are coordinated by the State Secretary/Director of Industries. The latter have been
requested to impress upon the Convenor of SLBC to make assessment of the needs of SSIs in the clusters in consultation with other
banks, formulate Annual Credit Plan for the identified clusters in their State and get it incorporated in the State Credit Plan. The State
Governments have also been requested to develop a monitoring mechanism for effective implementation of cluster Credit Plan.
20.9  The Committee welcomes the proposal for selection for 60 cluster by DC (SSI) and which has been forwarded to RBI for
clearance and instructing Public Sector banks for providing adequate credit flow. It is hoped that RBI would expedite the process
at the earliest. The Committee is of the strong view that the cluster development initiatives would lead to technology up-gradation
design development, up-gradation of skills, increased production and export and enhancement of competitiveness of the clusters.
A resilient monitoring mechanism is required to achieve the desired success on cluster approach.

22.0  CREDIT RATING SYSTEM FOR SSI
22.1  NSIC in consultation with the various stake holders i.e. Small Industries Associations, Indian Banks Association and various Rating
Agencies has formulated a Rating Scheme for Small Scale Industries in the country. The rating methodology shall cover a combination of
credit and performance factors including parameters measuring operational, financial, business and management risks. The scheme titled
as 
“PERFORMANCE & CREDIT RATING SCHEME FOR SMALL INDUSTRIES” has been approved by the Government in the month
of October, 2004. As per the approval of the Government, the fee charged by the rating agencies to carry out the rating of the SSI units
shall be subsidized to the following extent:

22.2  The Indian Banks Association has accorded its consent to support the scheme. NSIC has already empanelled six rating agencies i.e.
CARE, CRISIL , D&B, FITCH, ICRA and ONICRA to carry out the rating of the interested SSI units under the scheme. NSIC has
started implementing the scheme through organizing ‘Open Houses’ involving various SSI Associations, Rating Agencies and individual

22.3  The Committee is very positive in its expectation for the success of credit rating system for SI sector and in this regard the
role of credit rating agencies CARE, CRISIL , D&B, FITCH, ICRA and ONICRA would be crucial. The Committee recommends

25.0  MARKET SHARE OF SSI PRODUCTS
25.1  The Committee is of the view that for enhancing the market share of SSI products
in domestic and international market, the following areas need to be focused:-
            (i)     Providing full credit, technology up-gradation, modernization and marketing support to the SSI sector;
            (ii)    Infrastructure up-gradation in general, particularly in the major SSI industrial clusters;
            (iii)   Freedom from the plethora of rules and regulations existing in the SSI sector, which is known as Inspector Raj;

26.0  SWOT ANALYSIS ON THE WORKING OF NSIC.
         Strengths
            (i)     A National level organization with indepth knowledge of small industries sector;
            (ii)     The only ISO 9001 certified small industry facilitator in the Country and one of the few in Asia;
            (iii)     Integrated package of services, ranging from financial inputs to marketing of the final products manufactured by the small-
scale units;
            (iv)    Strong linkages with small industry organizations/associations within the country and several partner organizations
overseas;
            (v)    Proven track record in the area of international cooperation in small industries development and institutional capacity
building;
            (vi)    Network of offices throughout the country; and
            (vii)   Considerable physical assets base.
         Weaknesses
            (i)     Small resource base as compared to financial institutions and banks handling financial activities for SSI Sector;
            (ii)     No access to low cost funds renders NSIC uncompetitive in financing activities;
            (iii)    Surplus man power at lower levels, a large proportion of which is poorly educated and therefore, not easy to retrain or
redeploy;
            (iv)    Inadequate  skill levels at all levels in the organization to cope with the professional challenges especially competitiveness
issues;
            (v)    Limited options to induct professional and competent manpower due to existing surpluses and Government salary scales -
impacts on the core competency; and
            (vi)    Indiscipline and integrity problems in past eroded credibility.

            (i)     Opening of the markets has created large opportunities for small industries. The requirements of the sector will also grow

            (v)    Infomediary Services present an important untapped area of business opportunities. NSIC can create a niche in this field as

            (i)     Competition from commercial banks and other financial institutions in the areas of financing and few State-level

26.1  The major problems being faced by the NSIC are:-
            (i)     Surplus man power at lower levels, large proportion of which is poorly educated and therefore not easy to retrain and
redeploy. The Corporation is faced with the problem of a large employee base that possesses inadequate skills to operate
the schemes of the Corporation in present competitive environment. This also leads to high overheads (including staff
cost) per employee. Due to excess staff at lower level, it is not possible to employ /induct professional staff in required
areas like marketing, technology and other vital business development areas. In the last 5 years, 292 employees have
availed VRS but NSIC still has large pockets of idle manpower that is not willing to adopt this option.
            (ii)     A limited resource base, which is inadequate to service the small-scale sector spread across the country in comparison with
the other financial institutions and banks engaged in financing the small-scale sector.
            (iii)    NSIC does not have access to low cost funds which affects the profitability of the corporation.
            (iv)    Even though NSIC is expected to play a pivotal role in area of marketing, the bulk buyers from the Government
Departments/Agencies are not responsive in matters of making purchases through the small scale units registered under
NSIC Single Point Registration Scheme.
26.2  The Committee acknowledges of the role of NSIC. However, following measures may help NSIC in fulfilling its role more
effectively:-
            (i)     Greater flexibility to the NSIC Board to induct professionals in order to build the internal competency levels.
            (ii)    NSIC should be declared a nodal agency for purchases by Government Departments/Agencies. This will enable NSIC
to play an effective role in marketing the products of the SSI sector.
            (iii)   NSIC should be treated at par with SSIDCs in matters relating to allocation  of Steel and other raw materials. At
present, allocation of steel is made to NSIC only in those states where SSIDCs do not exist.
            (iv)   The Components of NSIC programmes should incorporate identification of new markets, Consortia and Brand
building, Quality assurance and rating Cluster specific catalogues.
            (v)    Business development services must extend in the areas of Marketing, Credit Technology, Infomediary services,
International partnerships.

40.0  PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY SIDO IN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF SCHEMES/ PROGRAMMES
ENCOURAGING SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
40.1  SIDO is implementing several schemes/programmes for the promotion and development of the SSI sector in the country. Most of
these schemes/programmes are aimed at augmenting the credit flow to the SSI sector and are linked with the banks/financial institutions.
The banks are, however, not favourably inclined to finance the SSI sector for various reasons like adverse risk perception, lack of credit
rating facilities, higher transaction cost in processing of large number of loan applications, etc. Moreover, some of the schemes are
optional for the banks to participate in their implementation. Furthermore, the implementation of the schemes/programmes is also
dependent on the willingness of the beneficiaries (i.e. the SSI units/ entrepreneurs) and the State Governments. The State Governments
have a major role to play in the implementation of some of the schemes/programmes by way of providing matching financial
contribution, Infrastructural facilities, fiscal incentives/concessions etc.
40.2  The Ministry of SSI has already initiated the process of formulating a scheme on credit rating, which includes providing financial
assistance to the SSI units for obtaining credit rating. The Ministry of SSI has taken up the matter with all the Public Sector Banks for
dissemination of information on schemes/programmes at the branch level and among the SSI entrepreneurs. The SSI Associations have
also been asked to play a pro-active role in increasing awareness about the schemes/programmes/facilities being implemented for the SSI
sector among the SSI entrepreneurs. The Ministry of SSI is in the process of finalizing a Draft Small and Medium Enterprises
Development Bill, 2005, which is aimed at minimizing the plethora of rules, regulations and laws to be complied by the SSI
units/entrepreneurs. The same would be introduced for the consideration of the Parliament shortly. Besides, a promotional package for
the Small scale sector is under preparation.
40.3  The Committee understands that most of the schemes/programmes as implemented by SIDO aims at augmenting the credit
flow to the SSI sector and are linked with the banks/financial institutions. To enhance the credit flow to the SSI sector and at the
same time improve the comfort level of the banks to extend more credit to the SSI units/entrepreneurs, there is a need to

42.1  The Credit Guarantee Scheme was announced on 30 August 2000 and became operational in January 2001.The Objective of the
Credit Guarantee Scheme is to ensure better flow of credit to small and tiny enterprises by minimizing the risk perception of financial
institutions. This will give greater comfort level to banks and also help financing without collateral security. The Mechanism by setting
up a corpus fund with contribution from the Government of India and the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) in the
ratio of 4:1. At present, the size of the corpus fund is Rs. 931.55 crore. The Operating Agency is the Trust set up by SIDBI/GOI and
serviced by SIDBI. CMD, SIDBI is the Chairman of the Trust; AS & DC (SSI) is the Vice-Chairman of the Trust; two other members are
Chairman, Indian Banks’ Association (IB A) and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Trust. The Modus Operandi is that the lending
institutions can have loans guaranteed by payment of one-time guarantee fee of 2.5 per cent and an annual service fee of 0.75 per cent of
the credit sanctioned to the Trust, the implementing agency. All Commercial Banks - public and private, select regional rural banks
(RRBs), North East Development Finance Corporation (NEDFC), National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) and SIDBI are eligible
under the scheme. Claim Settlement is done after 2-year lock-in period; settlement up to 75 per cent pending recovery proceedings,
balance 25 percent on completion of recovery proceedings. The extent of guarantee is 75 per cent of loans up to Rs.25 lakh. The
maximum risk cover is 75 per cent of the risk cover subject to a ceiling of Rs. 18.75 lakh. Interest rate payable by borrower not to exceed
3 per cent beyond PLR of lender.
42.2  It is estimated that the loans guaranteed by the Trust were instrumental in creating around 93,200 new job opportunities as at 28
February 2005. The major beneficiaries under the scheme are in the tiny sector comprising of rural artisans, self-employed entrepreneurs,
etc. The progress of the scheme is monitored by the Trust and the Ministry of SSI on monthly basis. The National Advisory Committee
(NAC) of CGTSI, consisting of representatives from the Government, SIDBI, RBI, IBA, banks, experts/professionals and small
enterprises associations, also reviews the implementation of the scheme periodically. IBA Review Forum also assists in implementation
of the scheme through coordination between the banking industry and Trust.
42.3  The Committee understands that one of the main objectives of the scheme is to generate more employment opportunities by
facilitating collateral free loans to small enterprises. However, despite the provision of the loans up to 25.00 lakh without
collateral/third party guarantee and the guidelines of the Reserve Bank of India thereto, Banks are reported to insist on the
collateral security and the third party guarantee. The committee has repeatedly recommended for a change of the mind set of the
Branch Manager, nothing fruitful has come out so far. The Committee directs all the Banks who are Members of this scheme to
implement the scheme so as to make it success.
42.4  The Committee has been apprised that under the scheme, it was envisaged that the corpus would be enhanced to Rs.2500 crore by
the end of Tenth Five Year Plan with contribution of Rs.2000 crore by the Government. The Corpus Fund was Rs.427.02 crore at the end
of FY 2002-03. With the higher plan outlay of Rs. 186.44 crore during 2003-04, the Corpus Fund was enhanced to Rs.686.19 crore at the
end of FY 2003-04. The Credit Guarantee Scheme is for contribution to Corpus Fund created under the Scheme. As the number of units
covered under the scheme increases, the liability of the Trust also increases on account of borrowers. As regards incurring of expenditure,
it may be pointed out that the scheme was operationalised on January 1, 2001 and only four years have elapsed since it became
operational. As there is a provision of two years lock-in period for claim settlement, so far only 81 claims have been received from MLIs
for settlement involving an amount of Rs. 1.70 crore. Of this, 36 claims have been settled with an outflow of Rs.39.66 lakh. During the
year 2003-04, a total number of 6603 proposals were approved for guarantee cover under the scheme.
42.5  The Committee takes note that under Major Head 2851 Credit Guarantee Scheme the Plan Outlay has been increased to
the tune of Rs. 180.00 crore in BE 2005-06 in comparison to 
Rs. 176.29 crore in RE 2004-05. The provision made under the scheme is for contribution to the Corpus Fund. The envisaged
level of corpus at the end of Tenth Five Year Plan is of Rs.2500 crore. But with a Plan outlay of Rs.900 crore in the Tenth Plan
and Rs.200 crore released during the Ninth Plan, the envisaged level of Rs.2500 crore cannot be achieved. The Committee is
anguished to observe that plan allocation is not made as originally conceived under the scheme. Therefore, in order to enhance
the comfort level of MLIs participating in the scheme, it is desirable that the corpus is enhanced to the envisaged level. With the
building of adequate corpus fund, the fears of MLIs could be allayed as still some of the banks have reservations about the
scheme because of their bad experience in the past with a similar scheme operated by the RBI.
42.6  While seeking guarantee cover from the Trust, the MLIs undertake to regularly monitor the functioning of units, which are covered
under this scheme. Moreover, the guarantee cover is to the extent of 75 per cent of the loan and the balance risk is borne by the banks. It
is, therefore, expected that the MLIs would ensure proper monitoring of the guaranteed accounts. The Trust obtains periodic data from
the MLIs regarding the status of the accounts covered under the scheme and can conduct inspection of accounts on sample basis.

49.0  ANALYSIS OF STATUS OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES IN NE & SIKKIM
49.1  The North Eastern Region and Sikkim have abundant natural resources and potential for small and tiny units. These resources can
be utilized for industrial development. The absence of motivated entrepreneurs has hampered the promotion and rapid industrialization.
The growth of small scale industries in the North Eastern States including Sikkim has not kept pace with the growth of SSIs in other parts
of the country. In order to accelerate the setting up of SSI units in this region, several steps have been taken by the Govt. which are
enumerated below:-
            (i)     Small Industries Services Institutes/Branch Institutes(SISIs/BIs) have been opened in all the North Eastern States & Sikkim.
            (ii)     Under the IID Scheme, Central grant (maximum Rs. 4 crore) is provided to the Implementing Agency for setting up IID
Centre in the North Eastern States and Sikkim as against Rs.2 crore to most of the States in India.
            (iii)     Under the Integrated Infrastructural Development Scheme, six IID Centres have been sanctioned in Assam and one each in
Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura.
            (iv)    A Tool Room and Training Centre at Guwahati has been set up to design and manufacture tools, dyes, zigs and fixtures etc.
and to impart training in tool and dye manufacturing, use of computers in design and manufacturing.
            (v)    Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship has been set up at Guwahati.
49.2 The Committee understands that the major areas of concern in the North Eastern Region and Sikkim are lack of
infrastructure like road and rail communication, shortage of power for industrial use, availability of skilled manpower, low
entrepreneurial skills, access to finance, technological obsolescence and lack of large scale manufacturing units which provides
ancillary opportunity to SSI community, therefore, the committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should take initiatives in this
regard by taking the matter with State Governments and DONER. The Committee is of the view that North Eastern Region and
Sikkim should be facilitated with focused entrepreneurship development programmes,technical training & skill up-gradation,
awareness of industrial opportunities for manufacturing in NER & Sikkim and supplying to the rest of the country, relatively
softer credit and marketing assistance programmes.

53.0  TINY AND MICRO ENTERPRISES
53.1  A provision of Rs. 460.30 crore has been made for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries in the Budget 2005-2006. There is no
separate allocation for the Tiny Enterprises in the Budget. However, for Micro Finance Programme a provision of Rs.5 crore (including
provision for NER & Sikkim) has been made in the Budget 2005-2006. Tiny Enterprises are such units which have investment in plant
and machinery upto Rs.25 lakh. As such all such industrial activities which are eligible for registration as SSI are also eligible for
registration in the tiny sector as long as its investment in plant and machinery is up to the prescribed limit of Rs.25 lakh. The majority
activities in Khadi & Coir Industry which are predominantly in rural areas and have investment below Rs. 25 lakh are covered under
Tiny/Micro enterprises in Agro & Rural Industries.
53.2  The Policy Measures for Promoting and Strengthening Small, Tiny and Village Enterprises, placed on the table of the House on 6
August, 2000 and Comprehensive Policy Package announced on 31 August 2000, while envisaging a separate package of facilities and
incentives for promotion of tiny industries included earmarking of 60 per cent of the total lending to the SSI Sector under Priority Sector
lending, raising of composite loan up to Rs.25 lakh, provision of 20 per cent or projected annual turnover as working capital loan,
concession in rate of interest from NSIC on composite loan of Rs.25 lakh, concessional rate of refinance to the tiny sector by SIDBI,
raising of project cost limit from Rs.25 lakh to Rs.50 lakh under the National Equity Fund (NEF) Scheme, enhancement of family income
eligibility limit from Rs.24,000 per annum to Rs.40,000 per annum under PMRY Scheme, earmarking of 50 per cent plots for tiny sector
under the Integrated Infrastructure Development (IID) Scheme, cluster development programme under the National Programme for Rural
Industrialization, preference in Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation, etc.
53.4  Government has announced under the National Common Minimum Programme that a major promotional package for SSI sector
will be brought out soon to support credit, technological and marketing support, freeing the SSI Sector from inspector raj, modernization
of coir, garments, food processing, leather, pottery and other cottage industries etc. This package will further strengthen and streamline
the Tiny Sector.
54.0  INDIAN TINY SECTOR’S COMPETITIVE RESILIENCE TO FACE THE CHALLENGES OF FREE IMPORTS AND
INTENSE COMPETITION
54.1  Small Scale Industries (SSIs) including tiny units in India have enough competitive strength to withstand the impact of free imports
and intense global competition. Government is fully aware of the WTO environment and have taken appropriate measures for preparing
the small scale sector including tiny sector to meet the challenges of globalization. Government is also constantly monitoring the impact
of the removal of QRs and WTO Agreements on the economy including the SSIs in the country. Though removal of QRs have exposed
the SSIs to a greater competition, yet the SSI sector including tiny sector has continued to grow. However, even after the removal of QRs,
protection to the industries is available in the form of raising Custom Duties up to the bound levels, imposing Anti-Dumping duties and
countervailing duties, taking safeguard measures, in case of surge in imports, etc. Further, the opening of markets by other countries, and
lowering of their tariffs will provide an opportunity to SSI including tiny units to give a big boost to their exports.
54.2  Some of the incentives & measures provided by the Government to enable the SSI including tiny units to compete in the globalized
& liberalized regime include raising the excise exemption limit from Rs.50 lakhs to Rs.l crore, a scheme of Capital Subsidy of 12 per cent
for investment in technology upgradation in select sectors, raising the eligibility limit for coverage under the Credit Guarantee Scheme
from Rs.10 lakh to Rs.25 lakh, continuation of financial support (up to Rs.75,000/-) for obtaining ISO 9000 & ISO 14001 certification up
to the end of Tenth Plan to enable the SSI to be competitive.
54.3  Field Institutions of Small Industries Development Organisation under the Ministry of SSI have been regularly conducting series of
Training Programmes to improve the skills of existing as well as would be entrepreneurs and their work force. This is in addition to a
number of Entrepreneurship and Management Development Programmes that are being conducted by SIDO’s Field Institution for
developing the latent desires of potential entrepreneurs to achieve something in to reality. All such Programmes are conducted throughout
the country by 28 Small Industries Service Institutes (SISIs), 30 Branch SISIs besides a number of autonomous bodies such as Product-
cum-Process Development Centres, Tool Rooms, etc. The trainings are primarily in the areas of Entrepreneurship Development
Programmes (EDPs), Management Development Programmes (MDPs, Skill Development Programmes (SDPs).
54.4  For acquiring marketing techniques and to promote marketing activities from SSI/Tiny Sector, SIDO participates in the Trade
