55.0  TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION OF SSI UNITS
55.1  Areas like revamping, R&D in technology upgradation, cost reduction, waste-avoidance etc. are diverse and highly specific to the
individual products and processes in the concerned SSI units. Therefore, these types of improvements can be brought about only by the
concerned units at their own level. However, to facilitate this process wherever required by them, Ministry of SSI has set up
organizations like Process & Product Development Centres, Tool Rooms and Training Centres and initiated schemes like Credit Linked
Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation. As indicated above, state Governments and industry associations are also provided
financial assistance for setting up facilities in this regard.
55.2  The following measures were undertaken during 2004-05 to increase the pace of technology upgradation in SSI sector:-
            (i)     Scope of the Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme( CLCSS) for Technology Upgradation of SSIs has been enlarged by addition of
14 new sub-sectors/products as well as new set of well-established and improved technologies under various sub-sectors
and products.
            (ii)     State Governments are being motivated to take advantage of the Scheme for financial assistance from SIDO to set up and
upgrade Mini Tool Rooms.
            (iii)    Industry Associations are being approached to set up product testing facilities with financial assistance under SIDO’s Plan
Scheme.
55.3  The functioning of Process and Product Development Centres, Tool Rooms, Regional Testing Centres and Field Testing Stations is
being geared up to meet the emerging requirements of the SSI sector.
55.4  The Committee recommends that activities like buyer-seller meets and vendor development programmes must regularly be
organized all over India, including the economically backward region to establish linkages between large and small enterprises to
accelerate and strengthen the partnership approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises. Apart from
Government Departments like Defence, Railways, coal, steel, Petro-chemical, food and food- processing etc., Public Undertakings
and Private Sector Industries should also be invited to participate in these events. Moreover, following course of action must be
taken for
            (a)    revitalization and regeneration of existing organization and revamping of existing organization and revamping of the
mechanism for technological up-gradation;
            (b)    R&D in technology up-gradation further steps required for designing;
            (c)     measures towards cost-reduction; and
            (d)    Steps towards avoidance of waste and non-value adding activities.
56.0  PROMOTION OF TECHNOLOGY BANKS AND ENCOURAGEMENT TO TECHNOLOGY PARKS.
56.1  Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) had set-up Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises(TBSE) in 1995 to help
SMEs to tap opportunities at the global level for acquisition of technology and establish business collaborations. TBSE has taken several
initiatives and put in place an effective mechanism to address the technology and collaboration related needs of the sector. Recognizing
the contribution of TBSE, Ministry of SSI, Government of India while announcing the policy package for SSI in the year 2000 indicated
that TBSE needs to be strengthened so that it emerges as a strong and vibrant “Technology Bank”. SIDBI initiated necessary steps for
institutionalizing TBSE as a full fledged “ Technology  Bank”. Several technology parks have been set up in sun rise areas such as
information technology, bio technology etc. by the concerned ministries in Government of India as well as States Government to promote
technology in SSI Sector.

57.0  POLICY OF RESERVATION
57.1  Small scale sector manufactures more than 7500 items. Out of that only 605 items are reserved for exclusive manufacture in small
scale sector. These items mainly are labour oriented with very less investment and low technological requirements. Most of these items
are produced in self employment ventures and do not attract big players in the field. However, some hi-tech export oriented items like
hosiery, hand tools, drugs & pharmaceutical and stationery have been provided with a higher investment limit in plant and machinery, i.e.
upto rupees five crores to enable them to meet the requirements of technology upgradation and face the global and domestic competition.
As such, the reservation policy does not discourage investment. On the contrary the policy is instrumental in employment generation and
meeting the concern of regional imbalances. Where ever it is felt that the reservation of any particular item needs to be dispensed with in
the interest of growth and development of the small scale sector, the issue is discussed with the stake holders and the respective
administrative Ministries, and depending upon the general opinion, the item is de-reserved with the recommendation of the Advisory
Committee constituted under Section 29B of Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951. Accordingly, the list of reserved items
have come down from 873 in 1984 to 605 as on date. There is a proposal to dereserve 108 more items during this year as announced in
the Budget Speech 2005-06, which will further shorten the list of reserved items.
57.2  The Committee hopes that the de-reservation of 108 items, as announced in the Budget (2005-06) would help the small scale
sector to meet the demand for technological upgradation, encourage research and development and make the sector competitive
to face the domestic and global competition. A status report on the practical implication in this regards may be furnished to the
Committee in its Action Taken Notes of the present Report.
58.0  FAIR PRACTICES CODE FOR LENDERS
58.1  There is a need for strict implementation of RBI Guidelines on Fair Practices Code for lenders. RBI should assess the situation and
make suitable amendments to strengthen the Fair Practices Code. The adoption of “Best Practices Code: as is applicable for payments to
large industries/corporate, for small and medium enterprises will help to a great deal in ensuring prompt payment and developing
coordinal relations between the supplier and buyer for long term business tie-ups.
58.2  The Committee understands that the adoption of “Best Practices Code” for large corporate dealing with the SME Sector on
the line of the code for payments for large industries/corporate” would greatly help the sector regarding timely payment to
SMEs. Despite RBI’s Guidelines on Fair Practices code for Lenders”, nothing has practically been achieved. No initiative has
been taken to address the issue of delay payment in the General Budget 2005-06. Under the circumstance, the Committee feels
that Government should come out with alternative arrangement i.e. secruitisation law to provide relief to the SSI sector from the
delayed payments.
59.0  ENACTMENT OF LIMITED PARTNERSHIP ACT
59.1  The Ministry of Company Affairs is likely to enact a law on Limited Liability Partnership. The issue is under their active
consideration. The Limited Liability Partnership will provide higher flow of capital in to the Sector, especially to the upcoming sections
like IT, Bio­ technology, Pharma, etc. It will also encourage venture capital.
59.2  The Committee is in agreement with the opinion of the Ministry of SSI that the Limited Liability Partnership will provide
higher flow of capital in to the Sector, especially to the upcoming sections like IT, Bio-technology, Pharma, etc. and would also
encourage venture capital. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of SSI should take up the matter of
Enactment of Limited Partnership Act with the Ministry of Company Affairs.
60.0  SPECIFIC EXPORT THRUST/POLICY MEASURES
60.1  As regards the steps undertaken to increase the export potential of SSI sector, the Development Commissioner (SSI) promotes
participation of SSI units in product specific as well as general exhibitions in India and abroad every year. Besides this, training in export
marketing and packaging for exports is also provided to SSI units. Sector Specific Market Studies are conducted for selected SSI
categories. In addition, publicity material for overseas publicity are also provided to the SSI entrepreneurs. No State specific study has
been conducted by the Development Commissioner (SSI).
60.2  The Committee feels that there is a need for the formulation of sector specific export thrust/policy measures and
establishment of more Export promotion zones to promote international trade of select SSI items especially ready made
garments, Leather products, basic chemicals, Marine and processed foods and engineering goods which account for 3/4
th of the
total export from SSI sector. This is required to promote international trade.

61.1  The recommendations of Abid Hussain Committee have been considered by the Government and follow up action in most of them,
like enhancement allocation of 60 per cent priority lending earmarked of SSI Sector to be provided to tiny wherein 40 per cent for tiny

revitalizing of State Financial Corporations and Small Industries Development Corporations, assistance on concessional rate of interest
for technology upgradation and modernization of SSI, implementation of Nayak Committee recommendations concerning credit supply,
particularly making available 20 per cent of annual turnover as working capital, enhancing of investment limit of Tiny Sector from Rs.5

62.0  CONCEPT OF FACTORING SERVICES FOR SSI SECTOR
62.1  Factoring services provide instant liquidity to industries, particularly to small scale and tiny sectors, prior to the maturity period of
various instruments drawn for supply or purchase of goods or services by assignment of debts or receivables to a factor. Factoring
services had played an effective role as an alternate mode of working capital finance for the past three decades in some of the countries.
The Factoring Services Legislation will help to mitigate the problem of delayed payments to SSI units and augment the flow of funds to
the SSI Sector.
62.2  The Ministry of SSI had discussed the matter with various stakeholders. However, it was felt that the proposed Act on “The
Factoring of Debts due to Industrial and Commercial Undertakings” covers all industrial and commercial undertakings including large
units. Therefore, the appropriate Ministry to take up the matter may be Ministry of Finance (Banking Division).
62.3  The Committee endorses the viewpoint of the Ministry of SSI that factoring services would provide instant liquidity to
industries, particularly to small scale and tiny sectors, prior to the maturity period of various instruments drawn for supply or
purchase of goods or services by assignment of debts or receivables to a factor. Since the Factoring services had played an
effective role as an alternate mode of working capital finance for the past three decades in some of the countries. The Committee
feels that the Factoring Services Legislation would also help to mitigate the problem of delayed payments to SSI units and
augment the flow of funds to the SSI Sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of SSI should also pursue
the proposed Act on “The Factoring of Debts due to Industrial and Commercial Undertakings” with Ministry of Finance
(Banking Division).

66.0  WORKING GROUP ON REHABILITATION OF SICK UNITS
66.1  The Working Group under the Chairmanship of Shri S.S. Kohli submitted its report in May, 2001 and all the major
recommendations were accepted by the RBI, including a change in the definition of sick SSI units, norms for deciding on the viability of
sick units, etc. Based on the accepted recommendations of the Working Group, the RBI has circulated the Revised Guidelines for
Rehabilitation of sick SSI units on 16th January, 2002 to all the Scheduled Commercial Banks for implementation. The revised guidelines
would enable the Banks to take early action for revival of the potentially viable sick SSI units.
66.2  The banks have been advised by the RBI to review the progress made in implementation of the revised guidelines on rehabilitation
of sick SSIs, based on Kohli Working Group recommendations, by their respective Boards annually as on March of every year and
intimate the position in this regard to the RBI. In this context, the RBI has informed:-
            (i)     All the banks have issued necessary instructions to their branches/controlling offices on rehabilitation of sick SSIs.
            (ii)     The banks have adequately delegated powers to take decision on sick SSIs.
            (iii)    The banks have put in place suitable mechanism for monitoring implementation of rehabilitation of sick SSIs.
            (iv)    The banks have put in place a system of periodical review of implementation of rehabilitation of sick SSIs.
66.3  Some of the banks are carrying out specialized studies to ascertain the reasons for sickness so that suitable rehabilitation measures
can be drawn up for sick SSIs.
67.0  A.S. GANGULY’S REPORT ON CREDIT FLOW TO SSI
67.1  The RBI has accepted some of the recommendations of the Working Group on Flow of Credit to SSI sector (Ganguly Working
Group) viz., adoption of cluster-based approach for financing SME sector, sponsoring specific projects as well as widely publicising
successful working models of NGOs by Lead Banks which service small and tiny industries and individual entrepreneurs, sanctioning of
higher working capital limits by banks operating in the North East region to SSIs, based on their commercial judgement due to the
peculiar situation of hilly terrain and frequent floods causing hindrance in the transportation system, exploring new instrument by banks
for promoting rural industry and to improve the flow of credit to rural artisans, rural industries and rural entrepreneurs and commended
them to the banks for implementation.
67.2  Further, based on the recommendations of the Ganguly Working Group, the RBI has advised all foreign banks that (i) the amount of
shortfall in priority sector obligation will be placed with SIDBI for a tenor of three years and (ii) the funds placed with SIDBI will have a
graded interest rate structure linked to the Bank Rate.

69.0  STRENGTHENING CREDIT DELIVERY SYSTEM AND SUPPORT SERVICES AGENCIES
69.1  The Government of India and the Reserve Bank of India have taken various measures to strengthen the credit delivery system and
to promote the healthy growth of the SSI/tiny sector. These include simplification of method of computation of working capital
requirements of SSI units on the basis of minimum 20% of the projected annual turnover for borrowal limits upto Rs. 5 crore, earmarking
targets for lending to tiny units, increase in the exemption limit for sanction of collateral free loans to all SSI units to Rs.5 lakh (further
increase in this limit to Rs. 25 lakh for units with good track record and sound financial position), enhancement of composite loan limit
from Rs. 50 lakh to Rs. 1 crore, opening of more specialised SSI branch under general norms and conversion of existing branches to
specialised SSI branches under relaxed norms (branches having 60 per cent or more of their advances to SSI sector) for providing better
services to this sector as a whole. To give the benefit of softer interest rates to SSI sector, banks have been advised to accord SSI units
with a good track record the benefit of lower spreads over the PLR and to re-set the interest rate downward keeping in view general
southward movement in interest rates. Further, Indian Banks’ Association have advised the banks to adopt the interest rate band of 2 per
cent above and below their prime lending rates (PLRs) for secured advances. The banks have been also advised to fix self-set target for
growth in advances to SSI sector. To make available timely credit to the sector, a time frame has been fixed for disposal of loan
applications i.e. upto Rs. 25,000/- within 2 weeks and upto Rs. 5 lakh, within 4 weeks provided the loan applications are complete in all
respects and accompanied by a ‘check list’.
70.0  STRENGTHENING OF SMALL INDUSTRIES DEVELOPMENT BANK OF INDIA (SIDBI) FOR EXTENDING
FINANCIAL AND SUPPORT SERVICES TO SSIS
70.1  Pursuant to the announcement made by the then Hon’ble Finance Minister on 9
th January, 2004 regarding creation of Small &
Medium Enterprises (SME) Fund with SIDBI as the Nodal Agency, SIDBI has structured a SME Fund for giving impetus to the growth
of Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) sector in the country. The SIDBI has operationalised the Fund with a corpus of Rs. 10,000 crore
with effect from 1st April,2004 to be utilized over the two years i.e. FY 2005 and FY 2006. To make available adequate financial
resources to the sector at competitive rates, the maximum rate of interest for the assistance out of the Fund would be 2 per cent below the
PLR of SIDBI under direct assistance [maximum 9.5 per cent p.a. at present]. 80 per cent of the SME Fund would be reserved for SSI
units having investment in plant & machinery upto Rs.l crore and balance 20 per cent to be utilized for other SSIs and medium sector
enterprises.
70.2  Apart form the above, the SIDBI is taking various strategic initiatives to improve the flow of credit to the SSI sector by broad
basing certain schemes in tune with changing requirements of the sector. Steps are also being taken to enhance the scale of operations
under direct finance schemes, strengthening and improving the functioning of State Financial Corporations (SFCs) besides, laying
emphasis on liberalizing the schemes and simplifying the systems and procedures to make them more market friendly and customer
oriented.
70.3  The Committee appreciates the role of SIDBI in taking various strategic initiatives to improve the flow of credit to the SSI
sector by broad basing certain schemes in tune with changing requirements of the sector, however, SSI sector remains for want
of adequate credit flow. Therefore, in order to extend financial and support services to SSIs, SIDBI should also get into direct
lending in a big way apart from refinance. For this, it is necessary that SIDBI is permitted to offer a total package of services
including opening up of accounts, cheque book facilities and other fund based and non-fund based services to the SSI units like
other banks rather than giving only term loans.
71.0  FDI FOR BETTER TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER IN SMES SECTOR
71.1  The Ministry has recommended the enhancement of equity participation/FDI limit from
24 per cent to 49 per cent in the case of SSI items where investment limit has been enhanced to Rs.5 crore. This would help in
encouraging FDI for better technology transfer in SME sector.
71.2  The Committee recommends that the Government give the green signal to the proposal of the Ministry of SSI in regard to
the enhancement of equity participation/FDI limit from 24 per cent to 49 per cent in the case of SSI items where investment limit
has been enhanced to Rs.5 crore as the would encouraging FDI for better technology transfer in SME sector.

CONTRIBUTION OF SSI IN THE NATIONAL ECONOMY
72.1  Though the State Governments are primarily responsible for the promotion and development of SSI, the Central Government took
several policy initiatives for small enterprises sector during 2004-05:
            (i)     The National Commission on Enterprises in the Unorganized/Informal Sector was set up in September 2004. The
Commission will, inter alia, recommend measures considered necessary for improvement in the productivity of these
enterprises, generation of large scale employment opportunities on a sustainable basis, linkage of the sector to institutional
framework in areas like credit, raw material supply, infrastructure, technology upgradation, marketing facilities and skill
development.
            (ii)     To facilitate technology upgradation and enhancing competitiveness, the investment limit (in plant and machinery) was
raised in October 2004, from Rs.l crore to Rs.5 crore, in respect of 7 items of sports goods, reserved for manufacture in the
small scale sector.
            (iii)     The Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Fund of Rs. 10,000 crore was operationalised by the SIDBI since April 2004.
Eighty per cent of the lending from this Fund will be for SSI units, at interest rate of 2 per cent below the prevailing PLR
of the SIDBI.
            (iv)    The Reserve Bank of India enhanced the composite loan limit for the SSI sector to Rs. 1 crore from Rs.50 lakh.
            (v)    A beginning was made to implement new scheme on ‘Performance and Credit Rating of Small Scale Industries’ through the
National Small Industries Corporation Ltd. (NSIC), with a one-time grant to SSI units towards part-reimbursement of the
rating fees,
            (vi)    With a view to integrating small and medium enterprises, facilitating their growth and enhancing their competitiveness
(including measures for freeing the sector from “Inspector Raj”), a suitable draft legislation was finalised.
            (vii)   Draft of a new “Promotional Package for Small Enterprises” was formulated. This would include measures to improve
credit, incentives for technology upgradation, infrastructural and marketing facilities, etc.
72.3  The Committee recommends that for streamlining and strengthening the contribution of small enterprises sector in the
national economy, the Government should focus the following strategy:
            (i)     Providing full credit, technology upgradation, modernization and marketing support to the SSI sector,
            (ii)    Infrastructure upgradation in general and particularly in the major small enterprise clusters; these would include
road connectivity, regular supply of power, common effluent treatment facility and water supply, etc.
            (iii)   Reducing the rigours of complying with the plethora of rules and regulations applicable in the small enterprises
sector, which is known as Inspector Raj.
            (iv)   Full support to the service industry to fulfill its true growth and employment generation potential,
            (v)    Training of existing and potential entrepreneurs and workers on a large scale in modern management practices and
skill upgradation through advanced training facilities for capacity building in the small enterprises sector.
74.0  ACTION PLAN FOR THE YEAR 2005-06
74.1  The Action Plan for the Ministry for the year 2005-06 is as under : -
            (i)     Formulation of a single legislation, i.e. Small & Medium Enterprises Development Bill to promote the growth of the sector
and free it from ‘Inspector Raj’
            (ii)     Formulation of a Promotional Package for the SSI sector
            (iii)    Examination of problems facing Enterprises in the Unorganised/Informal Sector through the National Commission set up
for this purpose
            (iv)    Facilitate credit flow to the SSI Sector - by implementing the Performance and Credit Rating Scheme for Small Enterprises,
through NSIC
            (v)    Infrastructure upgradation in major industrial clusters
            (vi)    Institutional  reforms in terms of: (i) Decentralisation; (ii) Simplification; (iii) Transparency; (iv) Accountability; and (v) E-
governance.
74.2  The Committee desires that as a precautionary measure to achieve the Action Plan for the year 2005-06, the Ministry of SSI
should review and monitor the progress of the work closely. The functioning of organisations under the Ministry, implementation
of Plan schemes and various developmental activities should be reviewed at various levels regularly. The Monitoring mechanism
to oversee the functioning of various organizations under the Ministry of Small Scale Industries should be made more effective.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE
COMMITTEE  —  AT A GLANCE
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES ON THE MOVE
         The Committee understands that the Small Scale Industries is today on the move world wide, therefore, Small Scale
Industries in India should be given top-priority by the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance in plan-allocation so
that small scale units may get adequate space for maturing into medium enterprises to catch the global trend. The Ministry of
SSI should provide the logistic support to the SSI sector. The Ministry of Small Scale Industries must strengthen the SSI sector to
enable it to remain competitive in market-led economy and generate additional employment opportunities. The Ministry should
assist the SSI sector in accessing (or provide) proper and timely inputs like adequate credit from financial institutions/banks;
funds for technology up-gradation and modernization; adequate infrastructural facilities; modern testing facilities and quality
certification laboratories; modern management practices and skill up-gradation through suitable training facilities; marketing
assistance; and level playing field at par with the large industries
sector.                                                                                                           (Para 1.4)
ORGANISATIONAL SET-UP AND RETRAINING OF STAFF
         The Committee feels that the organizational set-up of the Ministry must be made effective through reorientation of form
and retraining of staff to enable them to make full use of the opportunities and challenges fast emerging liberalization and
globalization process under post-WTO -regime by undertaking following steps:-
            (i)     more regular appraisal of policy initiatives for the SME sector in similarly placed large countries;
            (ii)    ascertaining best practices within the Central Government and also abroad for promotion and development of SME
sector and their adoption/adaptation in the Indian SME context;
            (iii)   closer and more structural interaction with the stakeholders;
            (iv)   improving synergies among the constituent organization of the Ministry and the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries;
            (v)    promoting constructive competitiveness among field-level organizations based on well defined objectives and action
plans; and
            (vi)   retraining of staff, as appropriate.
(Para 2.3)
         The Committee is constrained to observe that the Planning Commission has not accorded the financial requirement as
projected by the Ministry of SSI to the tune of Rs. 793.94 crore (inclusive of Rs. 3.35 crore for work outlay provided in the
Demands of M/o Urban Development for the year 2005-06 ) against which a plan outlay of Rs. 412.26 crores (inclusive of Rs. 3.35
crores of Ministry of Urban Development) has been accorded as a result of which reduced plan allocation would be made to the
schemes like Credit Guarantee Trust Fund Scheme (76 per cent) Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (80 per cent)
Technology Up-gradation (16 per cent) and Tool rooms (10 per cent) of their financial requirement causing a serious implication
to the promotion and consolidation of Small Scale Industries. The reduced allocation may already affect the implementation of
these schemes.                                                                          (Para 3.2)
         The Committee however understands the financial crunch with the Government and the consequent problems being faced
by the Planning Commission in judicious and equitably allocation among various Departments/Ministries as per their
requirement.                                                                                                                 (Para 3.4)
         The Committee is of the opinion that even the Planning Commission would appreciate the potential of Small Scale Industry
in the employment generation and its contribution to the poverty alleviation. It is not a secret that SSI sector is the fate-fixture of
common man as the SSI units require low investment but effects the lives of millions. Therefore, the question of resurrection of
the SSI sector would mean the improvement in the standard of living of millions. Moreover, the global trend of promoting the
SSI sector is an observable fact. The Finance Minister of India is even tired of stressing the need for providing SSI sector the
adequate space to grow and thrive as medium enterprises therefore, the Committee feels that the Ministry of SSI should get the
sufficient line allocation to implement its schemes/programmes. (Para 3.5)

of Finance, Planning Commission so that the financial requirement of SSI sector is well communicated to the Planning
Commission as per the actual requirement of SSI sector. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry of SSI should

needs of SSI sector.                                                               (Para 3.6)

THIRD CENSUS OF SSIS (2001-02) AND NEED FOR NATIONAL POLICY FOR SMALL INDUSTRIES
         The Committee is of the view that the national policy and programmes/ schemes should be suitable, and effective for
supporting the promotion and development of small scale industries. The main emphasis should be on easy credit availability,
technological Upgradation and modernization, Infrastructural development, marketing support, etc. Moreover, for uniform and
sustainable growth of small scale industries with an objective for greater employment creation and equitable distribution of
wealth all over the country, there is a need for a national policy for small industries. To address the needs in the changed
economic scenario, the Government must come out with a promotional policy package at the earliest. The findings of the Third
Census can be used for policy formulation as follows:-
           (i)      Liberalise credit policy to make institutional credit more accessible to SSI units, including the unregistered units.
           (ii)     Identify industries requiring technological upgradation which can be assisted either under the on-going
programmes/schemes or new appropriate schemes for the same.

FAIR PRACTICES CODE FOR LENDERS
         The Committee understands that the adoption of “Best Practices Code” for large corporate dealing with the SME Sector on
the line of the code for payments for large industries/corporate would greatly help the sector regarding timely payment to SMEs.
Despite RBI’s Guidelines on Fair Practices code for Lenders, nothing has practically been achieved. No initiative has been taken
to address the issue of delay payment in the General Budget 2005-06. Under the circumstance, the Committee feels that

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/171threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:36]
Government should come out with alternative arrangement i.e. secruitisation law to provide relief to the SSI sector from the
delayed payments.                                                             (Para 58.2)
ENACTMENT OF LIMITED PARTNERSHIP ACT
         The Committee is in agreement with the opinion of the ministry of SSI that the Limited Liability Partnership will provide
higher flow of capital in to the Sector, especially to the upcoming sections like IT, Bio-technology, Pharma, etc and would also
encourage venture capital. The committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of SSI should take up the matter of
Enactment of Limited Partnership Act with the Ministry of Company Affairs. (Para 59.2)
SPECIFIC EXPORT THRUST/POLICY MEASURES
         The Committee feels that there is a need for the formulation of sector specific export thrust/policy measures and
establishment of more Export promotion zones to promote international trade of select SSI items especially ready made
garments, Leather products, basic chemicals, Marine and processed foods and engineering goods which account for 3/4
th of the
total export from SSI sector. This is required to promote international trade.                (Para 60.2)
ABID HUSSAIN COMMITTEE REPORT
         The Committee was given an understand that recommendations of Abid Hussain Committee Report are still relevant for
the promotion of small and medium enterprises, as it has provided a road map for making the small enterprise able to grow on
its own and graduate in to medium enterprise. It recommended for single law of small enterprise, limited partnership act and
removal of regulatory barriers to the technological progress of the Sector are quite relevant. The Committee therefore, strongly
recommends that the Government in its proposed Small and Medium Enterprises Bill, 2005, should incorporate the provisions
pertaining to recommendations Abid Hussain Committee.         (Para 61.2)
CONCEPT OF FACTORING SERVICES FOR SSI SECTOR
         The Committee endorses the viewpoint of the Ministry of SSI that factoring services would provide instant liquidity to
industries, particularly to small scale and tiny sectors, prior to the maturity period of various instruments drawn for supply or
purchase of goods or services by assignment of debts or receivables to a factor. Since the Factoring services had played an
effective role as an alternate mode of working capital finance for the past three decades in some of the countries. The Committee
feels that the Factoring Services Legislation would also help to mitigate the problem of delayed payments to SSI units and
augment the flow of funds to the SSI Sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of SSI should also pursue
the proposed Act on “The Factoring of Debts due to Industrial and Commercial Undertakings” with Ministry of Finance
(Banking Division).                                                (Para 62.3)
TRENDS OF SICKNESS IN SSI SECTOR
         The Committee desires that RBI’S guidelines in regard to credit flow to SSI sector must be observed by pubic sector Banks
to facilitate additional capacity generation, expansion of existing units and improving capacity utilization diversification and to
enhance competitiveness of SSI sectors.                                                       
                                                                                                                                            (Para 67.4)
VENTURE CAPITAL FUNDING TO SSI UNITS
         The Committee desires that suitable and adequate steps must be undertaken for popularization of venture capital funding
to SSI units. Banks should feel encouraged in this regards as RBI has already announced that investment in venture capital
would be eligible for inclusion in priority sector lending.                                              
                                                                                                                                            (Para 68.3)
STRENGTHENING OF SMALL INDUSTRIES DEVELOPMENT BANK OF INDIA  (SIDBI) FOR EXTENDING FINANCIAL
AND SUPPORT SERVICES TO SSIS
         The Committee appreciates the role of SIDBI in taking various strategic initiatives to improve the flow of credit to the SSI
sector by broad basing certain schemes in tune with changing requirements of the sector, however, SSI sector remains for want
of adequate credit flow. Therefore, in order to extend financial and support services to SSIs, SIDBI should also get into direct
lending in a big way apart from refinance. For this, it is necessary that SIDBI is permitted to offer a total package of services
including opening up of accounts, cheque book facilities and other fund based and non-fund based services to the SSI units like
other banks rather than giving only term loans.    (Para 70.3)
FDI FOR BETTER TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER IN SMES SECTOR
         The Committee recommends that the Government give the green signal to the proposal of the Ministry of SSI in regard to
the enhancement of equity participation / FDI limit from 24% to 49% in the case of SSI items where investment limit has been
enhanced to Rs. 5 crore as the would encouraging FDI for better technology transfer in SME
sector.                                                                                                                                  (Para 71.2)
SPECIFIC STEPS WERE TAKEN DURING THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2004-05 FOR ENHANCING THE CONTRIBUTION

OF SSI IN THE NATIONAL ECONOMY
         The Committee recommends that for streamlining and strengthening the contribution of small enterprises sector in the
national economy, the Government should focus the following strategy:
           (i)      Providing full credit, technology upgradation, modernization and marketing support to the SSI sector.
           (ii)     Infrastructure upgradation in general and particularly in the major small enterprise clusters; these would include
road connectivity, regular supply of power, common effluent treatment facility and water supply, etc.
           (iii)    Reducing the rigours of complying with the plethora of rules and regulations applicable in the small enterprises
sector, which is known as Inspector Raj.
           (iv)    Full support to the service industry to fulfill its true growth and employment generation potential.
           (v)     Training of existing and potential entrepreneurs and workers on a large scale in modern management practices and
skill upgradation through advanced training facilities for capacity building in the small enterprises sector.
(Para 72.3)
ACTION PLAN FOR THE YEAR 2005-06
         The Committee desires that as a precautionary measure to achieve the Action Plan for the year 2005-06, the Ministry of SSI
should review and monitor the progress of the work closely. The functioning of organisations under the Ministry, implementation
of Plan schemes and various developmental activities should be reviewed at various levels regularly. The Monitoring mechanism
to oversee the functioning of various organizations under the Ministry of Small Scale Industries should be made more
effective.                                                                  (Para 74.2)

REPORT
 
The Coir industry is a traditional, labour intensive, export oriented and  agro based cottage industry.  The coir
industry originated in the State of  Kerala centuries ago and over the years it has spread to other coconut growing States
like Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal, Union Territories like Andaman & Nicobar Islands
& Lakshadweep etc. Coconut husk which was considered a throw away waste material is the basic raw material of this
industry.  The coir industry, therefore generates wealth from waste.  The coir industry employs more than half a million
people and majority of them are from rural areas and belonging to economically weaker sections of the society.  About
80% of the workforce are women.  It is of great importance to the coconut producing States in India as the industry
provides employment and livelihood to vast majority of the economically backward population with minimum
investment and contributes to the economy of these States.  This is because coconut husk, the raw-material for coir
industry is considered otherwise as a mere waste. The industry provides gainful employment mainly to rural

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/172treport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:39]
unemployed people where the scope for providing alternative employment is rather remote. The coir industry also
contributes to the valuable  foreign exchange earnings of the nation.
 
1.1       The emergence of new products like coir geotextiles  and coir composites as wood substitute have very good
potential.  Coir geotextile is used to prevent soil erosion and promote re-vegetation, as an effective soil conditioner and
biodegradable moisture retaining soilless growth medium which would find extensive application in greening projects,
agri-, horti- and flori-cultural   operations .   Similarly, coir composite has  extensive  application in the field of
construction and packaging.  Coir thus meet some of the market needs in respect of new products by way of geotextiles ,
garden articles and coir ply.
 
1.2       The expansion of cultivation of coconut in non-traditional areas in the States of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra
Pradesh, Orissa, etc has increased the availability of raw-material and coir industry is coming up in a big way in these
States contributing to rural employment generation through utilization of an agro-waste available in plenty.
 
1.3       In the pre-independent period, the industry was in the hands of foreign companies and production was highly
centralized merely catering to the requirements of exports.  The post independent period saw the decentralization and
fragmentation of the industry into small household cottage units.  It was in view of the socio economic importance that
the Coir Board was set up by the Govt. of India to safeguard the Indian industry including export. The Coir Board
extended its activities for development of coir industry in the State of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa,
West Bengal, Goa, Andaman & Nicobar Island, Pondicherry and Lakshadweep through its Regional Offices established
at Bangalore in Karnataka, Pollachi in Tamil Nadu, Visakhapattanam in Andhra Pradesh and Bhubaneswar in Orissa. 
 
 
 
 
1.4       Coir Board organised programme for developing skilled manpower by imparting training in various activities of
coir processing to the artisans in the above States, it opened sales outlets providing facilities to the small scale
manufacturers to sell their products through Coir Board showrooms & Sales Depots, introduced rebate system initially
and later it was replaced with Market Development Assistance Scheme to help the coir cooperatives and PSUs  engaged
in the manufacture and marketing of coir and coir products and  encouraged cooperativisation through specific schemes
to bring coir workers  in the cooperative fold and  ensure minimum wages.  With a view to safeguard the interests of the
industry, the Board had introduced minimum export price for price stabilisation and to prevent unhealthy competition
among exporters, Purchase Price to ensure minimum price to the small scale manufacturers and wages to workers,
import restriction to protect local industry, quality inspection to ensure quality of coir products. 
 
 
1.5       As part of empowerment of women, introduced Mahila Coir Yojana which provides motorised ratt/motorised
traditional ratt at subsidised rates to women artisans after giving  training in spinning coir yarn. 
 
1.6       Through R&D, the Board has developed the     motorised ratts, motorised traditional ratts and fully automatic
spinning machine which reduces drudgery in spinning and increases productivity and helps enhancement of wages of
coir spinners; Multi-purpose loom, semi-automatic loom and fully automatic loom for weaving mats, matting with
higher productivity;  ‘Coirret’ – a bacteria consortia; ‘Pith Plus’ – a fungal spawn, through its application the coir pith a
problematic waste product is composted for a genuine organic manures.  Coir geotextiles (Coir Bhoovastra) for
controlling soil erosion, protection of river embankments, road embankments, mud-wall, hill slopes; Coir composites to
produce coir ply a wood substitute for manufacture of furniture, doors, earthquake-free houses, panelling  and ceiling;
and instant lawn using Coir Bhoovastra, Coir Pith and grass.           The NRDC has been entrusted to patent the Coirret,
Pith Plus, Coir Geotextiles  and Coco Lawn developed by the research centre  of the Coir Board.  A number of novel
designs with attractive colour schemes have been developed for printing and weaving on coir products suitable for
different markets abroad. 
 
1.7       In line with the change of national policy and economic reforms etc. the Coir Board has reviewed its role.  The
Coir Board has assumed its new role of a promoter and facilitator in providing the industry and through increased
participation of the private sector in all activities.   The chanelisation of activities of the Coir Board by introducing

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/172treport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:39]
rationalized schemes under R&D and domestic market promotion, export market promotion, training, extension, Mahila
Coir Yojana and Quality Improvement, development of production infrastructure, welfare measures and
Cooperativisation, has been taken up for institutionalization   of the industry.   Restructuring of Cooperatives where the
workers are the members is necessary and the cooperativisation  scheme with the modification suggested in the report of
Institute of Rural Management, Anand (IRMA) is necessary to bring the coir workers in the cooperative fold to give the
coir industry a look of an organised sector. 
 
1.8       The Committee appreciates the role of  Coir Board in the overall development of coir industry in India
characterized by increased production, increased consumption, export and  employment in rural sector. 
Development of Coir Industries in India has led to  Women empowerment and welfare of workers. The role of
the Coir Board in the field of  R&D in coir sector has  strengthened, new products like coir ply, packaging
material and geotextiles .  Coir Board as a national organization has been  committed  to the sustainable
development.  The Committee hopes that the Coir Board would continue to make its lasting contribution in the
promotion and proliferation of Coir Industries not only in the Coir producing states but the non-traditional
zones also.
 
 
2.0       SWOT –analysis of Coir Industries
 
2.1       The strengths, weakness, opportunity  and threats of coir industry are;
 
Strengths
 
(i)
                  Abundant availability of raw material for industrial utilisation. Availability of skilled manpower.
 
(ii)                A renewable resource with inherent qualities  such as its biodegradability and eco-friendliness, which
advantages over synthetic products.
 
(iii)               An established and expanding export market.
 
(iv)              It provides employment for skilled and semiskilled workers, especially women, enabling empowerment of
women.
 
(v)                Virtual monopoly India enjoys as a producer of retted white fibre which are more suited for manufacture of
coir yarn, mats, matting, carpets.
 
(vi)              Scope for development of products out of coir for diversified use through R&D.
 
 
 
Weaknesses
 
(i)                 Obsolete production and process technologies.
(ii)                Slow pace of modernisation.
(iii)               Relatively high cost of production.
(iv)              The characteristic of coir limiting product diversification.
(v)                Inadequate credit flow and investment .
(vi)              Poor shipping infrastructure.
 
Opportunities
 
(i)
                  Increasing awareness for eco-friendly biodegradable products world over.
(ii)                Increasing awareness about need for erosion control and biodegradable Geotextile in erosion control
applications.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/172treport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:39]
(iii)               Opening up of markets through globalisation.
(iv)             The coir industry generates additional employment in rural areas through coir processing activities with
minimum investment and arrests migration of rural youths to urban areas.  
 
Threats
 
(i)                  Threats from synthetic products which are more attractive and sophisticated.
(ii)                Competition from cheaper natural fibres/ substitutes.
(iii)               Competition from other producing countries like Srilanka, Vietnam, Philippines and China. 
(iv)              Higher freight when compared to Srilanka.
 
2.2       The Committee recommends that the Coir Board would make a serious assessment of SWOT analysis of
Coir Industries.  Strength of the Coir industries must be capitalised and the opportunities ahead must be availed
of.  Similarly, strategy should be chalked out to combat the threats and overcome the weaknesses of the Coir
Industries.  The Committee has commended   contribution of the coir board in its 141
st  Report to chalk out
action plan for promotion and proliferation of coir industries in West Bengal and Andman  and Nicobar Islands. 
Similar action plan may be chalked out for other states  on the local logistics.

polluting the environment.  Its disposal was a big problem in all coir producing States.  The basic problems being faced

4.0       Cost reduction of coir products
 
4.1       Under the cluster development activities, it is proposed to promote the formation of consortium among the small
scale manufacturers and small and medium exporters so as to have a common approach in sourcing of raw material,
marketing of products etc.   This will enable them to reduce the selling cost of the products to the minimum extent
possible.  Under the UNDP Project recently concluded, the Coir Board in association with the Entrepreneurship
Development Institute of India, Ahmedabad had implemented a project on revitalisation  of coir industry by
demonstration of cost management strategies.   Under the Project, 4 consortia, 2 each for the small scale manufacturers
and exporters were constituted.   These consortia have been successfully marketing coir products in a cost effective
manner.  It is proposed to replicate the strategy in other coir producing sectors.
 
4.2       The Committee takes note of the basic characteristics and  problems of coir industries and the action
taken or be envisaged to be taken by the Coir Board and the Ministry of ARI.  The Committee is of the view that
with massive efforts and implementation of financial assistance scheme to encourage setting up of new units
would result into higher utilisation of husk from the present level of thirty seven per cent.    The Committee

5.2       During 2003-04 there was an increase to the tune of 15.53 per cent in the export value over the previous year.  It
was 10.02 per cent during 2002-03 compared to the previous year.  In the current year, (2004-2005) there was an
increase to the tune of 16.86 per cent in quantity-wise and 15.95 per cent in value wise. The increase in the export has
been satisfactory as the growth recorded is in the case of export of a traditional commodity.
 
5.3       During 2003-2004, the Gross Domestic Product of the coir industry was valued roughly at Rs.1750 crore and out
of which an amount of Rs.407.50 crore was earned as foreign exchange from export.  The GDP of the industry for the
year 2004-2005 is estimated to be Rs.1900 crore and out of which the export earnings amounted to Rs.450.00 crore
(2004-2005). The industry generates additional employment in rural areas through adoption of coir processing activities
with minimum investment and arrests migration of rural youths to urban areas.  The contribution of coir industry to the
national economy can be further increased by augmentation of utilization of coconut husk abundantly available in all
coconut producing states.   
 
5.4       Export during first 11 months of the current year (2004-05) totaled to 1,06,368 Tonnes valued at Rs.425.72
crore, the target being Rs.450 crore.  
 
 
5.5       Till the removal of the Minimum Export Price applicable on export of coir and coir products and removal of the
Minimum Purchase Price applicable  for the goods manufactured for export, the coir industry was operating in a
protected environment.  With the advent of globalisation  and liberalisation and resultant removal of Minimum Export
Price and Purchase Price the industry is facing severe price competition from among the exporters and manufacturers,
resultant deterioration in quality. This is besides the competition from synthetic and other natural products in markets
abroad.  Coir faces competition from products like Chinese Grass Mats, Rubber, Sisal etc.  In the domestic market also
liberal imports have created competition from substitutes.  It is export which helps to adjust the imbalance in the
domestic market. 
 
 
5.6       Presently there is no specific scheme to prevent competition from among the exporters and manufacturers.  
However, the following schemes are suggested to reduce the competition:
 
(i)
                  Formation of Manufacturers Consortia: Under this the Consortium may be given the margin money to
procure goods produced, store and supply it for exports according to the requirements of exporters for
procuring and stocking raw materials required for manufacture of  products by the small scale manufacturers,
establishment of Shearing factories, Smoke house etc
 
(ii)
                One time assistance for setting up of Common Facility Centres;
 
5.7       Collection, compilation and publication   of  prices of various products at the production centres . This would
enable the exporters to  quote price for various products after adding overheads and profit.  For this purpose it is
necessary to strengthen the Statistics Wing of the Coir Board.
 
5.8       The Committee understands that the coir exporters face competition in markets abroad from other
natural products like Chinese Grass Mats, Rubber, Sisal and coir products being exported by Srilanka, Taiwan,
Philippines etc. Synthetic products manufactured using improved technology and supported by publicity also
pose great threat to the coir exports. The Coir Geotextiles  are facing competition from Srilanka and synthetic
geotextile materials which dominate the market.  Therefore, the Committee feels that the Government should
provide assistance by reimbursing a portion of the expenditure incurred on brand based publicity abroad
projecting the eco-friendly nature of the coir geotextiles to meet this competition.

6.0       Marketing and Sales
 
6.1       Traditionally coir fibre, coir yarn, coir rope, coir products etc. have been marketed in India by a number of
private traders who book orders from places of consumption in various States in India and supply materials on
procurement from the producers in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.  The Co-operative Coir Marketing Federation in
Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are also engaged in the marketing of coir fibre, yarn and rope in the country.  In the
case of finished products of coir the major market players are a network of Showroom & Sales Depots established by
the Board in important places in India.  A number of producers in the private sector have their sales outlets established
through out the country.  The Apex Marketing Societies like Kerala State Co-operative coir Marketing Federation,
Karnataka State Coir Co-operative Federation and State owned Agencies like Kerala State Coir Corporation, Karnataka
State Coir Corporation, the State Industrial Coir Marketing Society of Tamil Nadu, etc., are also running a number of
sales outlets to market the products of coir in the country.  In addition to this the hawkers and mobile units are engaged
in the marketing of coir and coir products. 
 
 
 
7.0       Marketing Strategy
 
7.1       The Sub-Committee was apprised of the marketing strategy as chalked out and practiced by the Coir Board for
the promotion of Coir Industries as under:-
 
(i)
                  Identification of consumer needs through Identification of specific functional requirements and
modification of product quality and specification to meet the needs and Expansion of marketing outlets
 
(ii)                Projecting comparative advantages of coir products offer competing products.
 
 
(iii)
               Assessment of the market trends and changing taste of the consumer and to advise the industry for
production of products actually required by the consumer public.
 
(iv)              Product diversification and design development in association with national level organisation like National
Institute of Design etc.
(v)                Encouraging private participation in undertaking meaningful publicity.
 
(vi)              Popularisation of value added products through mail order literature and other products literature targeting
selective and prospective customers and Product promotion through publicity and propaganda measures
 
(vii)             Organisation of seminars and workshops with the objective of creating product awareness and Product
promotion through participation in Trade fairs and exhibitions
 
(viii)           Promotion of sales through innovative marketing strategies with the help of Market Development  
Assistance on a regular basis and Organisation  of Buyer-Seller Meet thereby encouraging the small scale
producers etc.
 
(ix)              Formulation of clusters among manufacturers to ensure a collective effort in marketing .
 
 
7.2       The Committee is of the view that steps being contemplated by the Coir Board to promote the marketing
and sales of coir products in the domestic market which interalia include intensification of promotional measures
like publicity through print and electronic media;    increased participation in trade fairs and exhibitions;
organisation of Buyer –Seller Meets in potential regions;  organisation of special sales campaign and festival
discount offer to promote sales; organising collective participation of manufacturers in selected trade fairs and
exhibitions;  popularisation of new products like coir geotextiles, garden articles, coir pith based products

8.0       R&D activities
 
8.1       Coir Board has been provided with Plan funds for organising S&T and R&D Programmes for the development
of the coir industry. The Plan S&T Programmes have been broadly classified into four sub-heads viz Modernisation of
extraction and processing coir fibre, Development of coir processing machinery, Product development & diversification,
Testing and services.
 
8.2       The research & development programmes are being implemented through the two premier research institutes,
Central Coir research Institute, Kalavoor in Kerala and Central Institute of Coir Technology, Bangalore in Karnataka.
As the in-house facilities in the research & development programmes are inadequate in all the departments of CCRI to
meet the requirement of the industry, collaborative projects are also undertaken with reputed R&D institutions engaged
in organising research & development programmes of similar nature. The scheme wise R&D programmes undertaken by
the Board and the details of the beneficiary industrial units, individual and the quantum of benefits achieved by these
units in terms of rise in production, increase in income, quality upgradation etc are detailed below:
 
8.3       Modernisation, extraction & processing of coir fibre and pith
 
8.3.1    Objectives of the scheme are:
 
(i)
                  Modernisation of coir industry by rendering it a clean & pollution free processing technology and the
upgradation of the quality of the fibre produced in the industry.
(ii)                Production of Coirret at the pilot scale laboratory at CCRI.
 
(iii)               To design, develop & standardise machinery for brown fibre production.
 
(iv)              To extend facilities in conversion of coir brown fibre into coir needled felt and testing of coir products.
(v)                Blending of synthetic fibre with coir fibre and evolve non-woven material for production of coir polymer
boards.
(vi)              Collaborative study with reputed organisations on bio bleaching and bio softening of coir fibre.
 
8.3.2    As a ongoing project, a pilot scale laboratory is established at CCRI for the production of COIRRET, a
consortium of bacteria for reducing the period of retting of coconut husk and conversion of green husk fibre into quality
of retted coir fibre. A collaborative research programme was organised for the development of coir composite board
using non-woven fabric and production of decorative board using coir matting as base material with Regional Research
Laboratory, Trivandrum.
 
8.4       Development of coir processing machinery
 
8.4.1    Development of coir processing machinery is an ongoing project under the S&T programmes. The machineries
were developed for processing of coir and popularising  in the industry for improving the productivity, reducing the

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

drudgery of the labour engaged in this sector, improve the earning of the workers and entrepreneurs   and quality of the
products intended for export.
 
8.4.2    In order to increase the utilisation of coconut husks from 35% to 50% produced in India, the main hurdle faced is
the high transportation cost of the raw material, coconut husk to the centralised  fibre extraction units.  There is no well
defined husk collection system existing in the industry as the coconut producers are not aware of the economic value of
the husks.  It is proposed to collect the husks available in the coconut producing sites and fibre extraction should be
organised at the site itself for reduction of transportation cost and cost of the end product.  Keeping this in mind, the
Board entered into a collaborative research project with the PSG College of Technology for the development of a
platform mounted mobile defibering machine. 
 
8.4.3    During the various market delegations to importing countries it was understood that the cost of the Geotextiles
exported by India is on the higher side than the competing countries such as Vietnams, Philippines, Sri Lanka etc.  The
existing technology available for the production of Coir Geotextiles  in India was mainly on traditional coir handlooms. 
As the production takes place in small and medium units, it is very difficult to bring down the cost of production as there
is a well defined wages structure prevailing in the coir industry in the product manufacturing sector.  Studies were
organised by Coir Board for reducing the cost of production of Coir Geotextiles  and also research was conducted for
developing a suitable.   technology  for production of woven geotextiles  without looms.   As a result the CCRI was
successful jn developing a technology for loomless weaving of coir geotextiles .  This technology was further improved
upon and a compact mild steel handloom viz. “Anugraha” was developed by the Institute. 
 
8.5       Product Development and Diversification
 
8.5.1    Product Development and diversified uses of coir are the major thrust area for R&D programmes.  For the higher
utilisation of raw material and production of value added items and for capturing export market and diversified uses of
coir.  The Coir Board has been undertaking various programmes under this head by expending the funds for organising
R&D and S&T activities.  Majority of the coir units functioning in the industry have been benefited by the outcomes of
these R&D projects and also to increase their quantum of export and improve the earnings by producing quality
products and implementing advanced technological developments which were the outcome of these projects. 
 
8.5.2    Research programmes were organised in collaboration with reputed research institutions such as National
Institute of Design, Ahmedabad , IIT, New Delhi. IPRTRI, Bangalore etc. for the development of novel and attractive
coir products especially for export purpose. Development of coir products using high count blended coir yarn was one of
the major achievement under this project. The outcome of these projects was well taken by the industry and most of the
exporters engaged in this sector have taken advantage for improving their performance in exports.
 
8.6       Ruberrised Coir
 
8.6.1    Due to the changing scenario and change achieved in the production sector of the coir industry especially in non-
traditional sector, it was highly essential to identify the areas for using coir for purposes other than the traditional use.
Rubberised coir was one of the items, which has been widely accepted as diversified uses of coir. Further the Coir Board
has imported and installed a needled felt plant at the CICT, Bangalore  for finding new user areas for brown coir fibre. 
The needled felt so developed has been used in different application areas in the field of Geotextiles  and as a Janatha
Mattress. This was also an achievement of the R&D work of the coir Board as the production of the Brown Fibre sector
has increased manifold, which led to the diversified uses of coir such as rubberised coir, needled felt etc.
 
 
8.7       Coir geotextile for soil bio engineering
 
8.7.1    The use of coir geotextile  for soil bio engineering purposes was one of the major breakthrough achieved during
the recent past under the R&D programmes undertaken by the Board. Coir geotextiles is being popularised in countries
in the Europe, USA, Japan, Korea etc.  However the exporters were not in a position to furnish any technical data on the
use of coir geotextiles for increasing their exports. Coir Board in collaboration with reputed organisations Border Roads
Organisations, Central Public Works Department, State Governments, National Highway Authorities, Road Research

8.7.2    A technology was developed under the R&D programmes undertaken by the Board to convert problematic pith

8.7.4    A collaborative research project was organised with M/s. Indian Institute of Packaging, Mumbai for the
production of low cost packaging material and is in progress.  They have developed a concept technology for the

50:50.  NRDC agrees to protect the patents assigned to Coir Board.

conversion of Pith into Organic Manure using Pithplus to two parties viz., 1) M/s. CADILA Pharmaceuticals India Ltd.,

"Key Areas of Action"
 
14.0     Restructuring of the Coir Industry
 
14.1     Excess production, low profitability, competition from identical products, low production technology, high
dependence on labour and trained industrial relations are some of the feature of the coir industry.  All these affect export
of coir and coir products from India warranting restructuring of the industry.
 
14.2     The Committee understands that the Low productivity of traditional technology, age old looms and
equipments, slow phase of modernisation, absence of a systematic collection of raw material, lack of adequate
credit availability, low level of capacity building, inadequate Infrastructural facilities, limited marketing skills,
lack of working capital are the bane of this industry.  The Committee, therefore, feels that  it is necessary to put
in  place  an integrated and complimentary set of measures to encourage and support coir industry so that they
become more productive  and competitive and development  and expenditure takes place in a sustainable and
sustainable  manner.
 
15.0     Creation of Utility Demand
 
15.1     There is lack of initiative  in the part of exporters for undertaking promotional efforts such as direct publicity,
brand promotion, efforts to enter  new markets etc. This is due to the poor nature of the industry.  The Committee feels
that the  Coir Board should undertake promotional campaigns in markets abroad projecting the eco-friendly
nature of coir products for which advance proposals will be given by the Coir Board and necessary approval
should be accorded by the Government even at the beginning of the financial year itself.

16.0     Modernisation for increased  productivity to face price competition
 
16.1     The technology adopted for production in the industry is very old. Production is undertaken mainly on
handlooms.  To achieve increased productivity it is necessary to introduce large scale Modernisation in the case of
textile industry. 
 
16.2     The Committee is of the strong opinion that a Modernisation Fund may be created for extending one time
financial assistance to the exporters  for modernisation of production, importing necessary machinery and
equipments including packaging and labeling machineries and also for setting up of R&D facilities.   This would

17.0     Capturing new markets through delegation, Market missions, publicity etc.
 
17.1     Export performance is still depended upon the demand for the product in the USA and E U countries. Any policy
changes in these countries would seriously affect export. The only alternate is to develop new and new markets in the
developing countries.The exporters are of the view that Coir Board should take the initiate to develop new markets.
Once the products are introduced to a market by 3 - 4 participation in exhibitions by the Coir Board, the exporters would

18.1     To be competitive in the field, product diversification is essential.   The poor nature of the industry does not
allow  large -scale diversification. The existing schemes do not allow any assistance for diversification of production.
Therefore, it is necessary to extend a one-time assistance to the manufacturers and exporters to adopt new technology
for production either by indigenously manufacturing the machines or by importing by reimbursing a portion of the
expenditure subject to certain ceiling, Coir Board may be allowed to implement such a scheme.
 
18.2     The Committee is of the view that the Coir Board should come out with the course of action required to be
undertaken for the product diversification through technology development and forward the same to the
Ministry of ARI for executing the projects. 
 
18.3     The Committee is also of the view that the technological upgradation/automation/quality control  etc. have

therefore necessary to extend assistance to the trade for export production, quality, design development, product
diversification etc.
 
18.4     The Committee feels that the Government may grant the Coir Board the status of an approved agency for
quality inspection of export products which would enable the buyers to utilise the services of the Coir Board for
quality certification.

24.0     Measures Required for Promotion and Proliferation of the Coir Industry
 
24.1       Raw material
 
24.1.1  Estimated consumption of coconut husk for coir production on an average is 37% of the total production of husk
in the country.  The absence of an organised collection mechanism often makes it difficult to the coir industry in major
producing States to mobilize adequate husk for coir production.
 
24.1.2  The Committee understands the need for enhancing the harnessing of coconut husk for coir production
from existing level of thirty seven per cent.  With a view to mobilize husk available in plenty in coconut
producing States and to increase the percentage of utilization of  coconut husk, the collection mechanism will
have to be streamlined with the active participation of NGOs, Self Help Groups (SHGs) etc. through introduction
of an appropriate scheme.  It would pave way for level of utilization reaching 50% thereby facilitating
production unhindered and to increase  output of coir fibre in the country.
 
24.1.3  Quality of end products manufactured depends to a large extent on the quality of inputs/raw material as also its
price competitiveness on the availability of raw material at reasonable rates without an element of escalation of the price
on account of involvement of middle men.  .  It was in this context that the idea of Raw Material Bank in coir sector was
earlier conceived to help Small Scale manufacturers in the private as well as co-operative sector.  Although it could not
be implemented for one reason or the other, the idea gains added importance in the present context of pursuing efforts
for re-generation of the coir industry.   Suitable assistance for formation of raw material banks at cluster level may be
provided through the Coir Board. 
 
24.1.4  The Committee is in agreement with the Coir Board in regard to Constitution of Raw Material Bank in
the coir sector to assist the Small Scale manufacturers in the private as well as co-operative sector.  That is
essential because access to quality raw material at reasonable price assumes great significance in the development
of enterprises in the unorganized/informal sector. 
 
 
24.2       Technology Upgradation – R&D efforts
 
24.2.1  Slow phase of Technology adoption / upgradation in the coir industry is one of the major factors hindering the
development of the coir industry.  In some areas of production, the absence of appropriate and acceptable technology
contributing to the growth and development of the coir industry.  An element of passivity on the part of  workers and
producers to adopt new production and processing methods is another reason for inadequate influence of technology
build up in the coir sector. 
 
24.2.2  There is scope for improvement of technology in areas  like extraction and processing of coir; development of
coir machinery; product development and diversification; testing and  extension.   Presently, the Research &
Development  work in the coir sector is  mainly carried out in the  research centres of the Coir Board viz. Central Coir
Research Institute, Alleppey,( Kerala) and Central Institute of Coir Technology, Bangalore.   Besides, R & D efforts on
a limited scale at public sector undertakings of the Govt. of Kerala and some of the private companies in the coir sector.
Presently the Coir Board has collaboration with 28 Research Institutes for carrying out research on different aspects of
coir. 
 
24.2.3  It is envisaged for entering into collaborative with a few more Research Institutes having expertise in the areas of
enhancing longevity of coir, blending fibre with allied fibre/wool to produce kaaleeno, bio-softening, bio-blending, coir
polymer composites as per the specific requirement of RDSO etc.
 
24.2.4  The Committee is of the opinion that the concerted efforts have to be made towards technology
improvement in the coir sector through research and development.  Improvement of the infrastructural facilities
and strengthening manpower available in research institutes of the Coir Board is necessary to address the

situation. Further, efforts towards areas specific collaborative research with due prioritization based on industry
needs, their better participation and that of nationally reputed R&D Organisations is called for. 
 
24.3     Development of Versatile Spinning Machine
 
24.3.1  Now coir yarn is spun throughout the coastal belt of Kerala on traditional hand-operated wheel (ratt ).  There are
a lot of limitations to this spinning system as  the contrivance used is region/quality specific requiring more man-power,
strain and characterized by low productivity.     The spinning machines available in the jute/sisal industry could be
suitably modified to process coir alone or in combination with other allied fibre.  Although a number of equipments for
spinning coir yarn have been developed and tried over the years with and without the use of power and through
improvisation of traditional ratt, the desired results could not be achieved to the best satisfaction of workers/producers. 
It may be required to source international expertise to develop such a versatile spinning system.  
 
24.3.2  The coir industry requires a versatile spinning machine compatible for production of different varieties of
coir yarn with higher productivity, less strain and  capable of undertaking commercial production.
 
24.4     Improvisation of the Existing Handloom
 
24.4.1  Different varieties of coir mats are produced on different types of looms.  One type of the loom cannot produce
the other types of mats, thereby reducing the scope of product diversification.  The CCRI is working on the development
of a versatile  handloom on which all the major four varieties coir mats can be woven.  The loom is also being provided
with pneumatic devices so as to reduce the strain of working on it. 
 
24.4.2  Popularisation of Eco-friendly dyeing and Effluent Treatment Plant
 
24.4.3  Coir yarn/fibre is dyed using chemical dye-stuffs.  The effluent arising out of this dye-stuff is also required to be
treated before letting off.  The Central Coir Research Institute of the Coir Board in collaboration with  IIT, New Delhi
has developed 16 novel shades out of natural dye stuffs. The details were disseminated to the trade.   In the next phase, a
pilot plant for production and distribution of natural dye-stuffs to the export oriented production centres of the industry
is to be set up.  This will enable the coir industry to source eco-friendly dye-stuffs locally. 
 
24.4.4  A cost effective technology for treatment of effluent arising out of retting of coir fibre and wet-processing needs
to be developed so as to meet the revised norms of the Pollution Control Board.  The  Coir Board pursues research
activities for the development of a technology using chemical treatment and also environment friendly root-zone
treatment technology. 
 
24.4.5  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI should extend all possible help to the Coir Board in
envisaging strategy for popularization of eco-friendly dyeing and Effluent Treatment Plan either through in-
house experiment or transfer/acquisition of required technology.
 
24.5     Popularisation of Coirret and Pithplus
 
24.5.1  The Central Coir Research Institute (CCRI) had developed a bacterial formulation viz. Coirret which can carry
out retting of coconut husk within a period of three months and treatment of green husk Coir Fibre (mechanically
extracted) within 72 hours to make it similar to retted fibre in terms of quality and colour.  As the traditional method of
extraction of fibre after retting is becoming unpopular in view of that process polluting the lakes and lagoons where
retting is undertaken, there is the need for popularizing the application of Coirret  for processing green husk fibre as an
alternative solution.  Besides the concern for pollution, the un-hygienic nature of work involved in retting and retrieval
of retted husk from the pits also results in new generation of workers drifting away from the work.  Field
demonstrations on the use of Coirret for faster retting without affecting the quality and strength of coir fibre need  to be
organised in many more places.  Coirret  helps in reducing the pollution by degrading leachates from the fibre upto
70%.   This in turn reduces the cost of effluent treatment either. 
 
24.5.2  The Committee desires that the Coir Board should take adequate research activities and field
