CHAPTER-VIII
 
 INSTITUTIONAL AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK AFFECTING THE SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
 
8.0       Legal framework affecting the Small Scale Industries is satisfactory
 
8.1       At present Small Scale Industries are governed by the Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951.
However, various authorities in the Central and State Governments as well as the local authorities formulate the
Acts/rules and regulations. These legal regulations can be classified into labour-related issues ; tax-related issues ;
finance-related issues ;location-related issues;  product-related issues ; environment-related issues and safety, security,
hygiene, health and welfare-related issues, etc
8.1.1    The regulatory frame work, particularly pertaining to labour-related Laws, is cumbersome. The laws, rules and
regulations that have accumulated over the last several years are many and their compliance is cumbersome. The burden
of inspections under various laws has proved to be too onerous for the SSI units to bear. They have adverse bearing on
the promotion and development of small scale industries.
 
8.1.2    The Committee understands that the plethora of laws, rules and regulations and the burden of inspections
under these, have affected the SSI sector adversely. Therefore, with a view to simplifying and streamlining the

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/173rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:41]
system of inspections under these laws, and also reducing the burden of statutory returns/ registers prescribed
hereunder, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005 (earlier referred to as the Small Enterprises
Development Bill) must be enacted without further delay. Following measures are therefore required to be taken
in order to give fillip to the promotion and development of Small Scale Industries: -
 
(a)
               A single Unified Act governing the rules pertaining to retrenchment and layoffs and social benefits for
employees.
 
(b)
               Enactment of Single Comprehensive Small Enterprises Development Act for SSEs similar to the
Industrial Development and Regulation (IDR) Act.
 
(c)
                Comprehensive Social Security Scheme for widening the social safety nets as proposed in SED Bill.
 
(d)
               Since the Inspector Raj is causing severe harassment to Small Scale Units, therefore, the provision made
in the proposed legislation for giving good bye to Inspector Raj to wipe out the tyranny  of Inspector Raj.
 
8.2       Awareness among SSI entrepreneurs about India's obligation under WTO regime
 
8.2.1    Government is constantly assessing and monitoring the impact of the removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs)
and Globalisation on the growth and development of Small Scale Industries (SSIs) in the country.  Though removal of
QRs have exposed the SSIs to a greater competition, yet the SSI sector has continued to grow. However, even after the
removal of QRs, protection to the industries is available in the form of raising custom duties upto the bound levels,
imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of surge in imports, etc.
 
8.2.2    Some of the incentives & measures provided by the Government to enable the SSI to compete in the globalized
and liberalized regime include raising the central excise duty exemption limit from Rs.50 lakh to Rs.1 crore, a scheme
of capital subsidy of 12% for investment in technology upgradation in select sectors, raising the eligibility limit for
coverage under the Credit Guarantee Scheme from Rs.10 lakh to Rs.25 lakh, continuation of financial support (up to
Rs.75,000/-) for obtaining ISO 9000 & ISO 14001 certification up to the end of 10
th Plan.
 
8.2.3    Removal of QRs does not automatically remove all the protection available to the domestic producers.  India can
regulate imports through adjustments in tariff within the bound rates.  Apart from tariff, action under anti-dumping and
safeguard measures can be taken to provide protection to the domestic producers.  For initiating anti-dumping action
and imposition of safeguard duty separate Directorates are already working under the Ministry of Commerce and
Industry  and the Ministry of Finance respectively. 
 
8.2.4    The Government has put in place several measures to help small enterprises become globally competitive. 
These include special focus on areas such as technology upgradation , infrastructure assistance through the cluster
approach, timely availability of credit, adoption of modern management practices, use of electronic infrastructure and
other IT applications, marketing and timely information dissemination, including sensitization of small industries to the
emerging challenges of trade liberalization.   Government is fully aware of the WTO environment and is taking
appropriate measures for preparing the Small Scale Sector to meet the challenges of liberalization/globalization.  Taking
a view of the whole situation, a new SSI policy including certain new schemes/incentives were announced during the
National Conference on SSI held at New Delhi 30-31 August 2000.
 
8.2.5    The WTO Agreement contains a number of provisions and annexes that have an impact on the industry.  It has
not been found feasible to monitor the detailed impact of these agreements sector specific and cluster-specific.  
However, industry units are encouraged to bring to the notice of Office of DC(SSI) either of their-own or through the
Associations so that the aspects of the WTO agreement that are not found suitable to them are brought to the notice of
Ministry of Commerce and Industry to take appropriate action in the matter.

entrepreneurs about India’s obligations under the WTO agreements and their impact on various sectors of small scale

attend the meetings. The representatives of the local SSI Associations should also be invited to the meetings of SLIIC,
which should play a major role in rehabilitation of sick units. SLIICs should discuss issues regarding delay in carrying
out viability studies and initiating nursing programmes of viable units as also progress in revival of units, which have
been placed under the nursing programme. In case of sick units where assistance is needed from other agencies, such
cases may be discussed in the SLIIC meetings. Further, the issues relating to the progress made in implementation of the
revised guidelines issued by the RBI based on the recommendations of Kohli Working Group should be discussed to
ensure that the banks strictly follow these guidelines for detection of sickness at an early stage and take remedial
measures for speedy rehabilitation of sick SSI units identified as potentially viable.
 
 
 
 
8.8       Raising equity participation from the existing 24% to 49%  (FDI) in SSI sector
 
8.8.1    The administrative Ministry to raise the FDI limit in equity participation is Department of Industry Policy and
Promotion (IPP), Ministry of Commerce & Industry, who do not have any such proposal at present.   However, the
Steering Committee on FDI in various Sectors, set up by the Planning Commission in August 2002, recommended
enhancement of equity participation to 49% in SSI Sector, which was discussed with the stakeholders.  Based on the
discussions with the Stakeholders and others concerned, the following views were communicated to the Department of
IPP:
 
8.8.2    “ The  Ministry has no objection to the enhancement of equity participation / FDI limit from 24% to 49% in the
case of SSI items where investment limit has been enhanced to Rs.5 crore.  FDI in this respect could perhaps be routed
through the FIPB Type agency with representation from stakeholders.  Details in this respect could be worked out in due
course.”
 
8.8.3    The Committee is of the considered view that the Department of Industry Policy and Promotion (IPP),
Ministry of Commerce & Industry may explore the possibility of  raising equity participation in the SSI sector
from the existing 24% to 49%  (FDI) for better technology transfer in SSI sector in which FDI can be encouraged
for sizeable investments towards larger returns.

8.11.1  The Anti-Dumping mechanism comes under the purview of the Directorate General of Anti-Dumping and Allied

including that falling under the SSI sector keeps a watch on the tariff being applied on the various products.

and massive imports.  There is also the provision for imposition of countervailing duty, if required.

SWOT analysis of Small Scale Industries is as follows:
 
 
 
            The Committee is of the view that for streamlining and strengthening the SSI sector in the national
economy, the focus should be on the following:-
 
(i)
                 Providing full credit, technology upgradation, modernization and marketing
support to the SSI sector;
 
(ii)               Infrastructure upgradation in general particularly in the major SSI industrial
clusters;
(iii)             Freedom from the plethora of rules and regulations existing in the SSI sector,which is known as
Inspector Raj;
 
(iv)             Full support to the service industry to fulfill its true growth and employment. generation
potential; and
 
(v)               Training of existing and potential entrepreneurs and workers on a massive scale.

Re-orienting the role of DC (SSI)
 
 
            The Committee, in the changing scenario of liberalization and globalisation, feels that  the role of the
Office of DC(SSI) should be reoriented, broadly on the following lines:-
    
 (a)    The DC (SSI) would need to be re-designated as the Central Development Commissioner for Small and
Medium Enterprises, [CDC (SME)] and he and his organization  (Small Industries Development Organization -
SIDO) equipped and   strengthened to view the sector as a composite whole, without losing focus on the need for
generation of employment as well  as the specific developmental/promotional requirements and inter-linkages of
each distinct component of the composite sector, e.g., tiny enterprises, small enterprises, etc., and the products
and services produced by them.
    
(b)  The Office of CDC (SME) would need to widen and continuously up-date its knowledge base regarding the
global trends in policies and Government interventions concerning the SME sector and recommend and
design/implement appropriate measures for continuously enhancing the competitiveness of the sector in India.  It
would also need to continually ascertain the “ best practices” in this field, within the country and abroad,  and

Key Areas of Massive Action  For Revitalization of SEs
 
Cluster Approach : A step  ahead towards synchronization  of SEs
 
 
            The Committee strongly believes that the Small Enterprises can be developed in cluster through the Small
Industry Cluster Development Programme. The common facilities like testing, infrastructure such as power and
roads, assured supply chain and credit should be provided within the clusters so that these enterprises can grow
without any hindrance. The small enterprises must be provided marketing assistance by organizing Vendor
Development Programme (VDP) to bring small and medium enterprises on a common platform to decide their
marketing strategy and to resolve their problems mutually.
(Para 1.6.5)
 
Technology management for SMEs
 
 
            The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that schemes for technology up-gradation for SMEs
should be made more functional and accessible to the existing entrepreneurs as well as the first generation
entrepreneurs.  Due budgetary provisions should be made for R & D so that outcome of the research work
should assist the entrepreneurs in cutting the cost of production as well as enhancing the value engineering of
SMEs product through product development and product diversification.  The Committee recommends that
public private partnership approach may be focused by the Government for infusion of latest technology in the
SMEs sector.
(Para 1.6.7)
 
Broad basing of the ownership of SSI enterprises
 
            The Committee observes that majority of SSI units are primarily proprietary concerns.  The required 
investment has been provided by the property owners themselves.  Such type of ownership pattern suffers from
severe limitations.  The main limitation that such units face is in their access to institutional finance and
development of the units is restricted by non-availability of finance at the time of need. In order to encourage
broad basing of the ownership of SSI enterprises, provision of some additional facilities for units going in for
company formation could be considered.  The SSI units going in for company formation should be provided
some additional facilities like incentives to form cooperatives, concession to create infrastructure, increase in
investment limit etc.
(Para 1.6.8)
 
Closer cooperation between large and small scale sector

            The Committee has been given an understanding that a large number of SSI units are not able to utilize

availability of raw materials, labour and marketing problems.  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that

assisting them in publishing their products and adivisng them about new and emerging markets would promote
and proliferate SMEs in India.

            The Committee observes that  there are absence of technical persons and trained workers in the SSI

need for increasing capitalization of SSIs  to enable them to procure better technical equipment, training inputs,

Adequate and timely supply of coal to Small Scale Industries
            The Committee takes note of the fact that Indian Small Scale Industries suffer from inadequate  supply of
coal to the SSI units. As per the extant policy, the supply of coal to the SSI units falls under the non-core sector. 
As a result, there has been huge mismatch between the demand and supply of coal to SSI sector.  As many of the
SSI units require timely and adequate supply of coal for running the units, non-availability of coal has adversely
affected to growth of SSI sector.
(Para 5.7.1)
 
            The Committee is anguished to note that Coal Companies are not maintaining separate statistics
regarding the supply of coal to SSI units.  The 16% of coal is supplied to non-core sector consumers including
SSI units under sponsorship and linkage based on the Maximum Permissible quantity (MPQ).   The Committee
feels that the requisite quantity of coal is not supplied under the sponsorship and  linkage based on MPQ which is
arrived at the average lifting of coal for the past three years, by the units.  Coal companies are supplying coal to
SSI units on the basis of availability of coal after meeting the requirements of core sector consumers like Power,
Cement, Steel etc. and often pro rata cuts are imposed in certain coal companies where availability of coal for
non core sector after meeting the requirement of core consumers do not permit the booking under MPQ.

of Coal and Chairman, Coal India Limited in the matter.  Having taken into consideration the mater placed
before the Committee and the evidence tendered by the witnesses, the Committee feels that following strategic
steps may be undertaken for adequate supply of coal to the SSI units:-
 
(i)
                        SE sector should be brought at par with the 'core sector' consumers;
(ii)                      The Coal Companies should establish Depots in each district/State for distribution/marketing of
Coal, either by themselves or through outsourcing with adequate accountability on the
outsourced entities.
(iii)                    Direct linkages should be given to the SSI units in all such districts which produce Coal.

                    Government should consolidate the Small Scale Industries in the country by   implementing

Railway as Preferred Mode of Transport
            The Committee is  however, constrained to observed  that  the Railways have done very little to encourage
the SSIs to choose railways as their preferred mode of transport.  As the rake load (2200-2300 tonnes) is the basic
transport unit of the Railways, the SSI units are not able to utilize the Railways for transportation of either the
raw material or the finished products due to smaller quantum. The introduction of movement of goods in rake-
load/train-load and running of point-to-point trains since 1982 created problems in transportation of raw
material/finished product of Small Scale units.  Moreover,  the closure of 79 marshalling yards between 1985 and
2000 due to rake-load/train-load movement restricted the collection/delivery of smaller loads originating from
adjoining sections.  Besides bulk volume of delivery are not accommodated at rural stations.  The container
services of the Railways, which can carry up to 24 tonnes, has also not served the cause of SSI sector due to
limited terminals in the country (52 locations throughout the country).  Due to these constraints, most of the SSI
units have to depend on roads for transporting raw material and finished products.

            Global Economy and Generation of Additional Employment
Considering the higher potential for growth in the SSI sector in terms of output,  employment and export,
the committee is of the considered that  the Government should strengthen and facilitate the SSI sector to enable
it to remain competitive in market-led global economy and generate additional employment.  In recognition of
employment generation potential, the SSI sector has been assigned a target of 12% of annual growth rate and
creation 44 lakh employment opportunities in the Tenth Five Year Plan.  Keeping in view the potential of Small
Scale Industries in India, the National Common Minimum Programme as announced by the Government on 27
th
May, 2004 stressed on providing full credit, technological and marketing support, infrastructure upgradation in
the major industrial clusters and to free the sector from Inspector Raj. But mere announcement would not
work.  Now the time has come, when the Government should keep its promises of consolidating the Small Scale
Industries in the country by implementing   the Action Plan to enable the sector to achieve the stipulated 12%
growth rate and accordingly provide employment generation opportunities to millions of youths in the urban as
well as rural areas. 
(Para 7.21.4)
            Erratic And Inadequate Flow Of Credit To Ssi Sector
The Committee is astonished to find the pathetic condition of the SSIs and the erratic and inadequate flow
of credit to SSI sector which  has been the key reason  for continuous languishing of this sector.  Although the
credit to SSI has increased from Rs.38,109 crore  for financial 1997-98 to Rs. 58,278 for financial year 2003-04 - a
growth of 53% but what concern the Committee the most is  the declining  share of SSI in Net Bank Credit over
the same period has from 17.5% to 10.4%.  No efforts seem to have been taken in the last seven years to arrest
the declining trend.  It was primarily result of lack of policy initiative by the Government and apathy of banks in
particular towards SSI lending. Various factors like high risk perception, higher transaction cost in processing
SSI loan applications, lack of credit rating facilities for SSI units contributed further to the woes of Small Scale
Industries.  Moreover, the non-adherence to RBI guidelines on SSI lending by the banks (e.g. inadequate/
delayed sanction of credit despite guidelines on computation of working capital requirements of SSI units/
prescribed time schedule for disposal of loan applications, insistence on collateral despite instructions from RBI
about no collateral for loans upto Rs.5 lakh and upto Rs.25 lakh for units having good track record, etc.) is
continuing till date.
(Para 7.21.5)
             Mortality Rate
The Committee express its concern that it is because of the inadequate credit flow to SSI sector, the
mortality rate is increasing year after year and sickness of SSI units is posing a matter of great concern.
Moreover, After the deregulation of interest rates regime from 18-20% in 1997-98, the lending rates have come
down to around   9-12% at present.  As per extant guidelines the banks are required to fix their own prime
lending rates (PLRs) and the maximum band over the PLR.  The existing guidelines for banks for lending SSI is
plus/minus 2% on PLR which translates into a range of 8.25% to 12%.  While interest rates for Large Scale
Industries are negotiable and are generally at sub-PLR.  Limiting to the plus / minus two per cent of PLR de-
motivated the banks  in general to lower the interest beyond PLR minus two per cent.
(Para 7.21.6)
Declining Net Bank Credit Flow To The Ssi

Strategy to ensure time
            The Committee, therefore, feels that  the foremost requirement is to extend timely and adequate credit  to
the  SMEs at reasonable rate of interests.  The following Course of Action may be adopted by the Government: -
(i)
                 Treating the Small Scale sector on the priority basis,  banks should fix self-set targets of
minimum 15% per annum for growth in advances to the SSI sector over the previous year's
achievements and in relation to the overall target set by them for growth in their Net Bank
Credit for the year.  Shortfall in achieving this target should be deposited with SIDBI by the
banks at rate of interest linked to "bank rate".
(ii)
               RBI should issue guidelines to banks to the adopt differential rates of interest under three
slabs of loans to Small Scale units as per the following rationalised pattern:-
Upto Rs.1 lakh                       Not exceeding bank rate plus 1.5%
Rs.1 to 2 lakh                         Not exceeding bank rate plus 2.25%
Rs.2 to 5 lakh                         Not exceeding bank rate plus 3%
Rs.5 lakh and above              Not exceeding bank rate plus 4%

             RBI should issue effective guidelines to be followed by the banks strictly for speedy revival of
potentially viable sick SSI units.  Test of viability of sick SSI units should be conducted with

debt restructuring whereby the outstanding debt of sick SSI units could be restructured
through various forms such as moratorium, rescheduling of debts, infusion of fresh capital,
etc.
(iv)
             Each public and private sector bank to set up at least a "SSI Desk" at each branch under a

(v)               Lead banks to set up Institutes for training of SE entrepreneurs in such districts where major SE
clusters are located.

(vii)
           Since SIDBI is meant solely for promoting SSI, there is the need to re-orient its role viz

         While extending credit facilities Bank should be advised to observe the credit history of the

Prime Minister Rozgar Yojna (PMRY)
 
1.1     The Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) scheme was launched on 2nd October, 1993 in the country. The objective of the scheme is to
assist educated unemployed youth from the weaker section of the society in setting up micro enterprises in all economically viable activities as per
the parameters of the scheme .The scheme is implemented in both urban & rural areas of the country from 1994-95 onwards.
 
1.2       The objective of the Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) is to mitigate the problem of unemployment amongst the
educated unemployed youth belonging to weaker sections of the society through setting up of self employed tiny units.
The annual target of employment generation under the PMRY is as per the target envisaged for the Scheme in the Xth
Plan document of the Planning Commission which envisages to create 50 million person years of gainful employment
opportunities over the Xth Plan. Accordingly, a target of 1.65 million person years over the Xth Plan or an annual target of
employment of 3.3 lakh persons or 2.20 lakh units per annum has been envisaged under the PMRY.

3.3       The Committee is not at all satisfied with the performance of PMRY in the States of Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal and

should keep monitoring over timely and effectively implementation of Schemes under its purview and accordingly apprise the Committee.
 
  
3.4     The analysis of the performance under PMRY during the last three years based on the reports received from RBI shows that  besides
other reasons, performance under the Scheme in States is positively correlated with the recovery of loan over dues under the Scheme. Other
reasons for failure of Scheme are competition from Central/State Govt. Schemes offering higher subsidy, difficulty in getting the desired
target group due to higher level of per capital income, non viable projects, reluctance on the part of banks to sanction and disburse loan,
militancy, etc.  The Committee, therefore, is of view that the Ministry of ARI in tandem with the banking division, Nationalized Banks and
the State Governments of Bihar, Jharkhand , West Bengal and Maharashtra should take suitable steps ensuring compliance with under -
mentioned yardsticks for better functioning of PMRY in these states:-
(a)
   Minimise the rejection ratio  by banks against no. of application received.
(b)   Avoid the stoppage/delay of disbursement  in  PMRY loans on flimsy   grounds
(c)    Quick disposal of application on the part of DICs  and forwarding the same  to banks

4.0       Working of Khadi Industries in West Bengal, Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Bihar
4.1       The financial assistance provided under khadi sales rebate and Interest Subsidy has largely helped the khadi sector
to enhance its performance over the previous year.  While the Interest Subsidy propelled the flow of working capital from
banks, the rebate element helped khadi institutions to boost sales and to get relief from the  blockage of working capital to
a certain extend. The Rebate and Interest subsidy are two important components used for the furtherance of the khadi
programme. The rebate is a promotional expenditure provided on  khadi sales for neutralizing the cost due to higher wage
component thereby to boost its sales. Similarly, the quantum of Interest Subsidy provided on funds availed from
Commercial Banks against ISEC issued by KVIC helps to enhance credit flow to khadi programme.
 
4.2     KVIC has launched an Insurance Scheme for the welfare of khadi workers which brings a sense of social security
among the khadi workers.  The portion of khadi grant is paid to Insurance Company as KVIC’s share of the premium
under this scheme. Similarly, KVIC has launched a Product Development, Design Intervention and Packaging (PRODIP)
for the betterment of khadi sector.  Certain part of khadi grant is utilized for this purpose also which in turn helps for the
furtherance of khadi sector.

Industries in these select States.   The Committee got an opportunity to interact with the representative of NGOs/Industrial Associations of the
respective States and the representative of the respective state Governments.

4.6       West Bengal
 
4.6.1    The Committee was informed that the West Bengal has established its status under Khadi programme for its unique art and craftsmanship.
The climatic condition and abundant local resources have widened the scope for the development of Khadi programme in the State. The districts of
Malda, Murshidabad, Nadia, Birbhum, Bankura, Hooghly, Purulia have the extensive coverage of the Khadi programmes, especially for silk &
Muslin Khadi.
 
 
 
 
4.6.2    The Committee was informed that Mulberry cocoon cultivation in the districts of  Malda, Murshidabad and parts of Birbhum had been
increased adequately and as a result of which, silk reeling and weaving unit have been concentrated in those localities. Further, a good number of
skilled artisans are also available in those area. As such, the scope of silk Khadi activities in those areas have been expanded considerably. Jiagunj,
Raghunathganj, Piarapur area of Murshidabad district is famous for the Garad varieties, while the Bishnupur in Bankura district is famous for the
exclusive Baluachari design. Besides Mulberry silk, Matka Silk, Tassar Silk are produced in good quality and in huge quantity also. In production of
silk Khadi the state contributes 36.37 per cent  of total silk Khadi production in KVI sector and ranks in 1st position in overall performance under
KVIC.
 
4.6.3    The Committee was further informed that another prestigious product of West Bengal is Muslin Khadi. Muslin Khadi has reached to its
fineness to the extent of 500 metric count and there is no competitor of this industry. The main characteristic of this industry is large-scale
employment of women artisans. Around 8,000 women artisans in the state are engaged in this industry. Muslin Khadi Industry has grown in the
districts of Murshidabad, Nadia, Burdwan and Malda.  In production of Muslin Khadi, the state ranks at the top contributing 55.25 per cent of the
total production of Muslin Khadi in KVI sector.

4.10     Bihar
 
4.10.1  Consequent to the   division of Bihar in the year 2000  almost the entire Industrial and rich mineral base along with many of the power
projects of the erstwhile state of Bihar  went to the newly  created   State  of Jharkhand, leaving Bihar an Industrially backward state.  The fact that
Bihar remained largely an agricultural  state   necessitated the  formulation   of a new Indusial Policy, 2003 for Bihar in order to give a boost and
impetus  to industrial growth.  However, with a large agricultural base and available huge manpower resources, Bihar, with a rich historical and 
cultural heritage, has good potential for agro processing, bio technology, tea processing,   software technology, tourism  and other allied industries 
along with handloom, sericulture and handicrafts. Insufficient infrastructure   development, inadequate supply of power, frequent floods, low flow of
capital investment  from outside, adverse C.D. Ratio are some of the major impediments in the industrial growth of the State.  Competition from
well-established products and services from other States and through imports such as through Nepal pose a threat to the viability of the local
industry.  But the State Government is alive to the situation and is trying hard to remove these impediments in conjunction with the Government of
India for creating a more conducive environment for industry and investment.
 
4.10.2  The Committee was apprised that the State Government have taken a series of steps for improving the investment and industrial climate in the
State, which  mainly  included the announcement of the Industrial Policy, 2003; announcement of the Stores Purchase Preference Policy, 2002;
reconstitution of Industrial Area Development Authority and establishment of the amalgamated Bihar Industrial Area Development Authority; and
restructuring of Public Sector Undertakings in the State.
 
4.10.3  Some of the recent developments that have taken place in the State on the industrial side include setting- up  of new units, and opening of
closed industrial  units   such as  Katihar Jute Mill, Rameshwar Jute Mill etc.  The State Government have also set up a Software  Technology   Park
in Patna which has stated  functioning.   On   the  food  processing side the Agri Export Zone has been notified and exports of Litchi has increased  
nearly eleven fold from a level of 35 MT in the year  2000-01 to 396 MT in the year 002-03.  It has also being decided to include Honey and
Vegetables in the Agri Export Zone.  A separate Agri processing side, adequate training ,  EDP courses etc.   are being  organized   to promote the
development of  food processing industries.  Similarly, having regard to the good potential for Tea in Bihar, especially in Purnea,   Kishanganj and

4.10.4  The State Government  have given priority to promotion of infrastructure for industry.  Some of the major initiatives include setting - up of
the Software  Technology Park, establishment of Growth Centres,  setting up of the Export Promotion Industrial Park at Hajipur, the  proposed Air

4.10.5  The Committee has been apprised that Bihar has about  1.32 lakhs weavers and nearly 34,000 Handlooms and Power looms Programmes for
development of  clusters of  weavers, establishment of  work-shed, provision of looms and equipments and other measures have been undertaken,   A
comprehensive handloom development project involving a total cost of Rs.8709.80  lakhs  has been prepared and sent to the Government of India for
approval.  Similarly, on the Sericulture side, schemes are being implemented for promotion and development of Tasar, Mulberry and Eri both by the
State  Government and through the Central Silk Board (CSB).  These  include    a composite Tasar and  Eri Development project for  Banka and
Jamui districts  by the CSB at   a  total cost of Rs.1434.00 lakhs and a mulberry project in Purnea and   Kishanganj districts at a cost of Rs.140.00
lakhs.  A Special composite project for sericulture development in the State   for Rs.3709.00 lakhs  has been sent to  the Central Government for
approval.
 
           
4.10.6  The Committee has been apprised that there is a large sugar industry in the State.   The total area under sugarcane in the State during the year
2002-03 was  R.2.54 lakh  hectares with sugarcane  production of   nearly 119 lakh tonnes.  There are  10 sugar mills functioning in the State, all of
them  in the private  sector,  with a combined capacity of nearly   37,700 TCD.  The production of sugar during  the year 2002-03 in   the State was 
4.08 lakhs tonnes.
 
4.10.7  The State Government is thus putting in all efforts for industrial development and promotion   of investment   in the State both in the
manufacturing and the services sector.  The Industrial Policy  2003 provides  the policy framework for the various schemes  that are being
implemented  with this objective.   The  special  package announced in  1997  for industries in the North-East by the Union Government   and for
Utranchal and Himachal Pradesh recently, needs to be provided for Bihar at the earliest.
 
4.10.8  The Committee understand that in post partition phase (since the year 2000),  Bihar  remained  an industrially  backward  state with
insufficient and poor infrastructure development , inadequate supply  of power, low capital flow, adverse C.D. ratio.  The announcement of 
new industrial  policy has not made any observable  headway.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view  that  the Central Government  in
tandem  with the state government has to start  from the stretch  for launching effective   industrial  growth and development  of the  state. 
Since the state  has   largely been remained  an agricultural state.  A   new beginning    can be  made in the areas of Agro -rural  industries
by initiating following course of action:-
 
(i)

(ii)               De-centralisation of setting up of software technology  park in each district of the state;
(iii)             Promotion and proliferation of  tea processing units in Kishanganj, Purnea and Araria;
(iv)             Institutional and logistic  support to Agro -Rural Industries, specially  Sugar Mills and its  backward linkages;
(v)               co-ordination with Central Silk Board (CSB) for development of TAsar, Mulberry, Eri development in Bhagalpur , Banka,
Jamui, Purnea and Kishanganj;
(vi)             Promotion of Handloom and powerloms programmes for development  of clusters of weavers, establishment of work shed   at
Panchayat level of each districts.  Government may approve the composite schemes  for  development   of Handloom and
sericulture in the state; and
(vii)           Having regard to the fact that Bihar is an industrially backward  state, the  special package announced in  1997  for industries in
the North-East by the Union Government  and for Utranchal and Himachal Pradesh recently, needs to be provided for Bihar at

difference of project cost up to  Rs. 25 lakhs over and above Rs. 10 lakhs is provided for setting up viable Village Industries projects.   For certain
categories of entrepreneurs such as women, physically handicapped, ex-servicemen and those belonging to SC/ST/OBC, minority communities,
North Easter Region, including Sikkim, hill border and tribal areas, Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Lakshdweep etc. margin money is @ 30% for
projects up to Rs. 10 lakhs.  The Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) is implemented with the active involvement of 27 nationalized
scheduled commercial banks, their Regional Rural Banks.  Now this programme has deeply percolated  its roots in the countryside and got unique
identity.

Prime Minister Rozgar Yojna (PMRY)
 
 
             The Committee is not at all satisfied with the performance of PMRY in the States of Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal and
Maharashtra, although slight     improvement has been  there during 2004-05 as compared to the last year for the corresponding period. 
The Committee observes that it is desirable that Ministry of ARI  in tandem with the Ministry of  Finance, banks and state Government 
should keep monitoring over timely and effectively implementation of Schemes under its purview and accordingly apprise the Committee.
 
(Para 3.3)  
          The analysis of the performance under PMRY during the last three years based on the reports received from RBI shows that  besides
other reasons, performance under the Scheme in States is positively correlated with the recovery of loan over dues under the Scheme. Other
reasons for failure of Scheme are competition from Central/State Govt. Schemes offering higher subsidy, difficulty in getting the desired
target group due to higher level of per capital income, non viable projects, reluctance on the part of banks to sanction and disburse loan,
militancy, etc.  The Committee, therefore, is of view that the Ministry of ARI in tandem with the banking division, Nationalized Banks and
the State Governments of Bihar, Jharkhand , West Bengal and Maharashtra should take suitable steps ensuring compliance with under -
mentioned yardsticks for better functioning of PMRY in these states:-

INTRODUCTION
 
  
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having   been  authorized   by the Committee, hereby present this  One
Hundred Seventy Fifth Report on Key Concern Areas of Small Scale Industries in Select States (Ministry of Small Scale Industries).

2.         The Committee visited Banglore, Hyderabad, Ranchi, Patna and Kolkata from 26 th September to 6 th October, 2004 and interacted with the representatives of
respective State Government, State Chamber of Commerce, Industrial Federations/Associations and Banks on problems and prospects of Small Scale Industries in the
respective States.  The Committee further undertook study visit to Bhubaneshwar and Ahmedabad on 21 st and 23 rd January, 2005 respectively to interact with the
representatives of the Government of Orissa and the Government of Gujarat to take stock of ground realities regarding the problems being faced by Small Scale Industries in
the Orissa and Gujarat.
3.         The Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries undertook study visit to Lucknow and Mumbai from 2 nd to 4th November, 2004 to interact with the
representatives of the State Government of Uttar Pradesh and the Government of Maharashtra , Associations and Banks on the issue of problems being faced Small and
Medium Enterprises in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra.
4.         The Report has been prepared on the basis of the information provided by the Government, SSI associations and banks and the feed back received during the
interaction with the representatives of select State Government, banks and Associations.  Chapter-I of the report deals with the Micro Analysis of Problems and Prospects of
SSI in the select states viz. along with the strategy for combating the problems.  Views/ suggestions of the SSI Associations/Federations have been given due importance
with the hope that the Ministry of SSI would examine and consider those issues in detail.   Chapter-II of the report deals the the Functional aspects of the
Schemes/Programmes undertaken by the Ministry of SSI to promote and proliferate Small Scale Industries in the country and their actual working in the select states.  Both
the chapters contain specific and general recommendations.   The Committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should peruse with the concerned Ministries/Departments for
implementations of observations/recommendations pertaining to them.
5.         The Committee in its meeting held on 09.05.2005 considered and adopted the Report.
 
3          I thank the Department of Public Enterprises for providing valuable inputs to the Committee.

CHAPTER – I
 
MICRO ANALYSIS OF PROBLEMS AND PROSPECTS OF SSI
 
(A)              ORISSA
 
Orissa is endowed with mineral resources like manganese, coal, iron ore, bauxite etc. Besides it has a vast coastline which provides the potential for harnessing marine
resources. Yet the state represents a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty. The quick estimate of Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) the State suggest that primary
sector constitutes nearly 38% of NSDP followed by Service sector (28%). Secondary sector (17%) and Tertiary sector (17%) in other words the rate of shift from agrarian
economy to industrial one is quite marginal for the State.
 
1.1 Liberalization and Globalization has changed the face of state economy and has thrown great challenge for SSI and they no longer operate under protected  environment,
but have to face harshness of competition both from within the country and outside. Such change requires technology up gradation, modernization, backward and forward
integration, skill development and better marketing. This requires funds for fixed capital and working capital need and the shortage of these funds seriously affects the SSIs
of Orissa leading to sickness.
 
1.1.1 The committee was apprised that Super Cyclone occurred in Orissa during the 1999 also greatly affected the SSI Units of Orissa. SISI, Cuttock  has undertaken a study
to diagnose the factors responsible for sickness in Orissa by taking some samples of sick S SI units which were identified for revival. The major reason for inadequate
working capital is the poor equity limit, lack of financial strength of landing institution and high interest rate. The major reasons for sickness of SSI units in the states are :-

showing healthy trends of growth in Orissa.
 
1.1.2 The Committee interacted with the representatives of Orissa Industries Association and Orissa Young Entrepreneurs Association in the presence of representatives of
Ministry of SSI, Government of Orissa and the Banks, The Committee came across that Orissa is having only 2% of SSI units in India and the share of Orissa in total Bank
finance to SSI units is only to the tune of 1.08 %. The associations pointed our following solutions for improving SSI sector in the state :-
 
(i)         The rehabilitation package should be implemented promptly within a time frame to revive the unit. It is fact that inadequate finance and untimely finance by the
banks whether term loan or working capital is responsible for sickness of SSI steps should be taken to strengthen the forum of SLIIC and the promotional agencies and the
financial institution to do pro-active role to overcome the difficulties faced by the units.
 
(ii)        As SSI units in Orissa were affected badly due to super cyclone, a special liberal package to the affected units by extending all types of concession, and also
extending the period of repayment should be drawn in consultation with Reserve Bank of India.
 
(iii)       Priority should be given by Nationalized Banks to finance potential SSI unit in a particular area.
 
(iv)       Compromised settlement of NPA: As the response from SSI unit in Orissa for NPA settlement is encouraging. So more time should be given to cover more number
of NPA units.
 
(v)        Different financial linked schemes like CGTSI, CLCSS, NEF, Composite Loan scheme, SME find of SIDBI Should be popularized in Orissa as most of the
entrepreneurs are not aware of these schemes.
 
(vi)       The innovative financing like venture capital, factoring services etc. should be popularized which will improve the position of the unit to get finance easily.
 
(vii)      Orissa State Financial Corporation which is the chief term loan provider to SSI unit in Orissa is in urgent need of financial restructuring, so as to clean up their
balance sheet. The mechanism of state government, SIDBI and the IDBI have to play a proactive role in this.
 
(viii)      There should be a liberalised OTS Policy by Financial Institutions for sick SSI.
 
(ix)       The forum of State Level Inter Institutional Committee i.e. SLIIC should be made more effective. The decision of the SLIIC should be made compulsory
implementation by other agencies concerned with revitalization of their units.
 
1.1.3 The Committee was informed by the representative of Orissa State Financial Corporation Employee’s Union that following relief an concession may be granted to the
state :-
 
(i)         Impress upon the SIDBIJIDBIICommercial Bank to waive the entire interest that has accrued on Financial Assistance to OSFC w.e.f. 1.11.99 to 30. 06. 2004.
(ii)        The interest payment of Rs.160.53 crores already made by OSFC to TDBIJSIDBI/ Banks may be adjusted against principal liabilities of these institutions after such
waiver of interest.
 
(iii)       To impress upon SIDBI to continue with refinancing under SMEs Fund, which is already made available to SIDBI by the Union Government.
 
(iv)       Development strategy for promotion of SSI units in economically backward district like Bolangir and Koraput, Kalahandi and extension of income tax and central
Excise exemption on the lines of North East and Uttranchal and Himachal Pradesh.

1.1.4    The Committee observes that Orissa demonstrates a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty as the state, despite having mineral and marine resources, has been
bereft of sustainable industrial growth and economic development. The Committee finds that the cherished Charter of the Planning Commission which was “to combine a
rapid rise in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing production and offering opportunities to all for
employment in the service of the community”, has not seen the light of the day in the state. The state has been devoid of planned development giving rise to the
economically backward district like Bolangir, Koraput and above all the Kalahandi.
 
1.1.5      No major efforts have been made to put the state on the industrial development track, and therefore there is the lack of ancialirisation of industries in the Small and
Medium sectors. Besides, the general problems like lack of Infrastructural development and marketing assistance and shortage of timely and adequate credit flow etc., the
state has also been the victim of natural calamities like super cyclone in 1999 which have actually devastated the Small scale industrial set up and thus arrested the industrial
growth and promotion and proliferation of small and medium enterprises in the state.
 
1.1.6    The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the financial institutions should come forward for providing timely and adequate credit flow to the entrepreneurs for
accelerated industrial growth and promotion of SMEs in the state. The Committee recommends that concerted efforts must be undertaken for popularization of venture
capital, factoring services and other financial linked schemes like CGYTSI, CLCSS, NEF and SME Fund of SIDBI.
 
1.1.7      The Committee further recommends that following key areas must be selected for effective action:
 
(i)        Strengthening the functional aspects of state level inter-institutional Committee (SLIIC) and promotidnal agencies;
 
(ii)    Financial restructuring of Orissa State Financial co-operation by seriously considering the proposal of adjustment of interest payment to the tune of Rs. 160.33 crore
against principle liabilities besides wavering of the interest;
(iii)        Extension of income tax and central excise exemption for setting up of SMEs in economically backward districts like Bolangir , Koraput and Kalahandi on NER,
Uttranchal and Himachal Pradesh line;
 
(iv)     Special liberal package to super cyclone effected SSI units like rehabilitation package and one time settlement (OTS).
 
(B) GUJARAT
 
1.2        Small Scale Industry in Gujarat has witnessed impressive development. There are
over 10,000 SSI registrations granted every year during last decade. As per 3rd Census,
Gujarat accounts for 11.2% of working SSI units in the country. The performance of S
industry in Gujarat, therefore, has been very impressive. The State Government has introduced various schemes to provide support to SSI as part of Gujarat Industrial Policy
2003. Providing interest subsidy @ 5% to new as well as existing SSI units for undertaking.  The small scale industry is facing difficulties with regard to credit flow from
financial institutions. The Committee was informed as under:
 
(i)         The investment in small scale sector is over Rs.450 crore. The credit flow from nationalised  banks does not match with investment taking place in SSI. Against the
total turn-overn of over Rs. 12,000 crore per annum by SSIs in Gujarat, the credit flow is hardly Rs. 1500 cr. The industry, therefore, suffers from inadequate credit flow.
 
(ii)        Higher rate of interest on term loan prevents availability of funds, as higher rate of interest, about 13% interest per annum is charged.
 
(iii)       Credit Guarantee Scheme for SSI has not become popular with banks and SSIs continue to face difficulties in providing collateral guarantee.
 
(iv)       Credit  Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation  of SS1s take off of this scheme has been negligible in Gujarat . The banks are not providing
assistance under the scheme, thereby depriving SSI units of the scheme introduced by Government of India.
 
(v)        Assistance for Cluster Development in Gujarat, there are 83 product clusters in small scale sector e.g. Rajkot for diesel engine; Jamnagar for brass parts industry;
Morbi for ceramic industry; Surat for power loom industry. Accounting for over 43% of investment, 48% of production and 47% of employment in overall figures of SSIs.
However, only one cluster has been taken up for assistance by Government of India under the scheme. There is a need to cover clusters in the state.
 
(vi)       Raw material shortage the small scale industry, especially the engineering industry, has been facing problem of availability of steel. The SSI requires about 2,70,000
MT of steel, 40,000 MT of rounds and 50,000 MT of wire rods problems of availability of steel.

1.2.1    The Committee interacted with the representative of Ahmedabad Foundry Cluster,
Morbi Chamber of Commerce & Industry, Wadhwan Industries Association, The Gujarat
Dyestuffs Manufacturers’ Association and Gujarat Chamber of Commerce & Industry. The SSI Associations, as a whole suggested for improving the status of SSI units with
the
following strategy : -
 
(i)         Rate of interest being charged by lending institutionals/banks to SSI be fixed at Bank Rate plus 2.0% for term loan and 4.0% for working capital.
 
(ii)        Moratorium on repayment of term loans provided to SSI units should be at least two years from the date of first disbursement and repayment should be spread over a
period of 6 to 8 years.
 
(iii)       One Bank Branch in every District catering exclusively to SSI.
 
(iv)       Operation of the Technology Development Modernisation fund scheme administered by SIDBI be extended to five years instead of three years.
 
(v)        National Equity fund of SIDBI covers projects upto Rs.25 lakhs. It is proposed that this limit be raised to Rs. 1.0 crore.
 
(vi)       The one time Settlement scheme should be extended for period of another 3 years with simplified norms i.e. installment for payment of dues should be extended to
36 months.
 
(vii)      Non Performing Assets (NPA) is considered on 90 days non payment of Interest/ instalment should be raised to 180 days as most of the SSI units are realising  their
proceeds after a period of 5 to 6 months.
 
(viii)      Revival of Co-operative Banking Sector.
 
(ix)       Exit Policy for the entrepreneurs of SSI Sector which provide.
 
(x)        Exit from the business. Provisions of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Act as of the developed world.
 
(xi)       One time settlement scheme which expired on 31 ‘ December, 2004 should be extended for another two years and 10% down payment should be asked instead of
25% from the entrepreneurs taking benefit of scheme.
 
(xii)      Restoration of S.S.I. Exemption on small scale ceramic to stand erect in cutthroat competition by large-scale industries.
 
(xiii)      The small Scale Unit, desiring modernisation by importing machineries form abroad shoud be given exemption from payment Custom Duty.
 
(xiv)     Grant loans at lower rate of interest for modernisation of S. S .1. Ceramic Unit and
 
(xv)      A passenger train from New Bhuj to Bareily via Morbi.
 
1.2.2    While the Committee is pleased to note the impressive development of Small Scale Industries in Gujrat, as almost ten thousand new SSI units are registered each
year, however, the Committee feels that the Ministry of SSI should act promptly in co-ordinating  activities with state Government, Banking division and steel sector for
combating the problems of inadequate credit flow, lack of infrastructure development and inadequate supply of steel in the engineering segment. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of SSI should invite from the state Government proposal under Integrated Infrastructural Development (LID) Scheme. Adequate impetus may
also be given for covering more cases under cluster development approach in the state. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of SSI should co-ordinate with
the steel units in public and private sector for ensuring timely availability of steel raw material to SSI units in the state.
 
1.2.3      The Committee desires that the proposal of extending the operational period of Technology Development Fund Scheme from 3 to 5 years may be suitably
examined.

(C) KARNATAKA
 
1.3       Karnataka has been pioneer in industry. In recent times, Karnataka has emerged as the knowledge and technology capital of the cQuntry making rapid strides in the
economy of the sate. IT and related industries, biotechnology and strong research and development institutions have given Karnataka a pride of place in the global market.
Growth of small-scale industries in Karnataka has been very rapid since 1982-83. As on 3 1’ March, 2003, 2,98,218 small scale industrial units have been registered with the
Directorate of Industries and Commerce. It is estimated that the investment is to the order of Rs.616374 lakhs providing employment for about 17,22,190 persons. Largest
concentration of small scale industries is in Bangalore Urban District, which is 53,665 followed by 27,084 units in Belgaum  District, 18149 units in Mysore district and
17,615 units in Tumkur district. Koppal has 3,451 in small-scale industries.
 
1.3.1 Problem being faced by SSI Sectors in Karnataka
 
(i)         Inadequate quality power supply,Lack of transportation in rural areas, lack of assured marketing facilities and huge domestic market still lie untapped,
 
(ii)        Raising inputs cost as compared to price of finished goods resulting into stagnant SSI sector;
 
(iii)       Lack of strong processing and mining technology back-up and poor technology and slow pace of technology upgradation due to poor R&D facilities.
 
(iv)       Vast scope for setting up of Electronic Units, Software, Hardware and Biotechnology in SSI field.
 
(v)        Delay in approval of Agree export zones at Chitradurga, Kolar, Bangalore, Tumkur and Bijapur.
 
            The Committee was apprised that the five Year “Perspective Plans” have been prepared by all the 27 Districts Industries Centres in the State highlighting mineral,
agro and human resource potential of the Districts. Keeping in view the needs of the industry,the following statregy may be adopted for promotion of SSI units :-
 
(1)        Financial assistance from Govt. of India towards industrial infrastructure projects, up gradation of surface transport infrastructure, augmentation of railway network
and connectivity to ports, upgradation of New Mangalore Port and assistance for expansion of Karwar Port (under Govt. of Karnataka).
 
(ii)        There is a backlog of Rs.429 crore of State Investment Subsidy payable to SSI units in the State. Government of Karnataka.  Suitable ways and means
advance/interest
free loan from Govt. of India to liquidate this arears preferably in one or two installments.
 
(iii)       Early approval of Govt. of India for the industrial clusters proposed.
 
(iv)       Early approval of Govt. of India to locate the Automotive Testing Facility in Bangalore/Dharwad of Karnataka.
 
(v)        Special Economic Zones Development Bill 2003 may be expedited;
 
(vi)       In addition to manufacturing exports, software and services exports from the State also be considered for the purpose of determination of quantum of financial
assistance to States under ASIDE scheme!
 
(vii)      Indian Institute of Technology (ITT) at Dharwad may be favorably considered.
 
(viii)      Central assistance for setting up of minor airports in uncovered destinations like Mysore, Bellary, Bijapur, Hassan, Karwar, Hampi, etc. would facilitate both
industrialization of backward areas as well as tourism sector.
 
1.3.2    The Committee observes that Karnataka is becoming the hub for proliferation of sun rise Small and Medium Enterprises units in the field of Bio-technology,
Electronic, Soft ware, the Committee, therefore, recommends that the State should be given top priority for encouraging investment in specific sectors in those select sectors
viz. Pharma, Automobile and Auto components, Textile, Garments, iT, ITES, Sugar, Food Processing, Engineering and Metallurgy (fron & Steel and Cement) with greater
R&D impetus for accelerating modernization and up-gradation of mining processing technology.
 
1.3.3    The Committee desires that the outstanding dues to the tune of Rs. 429 crore at state investment subsidy must be reimbursed to the state SSI units at the earliest.

(D) Bihar
 
1.4       After the partition Bihar, the development activities became un-organised and ultimately the entire Industrial activity shifted to Jharkhand state and Bihar remained
confined to agriculture and cottage Industries. Therefore, there should be a long term plan to develop the agriculture sector as well Industrialization in the State. On the line
of provisions and facilities provided to the North East States, Bihar should also be provided the economic and development package. The Central assistance should be
enhanced reasonably for the establishment growth centres. Under the integrated industrial development projects, there should be a change in financial assistance package in
which the ratio of Government of India and CIDB may be at 4:5 instead of 2:3. There is a need to make the growth centres/I.I.Dflndustrial  estates etc. tax free for a
considerable period of time for the consolidation of the Small and Medium Enterprises. For the development of agriculture based industries, the centre should provide
sufficient find separately for basic Infrastructural support.
 
1.4.1    As regards the institutional arrangements, the Committee desires that a branch of National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) be opened in the state. There is
further need to establish one centre in each commissionery which will prepare technology based project report for Industries based on Agriculture products. The Central
Government should open a centre in Bihar for export related enquiry, assistance and cooperation. For the marketing of handicraft products in International market, a centre
should be opened in Patna. As per the policy of RBI, CD ratio should be fixed a 70% for the Capital investment in the State. At present the raw material of Bihar is sent to
other states and the same is procured by the entrepreneurs of Bihar from such States. Therefore, the Committee desires that an inter-ministerial task force should be
established which may be coordinated by the Ministry of Small Scale Industry.

1.4.10 The Committee has been apprised that the main reason for closure of SSI units in the state are non availability of working capital, irregular supply of electricity, tough
competition in marketing of the products, non-up-gradation of the technology, problem in professional management system, lack of advertisement of their product in the
market, non rehabilitation of the sick unit at its appropriate time etc. Therefore, there is the need to arrange working capital for them, regular supply of electricity, provision
of priority in the Government purchases for the Small Scale Industries, provision to grant loan for technology up-gradation to SSI units and to give serious attention in the
basic facilities in these industrial areas. There is the need for developing and providing the important facilities such construction of roads, power supply, water, power plant,
quality testing lab and common facility centre etc.
 
1.4.11             The Committee is of the view that in the changing scenario of increased industrial activity, there is need to impart more training to the entrepreneurs of the
state in the field of Management, Cost effectiveness, Financial Management, advertisement and publicity, patent laws, new technologies in marketing, Inventory
Management etc. To have the global standard of entrepreneurship there is a need to provide additional basic Infrastructural facilities so that the entrepreneurs of the state can
be trained with such a high quality management training inputs which at later stage can be so strong that the identity and eiistence of entrepreneurs can be not effected by the
influence of World Trade Organization.
 
1.4.12              Status of Power supply to Industries
 
1.4.13         The Committee was apprised that Bihar has an installed capacity of around 3000 m.w. Thermal power accounts for over 90 per cent of the total generating
capacity in the state. Implementation of various power projects have been in different stages. These projects cover thermal power at Nabinagar, Chandil , Patna, Kursela and
Tenughat and Hydel Power at KoelKaro, Kadwan and Sankha. Government of India recently announced a package of new schemes worth Rs. 12,036 crores for the State
including assistance to power projects. Several pithead thermal projects are also on the anvil. The Eastern Region of the country (installed capacity 9000 m. .w.) with 6000
m.w. of power operates in an integrated mode as a single system. With the central share available from this system and inequity due to trade equalisation policy, the supply
of power has been erratic in Bihar. The State Government is aptly placing highest priority on the development of power sector in its economic planning to bridge the demand
gap. It is also encouraging private sector participation in power generation and power distribution in the State. Setting up of captive power plants, to meet the existing as well
as future demand for power of industrial units, is being encouraged in the state. Installation of Diesel Generating sets by entrepreneurs are also permitted for running the
enterprises. With the encouraging power policy pursued by the State Government, th industrial activity in the state would pick up in the years ahead.

(H)       UTTAR PRADESH
 
1.8       The Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries of the Committee on Industry interacted with the representatives of State Government on the issue of
status of Small Scale Industries in the state. The Sub-Committee was apprised that upto March 2004, about 4,91,435 units have been established in the State providing
employment opportunities to 18,79,547 persons. In addition there are around 10 lac  artisans and more than 1 lac handicraft units in the State. In the Agro sector, 4 agri-
export zones have been established in the State out of which two are for mango and one each for potato & Basmati rice. Development zones for honey, bananas, amla  &

1.8.1    The Sub-Committee interacted also with the representative of Federation of Association of Small Industries of India, Eastern U.P. Chamber & Industry, Provincial
Industries Association, Rajkiya Audyogik Asthan Sahkari Samiti Ltd., Laghu Udyog Bharti, Uttar Pradesh Small Scale Soap Industry Association, U.P. Pharmaceutical
Manufacturers Federation, Confederation of Indian Pharma Industry, Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association, Kanpur etc.
 
1.8.2    The Sub-Committee was apprised of the problems being faced by Small Scale Industries in Uttar Pradesh which are as under:
 
(i)         Lack of infrastructure facilities viz, continuous power supply, high cost of transportation of the raw material and finished goods, linkage with multifarous agencies
thereby their maneuvering capacity is very limited;
 
(ii)        Growth of SSI units in the present day is tardy, as entrepreneurs are hesitant to take up industrial ventures, so, there is dearth of applications coming up for SSI
Sector;
 
(iii)       Lack of technology for producing goods at competitive rates;
 
(iv)       SSI units are highly dependents upon the larger corporate sector;
 
(v)      SSI units are facing stiff competition, lower margins, lower prices etc;

1.8.3    The SSI Associations suggested following strategic course of action to remove the problems being faced by SSI units in Uttar Pradesh:-.
 
(i)         The availability of loan at right time is one of the fundamental requirements of the Industry. The CD. ratio of the State which is 30.4% as against 59.4% at the
national level clearly shows that the position of credit facilitates to the Small Scale Units is not satisfactory and that it requires constant monitoring.
 
(ii)        It is evident that nationalised banks are not taking adequate interest in advancing loans to SSIs. They still demand collateral securities up to the loan amounting to
Rs.25 Lacs which is against the norms. Necessary instructions to banks may be issued.
 
(iii)       In order to improve the global competitiveness of the domestic industries and also to provide for quality infrastructure, the Govt. of India has launche  Industrial
Infrastructure Up-gradation Scheme. The scheme lays down that 25% of the total cost of the project would be borne by other stakeholders of the respective cluster with a
minimum industry contribution of 15% of total project cost. It is suggested that the provision of 25% contribution as above may be relaxed and State Govt. or State Govt.
Institutions may be allowed to contribute the above share.
 
(iv) SIDBI provides guarantee against composite loan of Rs.25 Lacs under Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries. Under this scheme only a few special RRB,s
NSIC, NEDFI, SIDBI & few commercial banks who have entered into an agreement with the Guarantee Trust are authorised  to operate the scheme whereas SFCs have been
kept out. It is therefore, necessary that all the SFC’s and commercial banks may be permitted to participate in the implementation of the scheme.
 
(v)        It would be in the fitness of things that one consolidated & integrated code of rules should be applicable to the SSI units, so that they may not face complexities of
rules and hardship and utilize their time for productive purposes.
 
1.8.4    The Committee feels that Uttar Pradesh, like Bihar, has been bereft of actual industrialization and therefore the State has more or less become an agriculture state.
The Committee, therefore, views that massive efforts should be made for promoting  and 
proliferating Agro Rural Industries and Food Processing Industries in the State. Union Ministry of SSI and API should chalk out strategy for promoting SMEs in field in the
state and accordingly institutional support like opening up of agree export zones and opening up of Agricultural development centres must be provided in the state. Suitable
central assistance may be provided for R & D purposes in the field of agro rural industries.
 
1.8.5    The Committee is also of the view that adequate attention must be given to improve the working conditions of Handicrafts and Handlooms units in the state and
through diversification of products, the profitability of the handloom and handicraft units be enhanced. Suitable strategy should be undertaken for domestic marketing and
export of Lucknow’s Kurta and pyjama and Chicken print clothes to international market.
 
1.8.6    The Committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should examine the proposal whether under Industrial Infrastructure up-gradation scheme the provision of 25% of the
total cost of the project to be borne by the stakeholders of respective cluster may be relaxed and instead the State Government / State Government institution may be allowed
to contribute the share of the stake holders. The consent of the State Government in this regard may be sought and accordingly the Committee may be apprised of.

coding registration has been launched.
 
2.2       Working of credit linked Capital Subsidy Scheme
 
2.2.1    Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation in Small Scale Industries has been started by DC(SSI) in year 2000 which provides 12% subsidy
(subsequently raised to 15% ) to selected sub sectors on institutional finance for technology upgradation . The technology related needs for process modification and product
diversification can be fulfilled by SSI sector through the scheme. Action is being taken to enhance the scope of this scheme to cover more areas by O/o DC(SSI).
 
2.2.2    The purpose behind introduction of CLCSS is to motivate and facilitate SSI units to upgrade their technology through infusion of institutional credit. The strategy
adopted for this purpose is to provide 12% upfront capital subsidy on institutional finance availed to facilitate technology upgradation in small scale sector. The ceiling of
loans eligible under the scheme is presently Rs. 40 lakh.
 
2.2.3    The corpus fund created under the scheme is Rs. 600 crore for years of operation from Oct. 2000 to Sept. 30, 2005. Till February 2005, an amount of Rs. 23.86 crore
has been utilized under the scheme which includes an advance of Rs. 5 crore to SIDBI and Rs. 3 crore to NABARD for operationalising  the scheme. The slow progress
under the scheme is due to general inhibition on the part of SSI units to go for technology upgradation . The announcement made under General Budget for the year 2004-05
for enhancement in the rate of subsidy and the ceiling of loans eligible under the scheme will help to make the scheme popular among the SSI units.

2.3       Working of Credit Guarantee Scheme
 
2.3.1    The Credit Guarantee Scheme was launched with a view to alleviate the problems of collateral security faced by the small enterprises, particularly first generation
entrepreneurs, and to remove the impediments in flow of credit to Small enterprises sector. The problems in the implementation of the scheme pertains to low level of
awareness about the scheme amongst the field level officers of MLIs, negative mindset of the MLIs due to greater volume of administrative work in the small enterprises
lending and may be their bad experience in the past on a similar scheme, bankers’ traditional/usual comfort with collateral security and perceived high risk nature of small
enterprises sector. These problems of the bank branches need to be seriously addressed by the management of the banks. By enhancing the awareness about the scheme
among the field level officers of MLIs through seminars/training, the progress under the scheme could be improved. Furthermore, expeditious enhancement of the Corpus
Fund up to the envisaged level of Rs.2500 crore under the scheme would increase the comfort level of participating MLIs and encourage them to avail the scheme on a much

2.10.1 The export-import data obtained from Department of Commerce, Ministry of commerce and Industry indicate that India’s imports from China have increased to some

2.10.2    The Committee was apprised that MIs. A.C. Nielsen on behalf of Ministry of
done an evaluation study. As per the findings the said study, major potential export mar for SSIs exports are US, EU and Japan. The potential export-worthy items in the SSI
sec have been categorized into three broad categories:
 
(i)         Potential items produced by SSI units amongst the top 100 items imported by major markets, which do not figure in the top 100 items exported from India to these
major markets:- The product groups that hold potential for SSI exports are agriculture, marine and allied products along with engineering! electrical! electronic product
group. The study identifies Japan as a potential market for exporting agriculture, marine and allied products whereas the European union and the US can be tapped for
enhancing SSI exports of engineering/electrical and electronic items.
 
(ii)        Potential items produced by SSI units amongst the top 100 items imported by major markets, which do not figure in the top 100 items exported from India to these

EU as the potential markets for textile whereas Japan would be the ideal destination for export of chemicals product groups.

major markets:- The potential for SSI is in various product groups like agriculture, marine and allied, chemicals and allied, leather items, textiles and other items. The EU
has been identified as the potential market for textiles including sports equipments whereas export of leather items holds potential for the US and the EU.

2.11     Challenges of globalization and liberalization
 
2.11.1  The Committee desires that the Government should take measures for preparing SSI sector to meet the challenges of globalization and liberalization under the WTO
regime. However, the basic concern of the Committee is the protection and promotion of domestic SSI sector under the prevailing global market economy. Therefore, the
continuous and concrete efforts should be made by the Government to protect the domestic Small Scale Industries from the on-slaught of adverse impact of globalization and
liberalization through appropriate tariff adjustment, anti dumping measures and other safeguards. Simultaneously the process of strengthening SSI sector and acquiring the
requisite competitive resilience should be .enhanced on the ground level. The Committee is in agreement with the views of SSI associations I federations that the Ministry of
SSI should make efforts for Streamlining and strengthening the Anti-dumping mechanism
 
(i) Conversion of Quantitative restriction (QRs) into rationalised tariff regime for providing protection to the domestic SSIs;
 
(ii) Implementation of VAT and safeguard duties to protect domestic producers in consonance with WTO provision; and
 
(iii) Expeditious disposal dumping cases are anti-dumping actions thereto, in view of almost all SSI products under open general license (OGL) list.
 
212      Legal framework
 
2.12.1  The Committee desires that legal framework affecting the Small Scale Industries must be satisfactory in order to give fillip to the promotion and development of
Small Scale Industries Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa, Jharkhand. The following issues may be taken up on priority basis and the Ministry of SSI should pursue
with the concerned Ministries: -
 
(i)         A single Unified Act governing the rules pertaining to retrenchment and layoffs and social benefits for employees.
 
(ii)        Enactment of Single Comprehensive Small Enterprises Development Act for SSEs similar to the Industrial Development and Regulation (IDR) Act.
 
(iii)       Comprehensive Social Security Scheme for widening the social safety nets.

the Companies Act i.e. mandatory provision requiring the large enterprises to show in the entries of their Balance sheets the amount due for payment to the SSI units to
enable SSI units/suppliers to get payments as agreed upon.
 
(vi)       The SSI sector needs the Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Act, therefore, that the Ministry of SSI should continue to pursue for legislation of the Limited Liability

2.12.2 The Committee views that small scale industries is the engine of growth, therefore, SSI units must be given the space to grow into medium enterprises. In the context

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE
COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
ORISSA
 
            The Committee observes that Orissa demonstrates a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty as the state, despite having mineral and marine resources, has been
bereft of sustainable industrial growth and economic development. The Committee finds that the cherished Charter of the Planning Commission which was “to combine a
rapid rise in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing production and offering opportunities to all for
employment in the service of the community”, has not seen the light of the day in the state. The state has been devoid of planned development giving rise to the
economically backward district like Bolangir, Koraput and above all the Kalahandi.
(Para 1.1.4)
 
            No major efforts have been made to put the state on the industrial development track, and therefore there is the lack of ancialirisation  of industries in the Small and
Medium sectors. Besides, the general problems like lack of Infrastructural development and marketing assistance and shortage of timely and adequate credit flow etc., the
state has also been the victim of natural calamities like super cyclone in 1999 which have actually devastated the Small scale industrial set up and thus arrested the industrial
growth and promotion and proliferation of small and medium enterprises in the state.
(Para 1.1.5)
           
            The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the financial institutions should come forward for providing timely and adequate credit flow to the entrepreneurs for
accelerated industrial growth and promotion of SMEs in the state. The Committee recommends that concerted efforts must be undertaken for popularization of venture
capital, factoring services and other financial linked schemes like CGYTSI, CLCSS, NEF and SME Fund of SIDBL
(Para 1.1.6)
