Recommendation in 178th Report
 
1.         The Committee observes that since their inception the CPSEs had initiated a wave of industrialization in their adjoining region. The CPSEs
were direct mainstay for several small  scale ancillaries and supplies and many more indirectly. These Units had thrived on the orders from CPSEs.
The Committee is of the view that if the trend could continue this would have benefited both parent company and the ancillary units.
(Para 27)
Action Taken Report
 
2.         Originally, Ancillaries were established as suppliers for components to mother factories during 1960-70’s when manufacturing was at its
infancy in the country.
 
3.         Manufacturing industry started growing from 1980 onwards, with industries being set up viz, State Government Assisted, Small Scale and
Private Enterprises as small and medium Units. The larger units (automobile or capital goods like Machine Tools etc.) in turn commenced sourcing
their requirement of components and assemblies from these units, also, in order to obtain competitive process and advanced technology.
 
4.         Today the Small Scale Units, other than Ancillary Units established in the country have taken a lead to upgrade and equip their facilities with
modern high-tech machines viz, CNC machines, adopting processes and manufacturing methods that have significantly reduced the cost of
manufacture.
 
5.         Simultaneously with   this development, the requirements of the mother Industries’ also changed and in order to compete effectively the large
industries shifted to products of higher standards and higher technologies that require higher quality parts, in low volumes with shortened  deliveries.
 
6.         While these transformations were taking place the Ancillaries failed to upgrade the manufacturing facilities and with their existing old units
and machinery are able to take up only primary machining operations on the raw material supplied by the mother factories and are not in a position to
supply the high quality components required by the manufacturing industries.
 
7.         Today outsourcing has permeated to such an extent that finished components ready for assembly, are available. This has been the primary
reason for the shift that has taken place in out-sourcing by mother industries from Ancillary to other small scale and medium industries.
 
8.         However, the Ancillaries are still being supported by mother industries to the extent they are able to supply high quality parts. In addition to
the above mother factories have been providing technology support by way of engineering, inspection etc. despite the limitation for utilizing the
services of ancillaries as on date.
 
Further Recommendation of the Committee
 
9.         The Committee acknowledges the efforts made by the mother CPSEs to enable the ancillaries to meet their requirements. The Committee also
impresses upon the ancillaries to upgrade technologically and diversify their products and market profile so that the CPSE does not suffer due to the
drawbacks of ancillaries. The Committee is of the view that   in a competitive and open market, the CPSE is entitled to minimize its cost to remain
competitive, yet efforts should be made to utilize these  existing facilities by upgrading them.

Recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted the reply of the Government
 
Recommendation in 178th Report
 
1.         Considering the resource requirement of the HMT for its revival and the Committee’s consistent   emphasis on need to encourage the CPSE to
generate their own resources to assume full autonomy, also appreciating the long association of ancillaries with their present HMT Company and
taking a view of their offer to purchase the sheds at the price ascertained by State Government agency TECSOK as against the market prices which is
demanded by the HMT,  the Committee recommends that the CMD of the HMT, in exercise of the powers vested  in him, on taking a lenient and
favourable view  on demand of the ancillary owners, constitute a sub-committee in the Board of Directors to review the issue in consultation with
stakeholders within the parameters  of the Company’s financial requirements, such sub- committee should furnish its report to the Board of Directors
of the Company with in a time frame who may then take a final view on the issue in its earliest meeting.
(Para 29)

Director, HMT Machine Tools, Company Secretary and the Chief of Asset Management to examine all the relevant issues concerning the demands of
the HMT Ancillary Units Entrepreneur’s Association including the transfer of the industrial sheds. The Committee has submitted its report which was
deliberated twice in the Board Meeting of HMT Limited and the following works consider:

practices in regard to such matters. Moreover, any form of concession shown to the private entrepreneurs would attract serious objection and
comments form audit and C & AG.
 
7.         In case the Company was compelled to accept the demands from the Entrepreneurs Associations, the loss on account of the same would have
to be compensated / reimbursed by the Government in the form of grant.

9.         In view of the above, it is once again felt that the transfer of ownership of the industrial sheds to the existing licensees could be considered

accordance with the procedures laid down by BIFR. Surplus assets of land, is also being utilized by the PSEs to fund their own revival plans in a
number of cases presented to BRPSE/Government. The money realized through the sale of land etc. is ploughed back to fund the revival schemes of
such companies. While disposing off land, urban land norms as prescribed by the State Government are followed.
 
3.         As the land held by the PSEs is of varying types ie on limited time lease or free-lease or free-hold in their own name and is not a property of

4.         However, the Ministry of Urban Development has already initiated the process of formulation of policy guidelines relating to land held by the
Government including held by CPSEs/ Statutory/Registered bodies. These guidelines are at present under discussion/formulation. The intention is to

to all the land holding of Central Ministries/Departments. This would facilitate uniformity and common standards of efficiency and transparency in
land management and disposal practices in Central Government.
 
Further Recommendation of the Committee

Recommendation
 
Streamlining the ARI sector
 
The Committee understands that the Agro and Rural Industries need further reinforcing and strengthening through
streamlining the ARI sector and by ensuring timely policy interventions. The committee is of the considered view that
the contribution of this sector can be further consolidated and strengthened by ensuring timely and adequate delivery of
credit, technology upgradation, marketing support in the form of financial support for exhibitions, design intervention
and packaging, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of ARI should make strive in this regard.
The committee foresees that   amendment in the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956 would lead further
to streamlining and strengthening the activities in the KVI sector.

(Para: 1.5)
 
Action Taken
 
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries appreciates the recommendations of the Committee. Most of the credit flow to the
agro & rural industries is through banks. This is further supported by way of margin money subsidy under the credit
linked subsidy schemes of Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) and Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana
(PMRY). Under these schemes, loans are provided to the prospective entrepreneurs by banks after assessment of the
project reports and the margin money part of the project is borne by the Government through its budgetary allocations.
 
In order to improve credit flow to agro and rural industries sector, KVIC holds regular review meetings with banks to
ensure achievement of targets fixed under REGP. In addition, the following steps have been taken for improving credit
flow under the PMRY:
 
Reiteration of RBI guidelines on keeping interest rates at PLR or less.
Interaction with State Governments, RBI and Banks to reduce gaps  between sanctions and disbursements.
Issue of instructions by RBI to the banks to avoid under-financing of projects.
Similarly, the Ministry of SSI has taken up from time to time the issue of improving credit flow to the SSI sector with
the RBI. These issues include taking up measures like increase in the limit of exemption from collateral security, setting
of targets for growth in advance, opening of specialised SSI banks, time-frame for disposal of loan applications, etc.
These measures have also helped in the improved credit flow to the ARI sector.
Further to above, creation of an independent Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has reinforced and strengthened the
functioning of the ARI sector as a whole, by highlighting its present status and ensuring timely policy interventions
needed. The contribution of this sector can be further streamlined and strengthened by ensuring timely and adequate
delivery of credit, technology upgradation, marketing support in the form of financial support for exhibitions, design
intervention and packaging, etc. Further, to streamline and strengthen the activities in the KVI sector, the Khadi and
Village Industries Commission Act, 1956 has been amended.
 
Recommendation
 
Monitoring mechanism
 
The Committee finds that the monitoring mechanism at the Ministry level includes both structured as well as informal
but regular monitoring. Secretary (ARI) periodically monitors implementation of PMRY and REGP along with other
schemes being implemented by the Ministry.  Secretary (ARI) also monitors the implementation of the National
Common Minimum Programme. The Committee believes that the ministry of ARI would achieve the targets set in the
Action Plan for the year 2006-07 without any hindrances.(Para : 4.2)
Action Taken
The performance of the schemes being implemented by KVIC, Coir Board and PMRY and the declaration made in
National Common Minimum Programme are reviewed regularly at the level of Secretary in the Ministry. KVIC and
Coir Board are also reviewing the performances of their respective schemes at their level on regular basis. On the basis
of monthly and quarterly performances of progress in various sectors of development, appropriate follow up actions are
taken by the KVIC, the Coir Board and the State Governments.
 
With these efforts, in 2004-05, against the target of generating 5.25 lakh additional job opportunities under Rural
Employment Generation Programme (REGP), 5.30 lakh job opportunities were generated in the country. During 2005-
06, 5.68 lakh jobs opportunities were created against the target of 5.50 lakh. Thus, during 2004-05, and 2005-06, the
achievement under REGP has crossed the annual target. 
 
Similarly under PMRY, as per the data made available by the RBI, there has been significant improvement in the
implementation of the yojana in 2004-05 and 2005-06. As per the data made available by RBI, in 2004-05, against the
target of generating 3.75 lakh additional job opportunities under PMRY, 3.72 lakh additional job opportunities were
generated in the country and in 2005-06, 3.87 lakh jobs opportunities were created against the target of 3.75 lakh.

General Policy behind the budget proposals
 
The Committee notes that the policy behind the budget proposals for the year 2006-07, like the previous year, remains
the employment – generation with greater emphasis on REGP, PMRY and development of clusters under SFURTI. The
Committee is of the view that employment –generation would lead to increment in the purchasing power which in turn

Recommendation
Economic philosophy behind the budget proposals
 
The Committee is in agreement with the economic philosophy behind the budget proposals of the Ministry of ARI for
the year  2006-07 i.e. the Poverty alleviation and employment generation as  the keystone of the economic policy. The
Committee is of the view that fast growing India must invest in society, therefore, the purpose and policy of budgeting
should be aimed at widening the social safety net, as higher the economic development of a nation the greater the need
for a safety net. (Para : 7.2)
 
Action Taken
 
The economic philosophy behind the budget proposals (2006-07) pertaining to Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
conform to the needs of   on-going liberalization and globalization process. The liberalization of economy has enhanced
the competitive nature of the whole industrial set up in the country. Open market mechanisms have come in place of
regulated and protected nature of pre-liberalised economy. The challenge posed by globalised economy has enhanced
and enabled nurturing of the inherent competitive and resilient nature of the agro and rural industries sector. This sector
mainly consists of khadi, village industries, cottage industries (handicrafts), and coir, tiny and micro enterprises. The
products of this sector by their very nature are traditional, location specific and exclusively indigenous. This adds to the
specialized and exclusive nature of the sector as such and gives it a dynamic and resilient character. For example, herbal
products, organic manure, organic food, honey production, traditional crafts items, etc are so exclusive by nature that it
offers immense export potential which is almost noncompetitive in the world economy. The emphasis would be to
highlight the exclusivity of ARI products and its suitability to specific local area both for production as well as
marketing as it addresses the felt local needs and to develop quality diversification and aggressively enter the world
market. At the same time steps have been taken to continue and increase the social safety net through schemes such as
Khadi Karigar Janshree Beema Yojana, Shiksha Sahayog Yojana, Artisans Welfare Fund and a Welfare Fund for Coir
Workers.
 
Recommendation
 
Economic Philosophy behind the Budget proposals (2006-07)
 
The Committee is pleased to note that the economic philosophy behind the Budget proposals (2006-07) pertaining to
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries conform to the logistic of on-going liberalization and globalization process. The
Committee feels that in the euphoria of the rapid globalization humane economic consideration and approach remains at
the backburner, but, in the ideal situation as the growth gathers momentum, sooner or later, enough of it must trickle
down the poor. The Committee hopes that implementation of the budget proposals for the year would lead to enabling
of the poor to access to minimum standard of life. (Para : 7.4)

The Committee takes note of the economic philosophy of budgetary provision for this year aim at empowering the
people specially the poor. The Ministry have not yet indicated what special measure they are likely to take to give a

Action Taken
 
Compared to the initially approved outlay for X Plan which was Rs.2950 crore, the additional allocation under Annual
Plan till 2006-07 worked out to Rs.3584.46 crore which represented an increase of Rs.634.46 crore. Among the special
measures contemplated in 2006-07 are
the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) which is a scheme for integrated development
of clusters in ARI sector.  The scheme would be taken up in selected clusters of traditional industries in various parts of
the country.  Under SFURTI, it is proposed to develop 100 clusters (25 clusters for khadi, 50 clusters for village
industries and 25 clusters for coir industry) over a period of five years commencing 2005-06.  The Scheme would cover
an estimated 50,000 beneficiary families. The objective of SFURTI is to establish a regenerated, holistic sustainable and

will be developed in an integrated manner and will involve as well as lead to capacity building, training, skill
development, product diversification, quality improvement, common facilities, marketing assistance and increased sales
of the products resulting ultimately in empowering the artisans/weavers/workers in these sectors.

Recommendation
 
Export performance of coir and coir products
 
Having gone through the information provided by the Ministry with respect to  export performance of Coir & Coir
products, the Committee is not satisfied on this account. The Committee although finds that   the growth has been
between 10 to 16 percent in terms of value, but the fact remains that majority of coir products are showing declining
trend. The Committee’s worry is how to stop this trend. The Committee impresses  upon the Ministry to apprise the
Committee of the reasons for down trend in products take coir matting, coir geo-textiles, rugs & carpet, Rubberized
Coir, yarn etc., measures taken by the Coir Board & Ministry for export promotion especially when the protected regime
is over. The Committee would like to know whether the allocation for 2005-06 were spent and the expenditure so
incurred achieved the desired result.  The Committee would further like to know the projection for 2006-07 and the
modus-operandi to achieve the target.  (Para : 16.7.7)
 
Action Taken
 
The overall export of coir and coir products during the last 5 years showed an increasing trend both in terms of quantity
and value. During the year 2005-06, 136027 MT of coir and coir products worth Rs. 595 crore  was exported from
India.  It was only Rs.322 crore during 2001-02. The handloom mats, powerloom mat, coir PVC  tufted mat, coir pith,
coir geotextiles, rubberized coir, coir fibre have shown an increasing trend both in quantity and value compared to the
export of previous years. The export of coir yarn, handloom matting, powerloom matting, coir rugs and carpets, etc.
have shown a decreasing trend both in terms of quantity and value.  The coir yarn being the basic raw material for the
value added products, have been showing a decreasing trend during the last 3 years.  In the importing countries, mainly
selected member countries of European Union, coir yarn gets converted to finished products.  Due to the liberalization
policies implemented by the Government of India, the coir industry in India adopted certain imported technology and
machinery for the production of high quality value added coir products  for export purpose (eg. Tufting process).  Due
to various reasons like spiralling wage level and manufacturing cost of imported raw material, the manufacture of coir
products in the importing countries had declined drastically. The machinery used for production of coir products were
transferred to their counter part for setting up export oriented manufacturing units using coir yarn as the basic raw
material.  Sri Lanka is the only coir producing country in the world which is competing with India in the production of
coir yarn.  However, the export of value added products from Sri Lanka is not significant. Therefore, there is no
significant threat from Sri Lanka to the export of finished coir products from India.  However, the threat from China,
Brazil and Mexico in the floor covering market is on the increase particularly from jute, sisal and hemp products
originating from those countries.  In the case of coir geotextiles, the main competitors are Vietnam and Thailand,
besides Sri Lanka. 
 
The export of handloom matting, powerloom matting, coir rugs and carpets has been facing severe threat from other
natural and synthetic floor covering material which are available in the international market at competitive price,
attractive designs and patterns. The change in the concept of interior decoration as a consequence of increased usage of
attractive tiles and flooring materials also contributed to the low off take of such articles of coir.  Production of coir
floor covering blended with other natural fibre materials with attractive patterns and designs at competitive price is now
attempted.  It is also proposed to establish a design clinic exclusively for the coir and coir blended materials as a part of

General recommendations
 
Programme for "Bharat Nirman". 
 
The Committee is of the view that Implementation of programme for "Bharat Nirman".  Would go a long way forward
in developing rural connectivity and infrastructure, thus providing better access to the rural areas.  The programme for

Action Taken

Recommendation
 
Impact of globalisation and liberalization on the growth and development of Agro & Rural Industries in India
 
Government provides incentives to enable ARI  units to compete in the globalised & liberalised regime. The Committee
would like to know as how these incentives have led to  improving the quality of  ARI  products and made  them cost
competitive to enhance  sales of KVI products thereby meeting the challenges of open economy under the WTO regime.
The Committee would also like to know the impact of liberalization and WTO regime on the market scenario as 
responded by ARI  Sector as a result of  policy initiatives taken by the Government.(Para : 23.2.3)
 
Action Taken
 
The economic philosophy behind the budget proposals (2006-07) pertaining to Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
conform to the needs of   on-going liberalization and globalization process. The liberalization of economy has enhanced
the competitive nature of the whole industrial set up in the country. Open market mechanisms have come in place of
regulated and protected nature of pre-liberalised economy. The challenge posed by globalised economy has enhanced
and enabled nurturing of the inherent competitive and resilient nature of the agro and rural industries sector. This sector
mainly consists of khadi, village industries, cottage industries (handicrafts), and coir, tiny and micro enterprises. The
products of this sector by their very nature are traditional, location specific and exclusively indigenous. This adds to the
specialized and exclusive nature of the sector as such and gives it a dynamic and resilient character. For example, herbal
products, organic manure, organic food, honey production, traditional crafts items, etc are so exclusive by nature that it
offers immense export potential which is almost noncompetitive in the world economy. The emphasis would be to
highlight the exclusivity of ARI products and its suitability to specific local area both for production as well as
marketing as it addresses the felt local needs and to develop quality diversification and aggressively enter the world
market. At the same time steps have been taken to continue and increase the social safety net through schemes such as
Khadi Karigar Janshree Beema Yojana, Shiksha Sahayog Yojana, Artisans Welfare Fund and a Welfare Fund for Coir

The Committee believes that progress in regard to  "New Deal" for rural India in respect to rural development and

Action Taken
 
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries through its various employment generation programmes is already focusing on
setting up of industries in the rural areas in the non-farm sector.  The Rural Employment Generation Programme
(REGP) being implemented by this Ministry through KVIC since 1995 has successfully generated employment
opportunities for 33.74 lakh persons through setting up of 2,36,379 units up to 31 March 2006 (estimated).  Similarly,
under Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) since 1993, 36.89 lakh (estimated) educated persons have been
provided employment through 24.59 lakh self-employment ventures up to March 2006.
 
Since the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries is functioning in the rural sector, the interaction between farmer and
agro industries has improved substantially through the activities of the KVIC like bee-keeping, food processing
industries, handmade paper industries, etc. Similarly, the Coir Board through its various programmes has close
association by providing trainings for skill development and ratts for economic empowerment of rural poor.

The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) being operated by NABARD under Ministry of Rural Development

rural artisans and entrepreneurs.

The Ministry has reviewed the programmes under its purview.  The Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional
Industries (SFURTI) is much more comprehensive scheme for integrated development of clusters in ARI sector.  The
scheme would be taken up in selected clusters of traditional industries in various parts of the country.  Under SFURTI, it
is proposed to develop 100 clusters (25 clusters for khadi, 50 clusters for village industries and 25 clusters for coir
industry) over a period of five years commencing 2005-06.  The Scheme would cover an estimated 50,000 beneficiary
families. The objective of SFURTI is to establish a regenerated, holistic sustainable and replicable model of integrated
cluster-based development of traditional industries. This will primarily mean:
 
more competitive traditional industries with more market-driven, productive, profitable and sustained employment for
the participants;
strengthened local socio-economic governance system of the industry clusters, with the active participation by the  local
stakeholders that can help to continue undertake development initiatives by themselves; and
 
building up innovated and traditional skills, improved technologies, advanced processes, market intelligence and new
models of public-private partnerships, so as to gradually replicate similar models of cluster-based regenerated traditional
industries.
 
            The SFURTI is a Central Sector Scheme to be implemented by the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries, without
any State share.  The various components of the scheme include replacement of charkhas and looms for increasing the
productivity of khadi and weavers, Common Facility Centres (CFC) for ready made warp units for supply of ready-to-
use warps for weaving, post-loom facilities, viz., dyeing and printing, setting up composite ready made garment
manufacturing facilities to convert fabrics into ready-to-wear khadi products, product testing laboratory to enforce
quality standards,service and maintenance, processing and manufacture of village industry items like testing
equipment/laboratory to enforce quality standards specially for processed food items, service and maintenance and other
common infrastructure, etc., Product Development & Design Intervention for fabric designing for upholstery new
designs for high fashion garments, fabric development, embroidery in silk items, use of natural dyes, development of
new products specially for items like hand bags, shoes, new designs for pottery items; improved/new design for
packaging, specially for herbal and cosmetics, confectionery items, etc., Market Promotion Assistance for activities such
as organization of and participation in domestic/international exhibitions, participation in buyer-seller meets, renovation
and upgradation of marketing outlets, computerisation of sales outlets, bar-coding, etc.,  Capacity Building Measures for
undertaking following activities like exposure visits to other clusters and institutions (outside) to understand the self-
help actions, new products, technology, need based training within the clusters (related to global trade issues, skill
development, self-help, credit and other need based issues, support for establishment of cluster level networks (industry
associations) in the form of basic office infrastructure, including books, other need based support as emerge from the
diagnostic study, handholding support by NGOs/institutions of repute who would act as implementing agencies,
appointment of cluster development agents, who would work in the cluster for entire period of five years of cluster
development and technical support and guidance from reputed national level institutes having expertise in cluster
development such as Entrepreneurship Development Institute, Ahmedabad, NISIET, Hyderabad, IIE, Guwahati,
NIESBUD, Noida (UP).  While formulating the scheme of SFURTI, the Ministry of Finance and also the Planning
Commission had advised that “Schemes with overlapping objectives and coverage should be proposed for merger with
the new scheme to avoid duplication of effort, resources and responsibilities” .  Accordingly, considering the
comprehensive scope of SFURTI and the advise of Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission, it was decided to
subsume NPRI under SFURTI. However, a token allocation has been made for NPRI for 2006-07 to meet the
committed liabilities.

NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION
 
The Committee is of the view that National Programme on Rural Industrialisation was a unique programme aimed at
boosting  up the rural economy by creating more employment   avenues for the rural youth in the non-farm sector, and
arresting  the migration of the rural artisans to towns/cities, however, the performance under the NPRI Scheme has not
been very satisfactory due to meagre financial assistance of Rs 5.0 lakh per cluster for cluster-wise interventions, fill-in-
gaps arrangements, non-availability of credit-linked subsidy component, inadequate synergy with the
Ministries/departments with their own schemes in this area etc and the same has been  subsumed with the new Scheme
of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI). The Committee desires that the National Programme on
Rural Industrialisation should have continued with its set objectives, however, the Committee will wait and watch the
success of the new Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI).(Para : 19.5)
 
 
Action Taken
 
The Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) is a much more comprehensive scheme for
integrated development of clusters in ARI sector.  The scheme would be taken up in selected clusters of traditional
industries in various parts of the country.  Under SFURTI, it is proposed to develop 100 clusters (25 clusters for khadi,
50 clusters for village industries and 25 clusters for coir industry) over a period of five years commencing 2005-06.  The
Scheme would cover an estimated 50,000 beneficiary families. The objective of SFURTI is to establish a regenerated,
holistic sustainable and replicable model of integrated cluster-based development of traditional industries. This will
primarily mean:
 
more competitive traditional industries with more market-driven, productive, profitable and sustained employment for
the participants;
strengthened local socio-economic governance system of the industry clusters, with the active participation by the  local
stakeholders that can help to continue undertake development initiatives by themselves; and
 
building up innovated and traditional skills, improved technologies, advanced processes, market intelligence and new
models of public-private partnerships, so as to gradually replicate similar models of cluster-based regenerated traditional
industries.
 
            The SFURTI is a Central Sector Scheme to be implemented by the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries, without
any State share.  The various components of the scheme include replacement of charkhas and looms for increasing the
productivity of khadi and weavers, Common Facility Centres (CFC) for ready made warp units for supply of ready-to-
use warps for weaving, post-loom facilities, viz., dyeing and printing, setting up composite ready made garment
manufacturing facilities to convert fabrics into ready-to-wear khadi products, product testing laboratory to enforce
quality standards,service and maintenance, processing and manufacture of village industry items like testing
equipment/laboratory to enforce quality standards specially for processed food items, service and maintenance and other
common infrastructure, etc., Product Development & Design Intervention for fabric designing for upholstery new
designs for high fashion garments, fabric development, embroidery in silk items, use of natural dyes, development of
new products specially for items like hand bags, shoes, new designs for pottery items; improved/new design for
packaging, specially for herbal and cosmetics, confectionery items, etc., Market Promotion Assistance for activities such

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
Streamlining the ARI sector
The Committee understands that the Agro and Rural Industries need further reinforcing and strengthening through
streamlining the ARI sector and by ensuring timely policy interventions. The committee is of the considered view that
the contribution of this sector can be further consolidated and strengthened by ensuring timely and adequate delivery of
credit, technology upgradation, marketing support in the form of financial support for exhibitions, design intervention
and packaging, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of ARI should make strive in this regard.
The committee foresees that   amendment in the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956 would lead further
to streamlining and strengthening the activities in the KVI sector.
(Para: 1.5)
Monitoring mechanism
 
The Committee finds that the monitoring mechanism at the Ministry level includes structured as well as informal but
regular monitoring. Secretary (ARI) periodically monitors implementation of PMRY and REGP along with other
schemes being implemented by the Ministry.  Secretary (ARI) also monitors the implementation of the National
Common Minimum Programme. The Committee believes that the ministry of ARI would achieve the targets set in the
Action Plan for the year 2006-07 without any hindrances.(Para : 4.2)
General Policy behind the budget proposals
 
The Committee notes that the policy behind the budget proposals for the year 2006-07, like the previous year, remains
the employment – generation with greater emphasis on REGP, PMRY and development of clusters under SFURTI. The
Committee is of the view that employment –generation would lead to increment in the purchasing power which in turn

would boost the domestic market.(Para : 6.2)
Economic philosophy behind the budget proposals
 
The Committee is in agreement with the economic philosophy behind the budget proposals of the Ministry of ARI for
the year 2006-07 i.e. the Poverty alleviation and employment generation as the keystone of the economic policy. The
Committee is of the view that fast growing India must invest in society, therefore, the purpose and policy of budgeting
should be aimed at widening the social safety net, as higher the economic development of a nation the greater the need
for a safety net. (Para : 7.2)
 
Economic Philosophy behind the Budget proposals (2006-07)
 
The Committee is pleased to note that the economic philosophy behind the Budget proposals (2006-07) pertaining to
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries conform to the logistic of on-going liberalization and globalization process. The
Committee feels that in the euphoria of the rapid globalization humane economic consideration and approach remains at
the backburner, but, in the ideal situation as the growth gathers momentum, sooner or later, enough of it must trickle
down the poor. The Committee hopes that implementation of the budget proposals for the year would lead to enabling
of the poor to access to minimum standard of life. (Para : 7.4)
 
Welfare measures and meeting the social obligation
 
The Committee takes note of the economic philosophy of budgetary provision for this year aim at empowering the
people specially the poor. The Ministry have not yet indicated what special measure they are likely to take to give a
boost to their philosophy.  The increase in allocation for 2006-07 does not however give any indication to this effect as
it remains, more or less the same and it was in 2004-05 & 2005-06.  The Committee desires that the Ministry may
explain about this to the Committee. (Para : 8.3)
Gender sensitization Programme
 
The Committee wishes to pin-point that the Tenth Plan reinforced the commitment to gender budgeting to establish its
gender-differential impact and to translate gender commitments into budgetary commitment. It is a well-known fact that
the gender budgeting is perceived as a powerful tool not only for tracking allocation of resources but also ensures
implementation of issues and outcomes. The Union Expenditure Budget 2005-06 has also taken care of the fact and has
instituonalised Gender –budgeting in the budgeting in the budget document through Statement 20, Expenditure Budget,
volume –1 and at present, as per the source of the Economic Survey 2005-06, Gender budget cells have been set up in
35 department of the government of the Government of India.  The committee would like to know the response of the
Ministry of ARI to this cherished national policy and whether the Gender Budget cell has been set up in the Ministry of
ARI.(Para : 9.2)

Keeping in view the inflation and general increase in the income level and also the fact that some States like West
Bengal, Gujarat, Pondicherry etc.  Are running their own self employment schemes with better subsidy provision as
compared to PMRY, the Committee feels that the following modification in the existing criteria of PMRY scheme may
be considered:
 
Enhancement of the eligibility criteria of family income from Rs. 40,000/- per annum to Rs. 1,50,000/- per annum.
 
Enhancement in project cost ceiling under the scheme may be enhanced from Rs. 1,00,000/- to Rs. 2,00,000/- for
business sector and from Rs. 2,00,000/- to Rs. 5,00,000/- for service & Industry sector.
 
Enhancement in subsidy from Rs. 7,500/- per beneficiary (except for NER, J&K, Himachal Pradesh & Uttranchal) to    
Rs. 10,000/- per beneficiary other than NE States, J&K, Himachal Pradesh & Uttranchal. In case of NE States including
Sikkim, J&K, Himachal Pradesh & Uttranchal, the subsidy ceiling is already on the higher side i.e. Rs. 15,000/- per  
beneficiary.
 
The Committee is in agreement with the suggested modifications for improvement in PMRY. The Committee has

1.         The Committee strongly feels that the Government should come out with a transparent policy for unlocking of surplus
assets by the PSEs. The Committee feels that such a policy need to be uniform in respect of all the CPSEs which fall under
various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. If necessary the concerned State Government may be consulted
before the formation of the policy on this issue with a view to have broad consensus. The Committee considers that in absence
of a transparent policy, it would be difficult for the PSEs to generate resources by unlocking the surplus assets as it may
involve administrative issues and avoidable litigations.
(Para : 15)
Action Taken 
2.         There are 34 operating PSEs under the Department of Heavy Industry out of which 21 PSEs are loss making, many of
the loss making companies are sick and registered under BIFR. These sick companies have been disposing off their land as per
the directions of BIFR and in accordance with the procedures laid down by BIFR. Surplus assets of land, is also being utilized
by the PSEs to fund their own revival plans in a number of cases presented to BRPSE/Government. The money realized
through the sale of land etc. is ploughed back to fund the revival schemes of such companies. While disposing off land, urban
land norms as prescribed by the State Government are followed.
 
3.         As the land held by the PSEs is of varying types ie on limited time lease or free-lease or free-hold in their own name
and is not a property of the Central Government the policy of this Department is to encourage the PSEs to use such asset in
their own best interest.
4.         However, the Ministry of Urban Development has already initiated the process of formulation of policy guidelines
relating to land held by the Government including held by CPSEs/ Statutory/Registered bodies. These guidelines are at present
under discussion/formulation. The intention is to prepare a uniform policy for land management with a common set of
transparent and remunerative procedure for disposal which would be applicable to all the land holding of Central
Ministries/Departments. This would facilitate uniformity and common standards of efficiency and transparency in land
management and disposal practices in Central Government.  
Recommendation
5.         To consider the Cess as private sector’s contribution would be misrepresentation of fact. The Committee would like to
know the initial mandate for which Cess was levied, and if the NATRIP is covered within that mandate? The Committee is not
in agreement with the DHI’s assertion calling NATRIP a joint project by public and private partnership. As is evident from the
presentation given by the DHI, out of the total investment of Rs. 1718 crores only Rs 118 crores would be contributed by the
users from industry within three years, rest of the investment is to be made in one form or the other. The Committee feels that
the participation of industry should have been substantial to justify the public private partnership.
(Para: 44)
Action Taken
 
6.         Automotive Cess was levied by the Govt. since 1983-84  @ 1/8% i.e. 0.125% over and above the excise duty. It forms
part of the Consolidated Fund of India. Ministry of Finance allocates a portion of this fund through budget to DHI for the
Development Council for Automobile and Allied Industries (DCAAI). 
 
7.       As per para 9 of the IDR Act, 1951 the DCAAI may utilize the cess funds to promote scientific and industrial research
in the automobile sector, to promote improvements in design and quality of auto products, to provide training of technicians
and labour in the automobile industry and to meet such expenses in the exercise of its functions and its administrative
expenses. 
8.      National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRIP) envisages setting up of world-class automotive
testing and homologation facilities in India. The project principally aims at (i) creating critically needed automotive testing
infrastructure to enable the Govt. in ushering in global vehicular safety, emission and performance standards, (ii) deepening
manufacturing in India, promoting larger value addition leading to significant enhancement of employment potential and
facilitating convergence of India’s strengths in IT and electronics with automotive engineering, (iii) enhancing India’s
abysmally low global outreach in this sector by de-bottlenecking exports and (iv) removing the crippling absence of basic
product testing, validation and development infrastructure for automotive industry. This way NATRIP is covered under the
mandate of getting funds from the DCAAI under Cess allocations.
9.         Out of the investment of Rs. 1718 crore, Rs. 1090 crore is from the Plan support by the Govt. and Rs. 273 crore of this
Plan support is in the form of loan, which has to be re-paid back by the Industry. Rs. 510 crore is being contributed through
automotive cess and Rs. 118 crore will be collected through user charges. We agree with the view of the Department Related
Parliamentary Standing Committee that Cess cannot be taken as a contribution of the Automotive Industry. NATRIP is largely
a public project of developmental nature being financed by the Govt. funds for establishment of the facilities. The project has
been conceived, designed and being implemented in total tandem with the automotive industry and its running is also
proposed to be looked after by the autonomous bodies having complete involvement of the industry.
Recommendation

users from industry within three years, rest of the investment is to be made in one form or the other. The Committee feels that
the participation of industry should have been substantial to justify the public private partnership.(Para: 44)
 
            The Committee feels that the PSEs to become financially self-reliant must harness the export opportunities to earn their
own finances for revival.(Para : 114)
 
            It is the considered view of the Committee that the revival plans pertained largely to financial reconstruction, and
technology and marketing aspects are not contained in the revival plan approved by the Government. As the nodal Department
the DHI must monitor with the management of PSEs on  these aspects of revival. The Committee would like to be informed of
the steps taken by the DHI in this regard.(Para:10)

survivability of the PSEs, of the total required outlay of Rs. 1350.22 crores, a budgetary support of only Rs 450 crores has

restructuring of PSEs, only Rs. 27 crores could be spent till March 2006. The Committee also observed that of this lump sum

have been surrendered at the advice of Ministry of Finance. The Committee wonders if any worthwhile capacity building of
PSEs been done as part of intended sustainable restructuring. Also observing the smaller amount that have been allocated to

            The Committee notes with surprise that Rs. 44.60 crores meant for restructuring of CCI as Planned expenditure were

Financial year.  The Committee desires that  Government should ensure planned investment for capital expenditure.
Committee observes that the sheer quantum of such non-planned expenditures for revival suggests that revival packages have
focused largely on clearing the financial dues which the PSEs owe. Compared to which the Lumpsum allocations for the

wages. Though these are loans to begin with but the Committee also notes the abysmal record of PSEs in respect of Loan

by Rs. 116 crores. The non-Planned expenditure was increased to meet the salary dues of the PSEs.(Para : 32)

            The Committee observes that the Non-Planned expenditure has been higher than Planned Expenditure for last several
years. Meaning thereby that the expenditure is much higher on the committed liabilities as compared to new developmental
and capacity-building initiatives under Government sponsored schemes. Even the committed liabilities reflected under Non-
Planned expenditure, the majority of expenditure has been going to meet on year to year basis the financial obligations
incurred by PSEs. In view of the definition of Capital expenditure as provided by the DHI, the Committee only wonders if the
lump sum allocations of Rs 400 crores to support to clear VRS dues and salary dues to the workers could at all be termed as
Capital expenditure. The Committee desires that DHI may clarify the position.(Para : 35)
 
            The Committee has not been furnished any information regarding the criteria on which any expenditure is approved by
the Planning Commission and is reflected as Planned Expenditure where as other bulk expenditures are shown as Non-Planned
expenditures. The Committee desires to know whether such a division is random or based on any objective criteria.
(Para : 36)
 
            For Rs. 47.4 crores required for the two-year pilot scheme for textile and machine tools sector only Rs. 1 lakh token
amount has been allocated. No information has been given as to how the remaining finance shall be garnered. Further
Committee may be apprised of the method of identifying the beneficiary Units, delivery of funds and monitoring the

            The Committee observes from SWOT analysis that the PSEs consider increased competition in market as a major
threat also the technological drawback and inability to diversify the product profile are major constraining factors. The PSEs
still do not have marketing network so vital to retain the market niche and also to harness emerging. In absence of marketing
network and strategy, the PSEs continue to rely on Government and PSEs for orders, and have not been able to exploit new
business opportunities in private sector and export market. In order to face the increased competition, the PSEs have been
asking for consolidation, merger or Joint Ventures with other PSEs. However, these aspects have not been included in the

            The reply of the Department is too general and is not corroborated by the information on revival packages given to the
Committee by the Department.  The Committee expects the Department to be alive of the previous failed   revival packages. 
The Committee would like see the efficacy of the MOU system for the revived PSEs.
            The Committee seeks the elaborate response from DHI of its observations, queries and suggestions in its ATN.

independent assessment.
            The Committee cautions that DHI should bear the previous experiences in mind while assessing and ensuring the

performance of a PSE. The Committee also suggests that the respective PSEs should be given financial targets to be achieved

            Moreover, in view of the details furnished by the DHI of the Planned capital expenditure, the Committee wonders that
such meager infusion as the part of revival plan, would at all be sufficient to carry out technological upgradations and to

Report
 
 
1.         This One Hundred and Ninety Sixth Report deals with action taken by the Government on the One Hundred and Ninetieth
Report of the Committee.
 
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Department of Heavy Industries in respect of the recommendations
contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:-
Chapter -I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry.
Chapter -II- The recommendation/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's
replies.
Chapter -III- The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has either not accepted replies of the Ministry
or has asked the Ministry to review its reply.
Chapter -IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been received. In respect
of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV. The Ministry has either furnished the interim replies or mater has been forwarded to
other agency/Department whose reply is awaited or couched its language in vague terms like noted for compliance/guidance.
CHAPTER – I
Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry.
 
 Recommendation
1.         The Committee observes that of the PSEs recommended for revival maximum 16 cases belonged to PSEs under administrative
control of DHI, three PSEs under Department of Chemicals & Petrochemicals, two PSEs each of Department of Textiles and Fertilizers,
and one PSE each from the Department of Coal, Mines, Shipping, Scientific and Industrial Research and Ministry of Water Resources.
The Committee hopes that the administrative Ministries/Departments of these PSEs will ensure that the revival packages are implemented
earnestly and comprehensively as approved by the Government and that the targets as promised are achieved.  The Committee desire that

as the administrative Ministry of BRPSE, the DPE should pursue and coordinate with the concerned administrative Ministries/
Departments.
 (Para 61)
Action Taken
 
2.         The Resolution constituting BRPSE states that the implementation of the recommendations of the Board will essentially be the
responsibility of the concerned administrative Ministry/ Department, which shall in consultation with DPE monitor their timely
implementation. The recommendation of the Committee for effective   implementation of the revival packages is being conveyed to the
concerned administrative Ministry/Department. 
CHAPTER – II
Recommendation/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies.
Recommendation
 
1.         The Committee feels that the BRPSE was set up as a specialized body mandated to look into the possibilities and ways of the
revival of the PSEs.  It is irrelevant if it is a part time or full time body, till such time it is delivering on its mandate.  Though it was
empowered to seek independent advice, yet in practice the BRPSE is relying on the inputs given by the concerned administrative
Departments. The Committee would like to know about the cases where the BRPSE has consulted independent experts. The Committee
wonders that devoid of independent advice, if BRPSE’s role is only to ratify the inputs given by concerned administrative Department.
(para 8)
Action Taken
 
2.         The Resolution constituting BRPSE states that the administrative Ministry/Department would be responsible for preparing a
comprehensive package for revival/rehabilitation or closure of loss making CPSEs after due consultations with all stake holders. The
proposals submitted to BRPSE by the Administrative Ministries/Departments are generally based on the report of the independent experts
appointed by the CPSE/BIFR. The outside experts/consultants who were involved in the preparation the revival package of CPSEs are
invited to attend the meetings of BRPSE when such proposals are considered by the Board. The Board invariably seeks clarifications
from the experts on the sustainability of the revival proposal as also the reasonableness of the assumptions made in the projected
performance of the concerned CPSE. The Board also considers the comments of Chief Advisor (Cost)/ Controller General of Accounts on
the cases referred to them. Of the 35 cases recommended by BRPSE, in respect of 27 cases, the Board had the benefit of not only the
report of the independent consultants/operating agency appointed by the PSE/Administrative Ministry/BIFR but also their presence in the
meeting for providing necessary clarifications required by the Board. Further, when BRPSE felt the need for review of the revival
proposal submitted by the administrative Ministry/Department by an independent consultant, it had advised the concerned administrative
Ministry/Department to resubmit the same after vetting by an independent expert/consultant.
 
 
Committee’s Further Recommendation  
 
3.         The Committee has taken note of the exhaustive format in which revival proposal are submitted to the BRPSE. The Committee still
holds the view that BRPSE gets to know only a unilateral view. Most of the recommended cases pertain to financial and manpower
restructuring, with no detailed information being provided on the submission under the heading Future Prospects and its subheadings.
The Committee is of the view the BRPSE needs expertise for an extensive and objective appraisal of the proposals submitted before it. 
Recommendation
 
4.         The committee feels it is essential that the country shares the experience of other countries in reconstructing their public Sector.
The DPE could be a repository of such studies on the revival of Public Sector in other countries. The committee however desires that the
DPE should make an assessment of the benefits of such short-term programmes made.
(Para 22)
Action Taken
 
5.         As far as obtaining experience of other countries is concerned, Executives of CPSEs and officials of Government of India are
being sent to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE), Ljubljana, Slovenia for short term training programme and long
term training programme being conducted by ICPE.  Short-term programme is in the areas of corporate governance, strategic
management, total quality management and knowledge management.  In the long term course ICPE conduct MBA programme.  So far
about 300 Executives of PSEs, Government of India and other organizations in India have availed the benefits of short term and long-
term programme of ICPE.  The inputs derived during the training have helped participants from India in enhancing their management
skills.  As recommended attempt will be made to undertake study of experience of other countries in restructuring their public sector.
 
Recommendation
 
6.         The Committee observes that number of PSEs signing the MoU is highest 44 in Schedule A and the numbers gradually descend to
2 in Schedule D.  The Committee would like to have the comments of DPE on this trend.
(Para No.36)
Action Taken

Recommendation
 
11.       The Committee desires to know the ratings of the nodal agencies and the parameters of their performance.  Further Committee
observes that such training should be imparted in the vicinity of the existing parent company, so as to save the incidental costs that might
prohibit the VRS optee to join the training.  The Committee also observes that in several cases the location of such nodal agencies was

12.       The performance of nodal agencies is judged on the basis of achievement in terms of  assigned physical target and rate of
redeployment.
 
13.       CPSEs’ units are scattered in various states/UTs in remote areas where VRS may take place.  VRS optees after quiting migrate to
home state immediately.  The optees are therefore spread even in remote villages.  In the scheme, there is a provision of sensitization/
counselling programme under which immediately after separation from the CPSE, three days’ counselling is undertaken by the nodal
agencies in the premises of the parent company.  Under such programmes basic inputs and information /guidance by the personnel of the
CPSE/nodal agency are provided to the separated employees.  Through Counselling the optees are motivated to undergo the training
programme in the area of their interest, motivated to opt for alternative employment or preferably avail self employment opportunity. 
Training under the CRR Scheme is being conducted by the nodal agencies through Employees Assistance Centres (EACs) which are
located as close as possible to the location of VRS optees. As compared to 17 Nodal Agencies and 40 Employment Assistance Centres in
2001-02 there were 42 Nodal Agencies and 126 EACs in 2005-06.  For technical courses under Skill Development Programmes and
Entrepreneurship Development Programmes nodal agencies hire training institutes which have workshop facilities. Nodal agencies try to

Recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked

Recommendation

Recommendation
 
4.         The Committee has in a few cases observed that other stake holders like the State Governments, municipal authorities or

resolution of the Government to address the task of strengthening, modernising, reviving and re-structuring of PSEs and advise the
Government on strategies, measures and schemes related to them. The jurisdiction of BIFR is larger as it covers both public and private
sector enterprises, whereas BRPSE deals with only CPSEs. While BIFR’s role is restricted to only industrial enterprises, BRPSE may
also deal with non-industrial CPSEs. Further, Incipient sick CPSEs may be referred to BRPSE, so that its advice may help the enterprise
to avoid reference to BIFR.

inclusion of dependents of the VRS optees into the CRR  scheme.  The Committee requires the DPE to obtain the opinion of the Planning
Commission in view of the facts referred to above.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
 
Recommendation
 
1.0       Policy initiatives taken by Government during the financial year 2005-06
 
1.1       The Committee understands that alongwith agriculture and organized large industries, the small enterprises sector including
both SSI and services provide the largest employment generation potential in the country.  The Committee is of the view that
Government should make comparative assessment of Small Scale Industries vis-à-vis other Industries on the basis of growth rate, and
chalk out strategy for enhancing further the employment generation potential, maximizing contribution to national exchequer, in
order to combat the problem of poverty and improving the standard of living and thus making real contribution to the National
Economy.
Para (3.3)
Action Taken
 
1.1.1    The rate of growth in production of the small enterprises (SE) sector has been consistently more than that of the overall
industrial production as given in the table below:

1.11     Issues relating  Labour and Employment
 
1.11.1  Since the issues relates to Ministry of Labour and Employment, therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of
SSI should coordinate with Ministry of Labour and Employment at the earliest and effectively, and furnish the Committee outcome of
the efforts so undertaken by the Ministry.
Para (18.6)
 
Action Taken
 
1.10.1  (a) and (c)        These issues relates to Ministry of Labour and Employment and their reply/comments on same are stated
below:-
 
(i)         The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides provisions for investigation and settlement of industrial disputes and certain
other matters.  Chapter-VA of the Act provides provisions relating to lay-off and retrenchment of workman.  Lay-off compensation
is not required to be paid by the employer to the workman laid off in the industrial establishment employing less than 50 workmen. 
The chapter also contains provisions that an industrial establishment employing, on an average, more than 50 workmen is required to
give 60 days notice before affecting closure.  The provisions also include payment of retrenchment compensation equivalent to 15
days wages for every completed year of service by the workman and principle of last come first go in case of retrenchment.      Prior
permission is required by the  industrial establishment i.e. factory, mines and plantations wherein 100 or more workmen are
employed before effecting lay-off, retrenchment or closure.
 
(ii)        Social Security Scheme:   The Government has initiated several measures to provide social security to the workers in the
unorganized sector various labour laws like the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923, the Equal
Remuneration Act, 1976, the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment & Conditions of Service) Act,
1996 etc. are applicable to the labourers in the unorganized sector also.
 
            The Government has also set up the Welfare Funds to provide social security/welfare measures to certain categories of
workers i.e. beedi workers, certain non-coal mine workers and the cine workers.  The welfare measures include health care, housing,
educational assistance for childeren, drinking water supply etc.  The State Governments like Tamil Nadu and Kerala have
implemented Welfare Funds to provide adequate protection and social security to certain occupational groups.
 
            The Non-Governmental Organizations like SEWA also provide social security network for women workers in unorganized
sector.  The Government is also contemplating to enact “Unorganized Sector Workers Bill 2004” to provide for safety, social
security, health and welfare matters of unorganized sector workers.
 
            The Employees’ Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1956 also provide financial security for employees in an
establishment employing 20 or more persons.  Presently, the Act is applicable to 180 specified industry/classes of establishments.  As
on 31
st March 2004, there were 3,70,386 establishments and factories covered under the Act with a membership of 400.92 lakh under
the Employees Provident Fund Scheme both in the Exempted and Unexempted Sectors.  The ability to pay contributions is not
uniform across all sectors of workers and employers.  The proposal for increasing coverage by reducing threshold for minimum
number of employees would require consensus across the board among representatives of workers and employers.  The Ministry is
exploring ways and means to extend social security cover to identifiable groups, which are presently not covered.
 
            The Employees State Insurance Scheme under the aegis of the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 provides comprehensive
medical care and cash benefits in the contingencies of sickness, maternity, employment injury and death due to employment injury to
the workers working in power using factories employing 10 or more workers, and in non-power using factories, shops, hotels,
restaurants, cinemas including pre-view theatres, road motor transport undertakings, newspaper establishments and educational
institutions employing 20 or more workers in the implemented areas under the Act.  The employers covered under the Employees’

1.50.2  The Small Scale Industries (SSIs), including tiny units have enough competitive strengths to withstand the impact of free
imports and intense global competition under WTO regime as is evident from their past track record.  With a view to create
awareness about the WTO provisions and also for preparing them to meet the challenges of globalistion, Government launched the
awareness programme in the year 2000. Since then a number of sensitisation programmes, workshops, etc. on WTO its impact have

1.50.3  Government is constantly assessing and monitoring the impact of the removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) and
Globalisation on the growth and development of Small Scale Industries (SSIs) in the country.  Though removal of QRs has exposed
the SSIs to a greater competition, yet the SSI sector has continued to grow. However, even after the removal of QRs, protection to the
industries is available in the form of raising custom duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards
measures in case of surge in imports, etc.  This monitoring process will continue.

imports through adjustments in tariff  within the bound rates.  Apart from tariff, action under anti-dumping and safeguard measures

separate Directorates are already working under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and the Ministry of Finance respectively.
 
1.50.5  The Government has put in place several measures to help small enterprises become globally competitive. These include
special focus on areas such as technology up gradation, infrastructure assistance through the cluster approach, timely availability of
credit, adoption of modern management practices, use of electronic infrastructure and other IT applications, marketing and timely
information dissemination, including sensitisation of small industries to the emerging challenges of trade liberalisation.

sector will continue to grow.

objective to    double the flow of credit to the sector within a period of five years.  But the Committee expresses its concern that  since
the launching of the programme on 10
th August, 2005, the percentage net Public Sector  Banks  credit to SSI sector has declined from
10.4 % in 2004 to  9.8 in 2005 and further to 8.1 (provisional) in  2006  as furnished by the Ministry of SSI in its Action Taken Note
in response to the Committee’s recommendations in Para 62.1 of 189th Report   .  The Committee feels that the financial institutions  
must accord the intention  of the Government to provide adequate credit to  SSI sector.
(Para 3.2.7)

therefore, it is felt that the Ministry of SSI must be forthcoming in right earnest in the formulation of  policy intervention  for the
benefit of the SSI sector.  The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to indicate a time frame therefor.
(Para 3.2.8)
 
            The menace of Inspector Raj has posed serious threats to the growth of SSI sector which has been incorporated  by the
Committee in several reports and the issue has been voiced by the Prime Minister on several occasions but the Committee wonders
that clauses  9(2), 15 and 16 in the SMED Bill intended to make SMEs free from the Inspector Raj were dropped during Inter-
Ministerial consultations and Group of Ministers.    The Committee expresses its concern on how the Government proposes to curb
the adverse  impact of Inspector Raj on the SSI sector in the absence  of express legal provision.   The Committee, however would
like to know the time frame  by which the National Board for Micro, Small  and Medium enterprises is going to be constituted  and
what role it is likely to play in eliminating /reducing the rules and  regulations advocating Inspector Raj.
(Para 3.2.9)
 
Formulation of  National Policy for Small Scale Industries.
 
            The Committee feels that there is the need for Comprehensive National Policy for strengthening the Small Scale Sector,
although the process has already been  started since 1991 in the sporadic manner, the need is to consolidate and streamline the
national policy.  Keeping in view of the dynamic situation of the Indian SSI sector vis-à-vis domestic & international industrial &
economic environment, the Committee feels that that SSI policy must have been revisited and revitalized  incorporating components
viz programmes for infrastructure development, technological upgradation, marketing support, easier access to credit and scientific
management for inter-sectoral cooperation for ensured promotion and proliferation of SMEs. 
(Para 3.3.1)
           
            The Committee reiterates that the National Policy for Small Scale Industries must have been revisited and revitalized 
incorporating components viz programmes for infrastructure development, technological upgradation, marketing support, easier
access to credit and scientific management for inter-sectoral cooperation for ensured promotion and proliferation of SMEs.   The
Committee appreciates  the promulgation of MSMED Act, 2006 and the in-built  provision therein regarding  the National Board for
Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises but the need for Comprehensive National Policy for SSI sector is required to consolidate the SSI
Sector vis-a-vis domestic & international industrial & economic environment.  The Committee therefore, recommends that a
comprehensive National Policy for SSI sector be prepared in the light of recently enacted MSMED Act. 2006.
 (Para 3.3.3)

REPORT
 
1.
                  The Committee while assessing the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises, Department of Public Enterprises
(DPE) also undertook the examination of the policy of ‘Professionalisation’ of the Boards of the Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs). 
 
2.
                  The Committee was informed by the Ministry of HI & PE that “the PSEs need to be restructured in the new liberalized regime to make them
competitive.”  In a query regarding the viable alternative to the privatization of PSEs.  The Committee was informed by the Ministry that alongwith
other factors like greater functional autonomy, Professionalisation of Boards of PSEs could provide a viable alternative to the privatization. 
 
3.
                  The Committee was also informed that the policy of Professionalisation of Boards was designed “to distance them (PSEs), to the extent possible
from administrative Ministries.”  To this objective the known expert independent Directors were included in the Boards of PSEs.  It was envisaged by
the Government that a Board managed company should be able to take prompt decision and facilitate the implementation.
 
4.
                  The Committee was informed by the DPE that emphasis was laid on inclusion of such persons from outside into the Boards who had experience
in the industry or academics or research in the relevant fields. The policy advocated that measures were required to be taken to make these enterprises
more growth oriented and technically dynamic which was not possible without inducting professionals on the Board of Directors. The non-official
Directors to be inducted on the Board were to be drawn from the public men, technocrats, management experts and consultants and professional
managers in industry and trade with a high degree of proven ability.
Composition of Board of Directors of Public Sector Enterprises.
 
5.                  The Committee was apprised that the Boards of PSEs generally consisted of Directors of three categories :
 
(i)                  Functional Directors: - These are full time operational Directors responsible for routine functioning of the Enterprise . The Economic
Administrative Reforms Commission (EARC) had recommended that each Board should have an adequate number of Functional Directors
on it. This was considered by the Government and the Bureau of Public Enterprises had issued guidelines in 1984 that the posts of Director
(Finance) and Director (Personnel) be created in all Schedule A' and Schedule `B' enterprises and on a selective basis in Schedule `C'
Enterprises. Apart from these two functions, the enterprises could have representation at Board level for other disciplines such as production,
marketing, project, planning etc.
 
2.             The Committee held elevan meetings to consider and examine the subject. In the course of its examination, the Committee held detailed discussions with the representatives of
the Ministries of Defence, Civil Aviation, Petroleum and Natural gas, Power, Telecommunication, Chemicals & Fertilizers, Shipping and Railways and the CPSEs under these Ministries.
The Committee also interacted with various CPSEs during its visit to their headquarters.  The Department of Public Enterprises too attended these interactions as the nodal Department
which issues the guidelines on the subject. 
 
3.             The Committee’s recommendations and observations are reflected in the end of this Report.
 
4. The Committee acknowledges the cooperation by the Department of Public Enterprises   and the Ministries of Defence, Civil Aviation, Petroleum and Natural Gas, Power,
Telecommunication, Chemicals & Fertilizers, Shipping and Railways and the CPSEs under these Ministries.

The number of such Directors on a Board should not exceed 50% of the actual strength of the Board. In cases where the number of
Functional Directors on the Board is more than the 50% of its actual strength (not sanctioned strength), Administrative Ministries will
immediately undertake a review of the strength of the Board in consultation with Department of Public Enterprises and PESB. On such
Boards where the posts of Functional Directors do not exist, Administrative Ministries will take immediate steps to create such posts in
accordance with the prescribed guidelines.
 
(ii)
                Government Directors: They are appointed by the Administrative Ministries and are generally the officers dealing with the concerned
enterprise. In most cases there are two such Directors on a Board; the Joint Secretary or Additional Secretary dealing with particular
enterprise and the Financial Adviser of the Ministry. The question of representation of Government Directors on the Boards of PSEs was
examined by the Arjun Sengupta Committee and following its recommendation, the Bureau of Public Enterprises have issued guidelines in
1986 that the Administrative Ministy concerned should not have more than one nominee Director on the Board of a PSE.
 
As per the guidelines of DPE the number of the Government Directors on the Board of Directors of an enterprise should not exceed one-sixth
of the actual strength of the Board. It will be preferable to have only one Government Director from the concerned Administrative Ministry
on each Board. The choice of the nominee Director would vest with the Administrative Ministry of the concerned Enterprise. In case of PSEs
where it is considered essential to give representation on the Boards to other concerned Government agencies/Ministries/State Governments,
only one representative from the Group could also be appointed on the Board as part-time Government Director. The number of Government
Directors on a Board should in no case exceed two.
 
In this regard, the Committee took note of the DPE’s OM No. 18(24)/2003-GM-GL-49 of 4
th December 2003 on “Role of Government
Directors, that states
 
“ … the association of Government officials with the Boards of Public Enterprises can be of advantage as this provides for a liaison role and
a channel of communication between Government and the Public Enterprises. They have also emphasised that the dual role of a Government
Director should be clearly recognised – as a Director of the company and as a representative of the Government. He should be allowed to
function freely and use his own judgment without any formalised briefing by the Ministry before a Board meeting with discretion whether to
seek a briefing or make a report. The Government Director should identify himself with the objects and goals of the enterprise, engage in
joint thinking on equal terms and not assume a superior status. He should not reserve his position on matters before the Board. However,
others on the Board should not expect him to commit the Government in respect of matters which require to be referred to the Government.
In all subsequent examination of the Board approved proposals, his role should be mainly elucidatory and he should not sit in judgment over
the Board. Reference to the Ministry for approval, sanction etc. should be addressed to the Government representative on the Board whose
responsibility should be to process the matter and obtain the necessary Government approval promptly.”
 
( iii )            Non-official Directors : -  The induction of Non-Official Directors on the Boards of PSEs has been considered essential by various
Committees and Commissions in order to make the Boards more professional. They are to be drawn from the public, technocrats,
management experts consultants and professional managers in industry and trade with a high degree of proven ability. As per DPE’s OM No.
18(6)/91-GM dated the 16
th March, 1992 that provided the outside professionals should be inducted in the Boards of PSEs as part time non
official Directors and that number of such Directors should be at least 1/3 rd of the actual strength of the Board.  The policy was further
defined by DPE OM No. 18(6)/2000-GM dated the 26.11.2001.  As per the O.M. in case of the listed PSEs headed by the Executive
Chairman   the number of non-officials Directors should be at least half of the strength of the Board.  
 
6.
                  The Committee was informed that a Panel of suitable persons who could be considered for appointment as Non-Official Part-Time Director on
the Boards of PSEs is maintained centrally by Department of Public Enterprises. This Panel is prepared in consultation with PESB and the Secretary of
the concerned Administrative Ministry.
 
7.
                  The Committee was also informed of the eligibility criteria for the non-official part-time Directors.  As such non-official part-time Directors
should be in the age group of 45-65 years which can be relaxed up to 70 years for eminent professionals after the reasons for extension are recorded in
writing. The minimum qualification for the part time non-official Directors is graduation from the recognized University with an experience of not less
than 10 years at the level of Joint Secretary and above in the Government or CMD/MD in Corporate Sector/PSE or a professor in an Academic
Institution or a professional of repute including the chartered accountants/cost accountant at the level of Directors of the Institute or the Head of the
Department.
 
8.
                  The Committee was further informed that in case of selecting the Academics as Part-time non-official Directors, their area of specialization is
relevant to Company and this should also be borne in mind.  As such academics from the disciplines like management, finance, marketing, technology,
human resource or law were considered relevant.
 
9.
                  The Committee was informed that the Government made exercise of functional and financial autonomy by Navratna and Miniratna  PSEs
incumbent upon professionalisation of their Boards. It was made pre-requisite to include atleast 1/3 of total Directors as independent Directors subject to
minimum four incase of Navratna and three in case of Miniratna Enterprises for them to exercise enhanced financial powers.
 
APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS
